f19df87757688a0b: ISTANBUL: A landslide triggered by heavy rainfall caused a rock spire to collapse in Turkiye's Unesco World Heritage-listed Cappadocia region on Thursday, bringing the death toll to three, officials said.
Turkiye's Cappadocia region, a magnet for tourists from around the world, is home to cone-shaped rock formations known as "fairy chimneys", created by ancient volcanic activity.
"According to initial findings, two people were killed and five others injured in the incident," Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said on X.
Rescue teams later pulled another body from the rubble, bringing the death toll to three, Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said.
One of those killed was a foreign national while the other two were Turkish, he added.
"Search and rescue teams are continuing intensive, coordinated operations to locate any other victims who may be trapped under the debris," the minister said.
Television footage showed heavy machinery digging through the rubble as rescue teams gathered at the site in an effort to recover people.
Excavators and rescue workers worked into the night at the site, using powerful floodlights as the search operation continued.
Rescue teams were also conducting careful listening operations to determine whether anyone was trapped beneath the fallen rock fragments, periodically calling for silence.
The incident occurred at 3.15pm local time (1215 GMT) when a landslide triggered a rockfall in the town of Goreme near the open-air museum, local governor Kok said.
The area was closed to the public following the collapse, according to reports.
Eyewitnesses described hearing a loud noise as the rock spire near a car park collapsed, sending up a huge cloud of dust.
- RESTORATION -
Turkiye's culture and tourism ministry has launched restoration work in the region to help preserve the fragile rock formations from climate-related damage, natural erosion and human activity.
In 2024, another rockfall was reported in Cappadocia, although no injuries were recorded.

A Unesco heritage site since 1985, Goreme national park and the rock sites of Cappadocia are "a landscape of harmony combining human interaction and settlement with dramatic natural landforms," according to the UN agency.
Some of the cones and pillars have experienced earthquake damage, but this is seen as a naturally occurring phenomenon.
"Overuse by tourists and some vandalism have been reported and some incompatible structures have been introduced," it said on its website.
The Cappadocia region is also home to rock-carved underground cities and early Christian churches.
In 2025, some 4.5 million domestic and foreign tourists visited the region, according to tourism ministry figures.

Hot-air ballooning in Cappadocia is a thriving industry that sees dozens of balloons take to the skies on clear mornings. But concerns have been raised about safety following a series of fatal accidents.
In 2022, two Spaniards were killed and three others injured when their hot-air balloon crashed in high winds.
"Winter Sleep", the acclaimed drama by Turkish director Nuri Bilge Ceylan that won the Palme d'Or in 2014, was set in the Cappadocia region.--AFP

f9e20844dba6e165: JOINT BASE ANDREWS, United States: US President Donald Trump on Thursday stepped up criticism of Brazil's "disgraceful" presidential election, declining to say whether he recognised leftist Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's victory over right-wing ally Flavio Bolsonaro.
Senator Bolsonaro fled to the United States to start a self-imposed exile on Wednesday and insisted that he is his country's rightful leader despite his defeat in the presidential run-off.
"I think the election was a disgrace in Brazil," Trump told reporters when asked if he accepted incumbent Lula's victory, as the US leader headed on a midterms campaign trip.
"I don't want to comment on it right now, but I thought the election was a very great embarrassment to the people of Brazil," Trump added.
"I watched the election. I let it be. I was asked not to take sides by the president, the current president. I didn't take sides, but when I watched what went down in Brazil, it was a disgrace."
Trump pointed to the reaction of the Brazilian stock market, which dropped after Lula's victory, adding: "I thought it was a very disgraceful situation for Brazil."

The US leader's stance appeared to have hardened from as recently as Wednesday, when he said Brazil's election was "very strange" but added that he "won't get involved" in Flavio Bolsonaro's claim to the presidency.
Bolsonaro's defiance on arrival in Florida on Wednesday signaled continued upheaval for Brazil, where Lula won a dramatic runoff election Sunday.

"I am the elected president, and the criminals who stole Brazil's election are part of a criminal organisation that has established a tyranny," Bolsonaro said in the statement published on his X account, slamming "electoral fraud."
Trump's administration has strong links to Bolsonaro and his hard-right father Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest in Brazil after attempting to overturn his own electoral loss to Lula in 2022.
The US president's reaction has meanwhile sparked speculation about how he will react to a possible Republican loss of Congress in tight US midterm elections that take place next week.

Trump, 80, has ramped up allegations of election fraud, reviving memories of his baseless refusal to accept his 2020 election defeat and the subsequent attack on the US Capitol by his supporters on Jan 6, 2021.
Details of how Bolsonaro, accompanied by his wife and daughters, made it to US soil are still emerging.
He is under investigation in his home country over alleged corruption and money laundering.
With his current parliamentary immunity about to expire, he was ordered to surrender his passports but left anyway, reaching the United States via Argentina and Ecuador.

The US Department of Homeland Security – which under Trump has led a major campaign against what it calls an immigrant "invasion" from Latin America – said in a statement that the Bolsonaro family members were inspected and cleared "with applicable immigration laws and procedures."
Lula, who won Sunday's election with 51.8 per cent of the vote, called Bolsonaro's departure a "shameful" act.--AFP
b594a01ae908e062: America's national laboratories are leading a consortium to move advanced battery storage technologies from the lab into domestic manufacturing.

Dubbed the Battery Manufacturing Accelerator, or BattMan (no, really), the initiative aims to bring together a bunch of national laboratories, universities, and companies to overcome barriers in scaling up new battery technologies.
Novel battery storage solutions are needed for applications in the electric grid, datacenters, and electric vehicles, as electrification gradually extends across industry.

Batteries have a far lower energy density than fuels such as petroleum, so the hunt for better materials never stops. Researchers also want to improve on the safety of flammable lithium-ion cells, cut production costs, speed up charging, and reduce reliance on scarce raw materials.

"The advances we make today in battery manufacturing technology will determine America's energy security and economic competitiveness for decades to come,” said Audrey Robertson, assistant secretary of Energy at the Department of Energy (DoE), which is overseeing the program.

Researchers continue to develop new battery materials and chemistries, yet many promising technologies face obstacles on the way from the laboratory to commercial production. According to the DoE, BattMan will tackle that problem by combining super intelligence - known outside of the Trump administration as AI - with advanced manufacturing into a coordinated, data-driven innovation ecosystem.

Pacific Northwest National Laboratory leads the consortium, along with Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Argonne National Laboratory and National Laboratory of the Rockies. Academic partners include the University of Washington, Binghamton University, University of Alabama, Arizona State University, and University of Michigan-Dearborn.

The accelerator is also building ties with battery and materials manufacturers, and hopes to sidestep critical minerals supply problems by finding battery materials among more abundant, domestically sourced elements.

ORNL is contributing its Battery Manufacturing Facility (BMF) R&D center and plans a smart test bed with advanced sensing, real-time monitoring, and data analysis to trial both wet and dry electrode manufacturing.

BattMan will also introduce autonomous pilot lines that combine sensing, process monitoring and intelligent control systems to improve product quality and reduce variability in the manufacturing process. The goal is an AI-based manufacturing platform that spots production irregularities as they occur and adjusts parameters on its own to prevent defects.

“The BattMan Accelerator is exactly the kind of coordinated national effort that turns scientific breakthroughs into economic and energy security advantages,” claimed distinguished R&D staff member Chins Chinnasamy, the consortium lead for ORNL.
Organizations interested in becoming part of BattMan can visit the program website to learn more. ®

The status of 81-year-old has long been a sticking point for the 11-nation Asean bloc, which has frozen Myanmar's leaders out of its summits since the putsch.

This year, analysts say authorities have allowed Suu Kyi increasing – albeit still extremely limited – contact with the outside world in a bid to shake off their pariah status abroad.
Last week, there were two rare updates on Suu Kyi.
On Monday, authorities in Myanmar said she received a package from Britain's King Charles, including two books about soil and a "sealed diplomatic communication" from the monarch.
Her UK-based son Kim Aris was then allowed a 20-minute consular phone call with her last Thursday, their first spoken communication in more than half a decade.
He told AFP his mother sounded "fairly healthy" but he feared she was being used as a pawn to improve the public image of those detaining her.

ed7aa8e92eb913c1: A major US federal agency has repeatedly left sensitive information in its Google Drive accessible to employees and contractors who had no legitimate business need to see it, and auditors aren’t happy.

The General Services Administration (GSA), which handles contracting, procurement, property management, and other elements of basic operations for federal agencies, has faced repeated findings of inadequate protection for controlled unclassified information (CUI) since at least 2014, according to a report from the agency’s Office of Inspector General. Again.

Controlled unclassified information, in the US federal government's parlance, is information that isn't classified but requires protection or restrictions on its distribution under applicable laws, regulations, or government-wide policies. Access is generally limited to individuals with a legitimate government need to know. According to the OIG report, that can include things like physical security info for government buildings, personally identifiable information (PII) of government employees, and proprietary business information, all of which the GSA has left exposed.
According to the report published this week, employees and contractors have approximately 2.5 million documents stored in GSA's Google Drive.

“During a limited search of GSA’s Google Drive, we found 116 files containing CUI that were improperly shared with all GSA users,” the report notes. That’s a limited search, mind you, and the OIG has plenty of reason to believe there’s more than just that sitting open for anyone with access to the GSA’s Google Drive instance to sneak a look at.

The OIG said that GSA is failing to properly manage the third-party tool it has in place to prevent data loss and detect CUI exposures, with annual reviews of search terms incomplete or undocumented, many relevant search terms not implemented, and a failure to enable an available optical character recognition feature that could help detect CUI in scanned documents. Additionally, the GSA was apparently “unaware of the tool’s file size limitation of 15 megabytes,” meaning that even if the GSA was properly using that tool, some large files would still be skipped.

“We also found that GSA lacks: (1) an approval process for properly sharing sensitive information and (2) a standard naming convention that could more effectively prevent exposures of CUI in GSA’s Google Drive,” the OIG added.
As for what was exposed … it’s not great.

According to the audit, site plans for buildings in Washington, DC were part of the improperly access-controlled files, with data that includes entrances and screening techniques, as well as the location of sensitive areas, like gun lockers. A progressive collapse analysis that "describes the building’s collapse vulnerabilities, defense vulnerabilities, and critical failure locations” was also exposed.

PII of government individuals was also exposed, including social security numbers, addresses, dates of birth, and contact information. Proprietary business information was also exposed, “including proprietary research and vendor proposals with technical and pricing information.”

This might not have been publicly accessible, but it’s still a shocking lapse of data control, especially given that contractors with access to the GSA’s Google Drive could potentially view proprietary information belonging to competing vendors, giving them an unfair advantage if they used it.

To make matters worse, this isn’t the first time the GSA has been dinged by its own inspector general for such lousy data protection practices. According to the report, it was 2014 when the OIG first spotted such bad habits.

“In August 2014, we first reported that GSA did not protect sensitive information on child care centers, courthouses, water sources, building automation systems, and security and fire alarm systems in its Google cloud computing environment,” the OIG noted. “We issued additional reports citing concerns regarding GSA’s ability to protect sensitive information in its Google environment between 2015 and 2017.”

Auditors flagged another set of improperly shared Google Drive files in April 2025. While the GSA’s chief information officer agreed with the auditors’ seven recommendations to fix the problems, the report doesn't establish whether the corrective work has been completed. We reached out to the GSA and the OIG’s office for an update, but didn’t hear back from either. ®

86b128a7f6a3f101: FRANKFURT: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down in February, months before her term ends, officials said Thursday, kicking off a race to succeed her against a turbulent backdrop in the eurozone and further afield.
"It has been a great pride and a huge privilege to serve this institution," Lagarde posted on X, announcing that she would resign nine months before her term officially ends in October 2027.
"I think that I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," she said.

Lagarde's early resignation opens the way for European leaders to choose a new ECB chief before French presidential elections in the spring, with officials fearing that a far-right victory could complicate talks to pick her successor.

But it also comes at a difficult time in the eurozone as worries mount about France's public finances and the central bank seeks to navigate the energy shock triggered by the US war on Iran, with inflation currently almost double the ECB's two-percent target.
European Union chief Ursula von der Leyen thanked Lagarde "for everything you have done for Europe and the euro."

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Lagarde had led the bank "with great aplomb during challenging times" and French President Emmanuel Macron thanked Lagarde on X for her service "during a period marked by numerous crises."
Lagarde, who previously headed the International Monetary Fund and served as French finance minister, did not say what her next move would be.

But she has ruled out running for the French presidency herself, and has been tipped to take the helm of the World Economic Forum, which organises the annual summit of politicians and business leaders in Davos, Switzerland.
- 'I DON'T THINK I CAN REMAIN NEUTRAL' -

Lagarde, who served in the governments of France's centre-right presidents Jacques Chirac and Nicolas Sarkozy, has also hinted that she could get involved in campaigning for the presidential vote, saying it was important to have a "European voice" in debates.
Speaking at the end of a regular ECB monetary policy press conference Thursday, Lagarde said she was quitting so that she could intervene in politics.
"I want to have the freedom of speech, the freedom of expression and the freedom to engage on matters that are not monetary policy matters," she said.
"I don't think that I can remain neutral. I don't think that I can be comfortable in that neutrality at the present time."
Her tenure was marked by repeated geopolitical upheavals that often left policymakers struggling to fulfil the ECB's main task of keeping consumer prices in check.

The Covid-19 pandemic, Russia's invasion of Ukraine and subsequent energy shock – which pushed eurozone inflation to a record of over 10 per cent – the US tariff blitz and now the fallout from the Iran war all severely tested the institution.
The ECB's governing council, which sets interest rates for the 21-member single currency area, faced criticism, in particular during the 2022 inflation surge, for responding too slowly.

But officials also won praise for seeking to overhaul the central bank so it is better prepared for a more uncertain world, introducing new crisis-fighting tools and seeking to communicate its decisions more clearly.
- SUCCESSION RACE -
Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, said the process to appoint Lagarde's successor would begin immediately to ensure a "smooth transition."
The frontrunners to succeed her are seen as former Dutch central bank chief Klaas Knot and Spain's Pablo Hernandez de Cos, currently head of the Bank for International Settlements.
One EU diplomat, speaking anonymously, said Knot was seen as the preferred candidate, as he was an experienced crisis manager and a good communicator.

But there are likely to be frantic negotiations in coming weeks between European capitals as several top ECB officials are due to be replaced – Lagarde, executive board member Isabel Schnabel and chief economist Philip Lane.

Holger Schmieding, chief economist at the bank Berenberg, predicted that EU leaders would try to fill the vacancies "as a package, no later than the EU summit of Dec 17-18, and possibly beforehand."--AFP

d052e41b141e82f1: MONTREAL: The EU and Canada want to bring their relationship to the "highest level possible" as they face a "world of growing rivalries", the 27-nation bloc's chief said Thursday ahead of a meeting with Canadian leader Mark Carney.
Brussels and Ottawa are to lay the groundwork for an ever-closer partnership at a two-day summit in Montreal, as they navigate uncertain ties with the US and China.

"We both want to bring our relationship to the highest level possible," von der Leyen said, doubling down on the prospect of Canada becoming the EU's "first associate member" despite an intra-EU squabble over the term.
"Our idea is simple: it is an 'association without accession'," she told an event organized by a research institute.
Von der Leyen first suggested Canada could become an "associate member" last month, but the title doesn't exist in EU treaties.
Some member states led by Germany successfully pushed to drop the term from a joint summit statement, after prolonged wrangling which threatens to take the shine away from the Montreal talks.

Canada and the EU have both been rattled by US President Donald Trump's second term. Trump's tariffs have hammered the Canadian economy, while the president's repeated annexation threats have caused outrage.
Prime Minister Mark Carney has warned relations will not return to a pre-Trump normal and told Canadians that reducing dependence on the US is an urgent priority.
Ahead of the summit, he promised "a new, ambitious alliance" with the EU.
The EU has equally faced US tariffs, and Trump and his top allies have piled criticism on European political leaders.

China's growing economic heft has also unnerved Brussels, which has moved to protect its industry from what it views as unfair competition from rivals subsidized by Beijing and ease its dependencies on Chinese goods and raw materials.
"In a world of growing rivalries, sovereignty and independence are no longer just the freedom to act alone. It is the capacity to act together," von der Leyen said.
"When trade becomes a tool of economic pressure, families pay the price, from the supermarket shelf to the cost of a new car. We are seeing in real time our sovereignty being attacked."
Brussels and Ottawa could either "go it alone" or "take a more strategic approach with trusted partners that face the same challenges," von der Leyen said.
What could be agreed?

The EU and Canada already share a free-trade pact, but it has not been fully implemented, and Canadian officials have said businesses are pursuing new opportunities in Europe to offset US tariff-related losses.

An EU official, speaking on condition of anonymity, said the new Canadian partnership would align policies in areas such as climate, energy and artificial intelligence, allowing Ottawa to participate in some EU programs.
Canada has huge stocks of the critical minerals needed for green technologies such as batteries and wind turbines that Europe sources mostly from China.

But Canada needs massive infrastructure investment to jump-start its mining industry. The summit could lead to an agreement allowing the European Investment Bank to back Canadian critical mineral projects.
A digital trade deal allowing faster and cheaper online transactions is expected to be unveiled in Montreal.
Ottawa and Brussels are also understood to be working to have Canada participate in the EU's Erasmus youth program, which allows university students to spend a semester abroad, among other things.
Carney said this week he wasn't concerned about associate-member status, or "specific names" to characterize the new alliance.
"What matters is the difference that it will make to the lives of Canadians," Carney said.
8616f263c2158d16: IN war-ravaged Gaza and the occupied West Bank, many Palestinians were less focused on who would win Israel's election than on whether anything would really change.
Whether Benjamin Netanyahu clings to power with his far-right allies or centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot comes out on top, few see much reason for hope in the Tuesday vote.
"We fear these elections could bring an even worse leader," said Huda al-Houli, a displaced resident of Khan Yunis in southern Gaza.
Such an outcome, she said, would only bring "more destruction and devastation" to the Palestinian territory.
Still, Houli said she hoped a more "human voice" would emerge in Israeli society and demand an end to the conflict, regardless of who forms the next government.
In Ramallah, in the West Bank, Ahmed Awad, 67, was equally sceptical.
"Whatever the result, and even if the politicians change, I don't think there will be any radical or dramatic shift in policies towards the Palestinian-Israeli conflict," he said.
With 85 per cent of ballots counted from Tuesday's vote, Netanyahu's camp remained ahead but without a clear majority, leaving uncertainty over Israel's next government.
The first election since Hamas's Oct 7, 2023 attack comes after years of right-wing and far-right rule marked by the war in Gaza and rising settler violence in the West Bank.
For Netanyahu, fighting for his political survival, several paths remain open: renewing his alliance with the far right, building a broader coalition or facing yet another political deadlock.
Far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir has already signalled that, if the current coalition survives, he would seek the defence portfolio and push for the expulsion of Gaza's population.
Not everyone has given up hope.
"Whatever happens, it will surely be better than what we've lived through in recent years," said Abdallah Abu Rahma, 54, from Ramallah.
But if Netanyahu remains in office, he added, "any coalition he forms, he will continue down the same path".
A government led by Eisenkot, a former army chief, could rein in the influence of the pro-settlement far right, said researcher Beth Oppenheim of the European Council on Foreign Relations.
It could also ease pressure on the Palestinian Authority and take a more flexible approach on aid and a ceasefire in Gaza.
But she warned against expecting too much.

There would be "nothing transformative", she said, and certainly no major shift on Palestinian statehood or the peace process, issues that have largely disappeared from Israeli political debate since Oct 7.
A renewed Netanyahu coalition with far-right partners would likely mean more of the same, including settlement expansion and impunity for settler violence, Oppenheim added.
"I think we need to have quite low expectations when it comes to seeing any major changes in policy from a different government," she said.
Even a Netanyahu defeat could leave Palestinians worse off in the short term, argued Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine-Israel programme at the Arab Center Washington.
"There is every reason for Palestinians to be concerned," he said.
Eisenkot himself served in Israel's wartime cabinet during the Gaza offensive, Munayyer noted.
A fragile alternative coalition under constant attack from Netanyahu and the right could try to prove it was tough enough by taking a harder line on Palestinian issues.
In the West Bank, violence could rise if the far right loses power, with settlers potentially acting out against a new government, he explained.
"It's important to understand that most settler violence in the West Bank is structural. It's not about the government in charge," said Munayyer.
"Settlers live in places that surround the Palestinian population. The Palestinian population is vulnerable to the settlers, who are armed, whereas the Palestinians overwhelmingly are not."
In Gaza, Adnan Al-Assar said he harboured few illusions.
"Netanyahu may win," he said. "But whatever happens, they all follow the same overarching policy, directed against the Palestinian people."

c8e42abc4890ea99: MICHIGAN'S tight race for an open United States Senate seat will help determine control of the chamber while testing two broader questions: whether identity-based attacks on a Muslim candidate can succeed in a battleground state, and how willing Democratic voters are to embrace the party's progressive wing.

Republican Mike Rogers has sought to portray Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, who would be the nation's first Muslim senator if he wins the Nov 3 election, as sympathetic to Islamist extremism, which El-Sayed denies and supporters say is Islamophobic.
Rogers has also argued that El-Sayed's support for universal healthcare and other progressive policies places him outside the political mainstream.

El-Sayed, a former public health official, has focused his campaign on lowering costs for working-class Americans while seeking to tie Rogers to President Donald Trump, even as Rogers has broken with the president on some issues in the campaign's closing weeks.
Trump has falsely accused El-Sayed of being a Muslim extremist, while Rogers has tried to tie him to the Muslim Brotherhood.
Branches of the Brotherhood, one of the Arab world's oldest and most influential Islamist movements, were designated as terrorist organisations by the Trump administration this year.
El-Sayed has disavowed the group and denied any connection with it.

Pollsters and political strategists​ say the attacks are aimed at dissuading Jewish and Black voters in the Detroit area who backed his primary opponent, Representative Haley Stevens, from voting for him.

"He's a Muslim-American and so Rogers is attempting to do his best to portray El-Sayed as an outsider who's dangerous," said Jonathan Hanson, a political scientist and public policy lecturer at the University of Michigan.
Michigan's Senate seat is critical to both parties' efforts to control the chamber. Republicans hold a 53-47 Senate majority heading into Tuesday's election.
Independent analysts rate the race a toss-up. The RealClearPolling average shows El-Sayed ahead by 2.5 percentage points in a state Trump carried by 1.4 points in 2024.
Advocating policies to curb corporate influence and expand the social safety net, El-Sayed, 41, has emerged as one of the Democratic Party's most prominent progressives.

He describes himself as a capitalist and rejects the socialist label, but a victory on Tuesday would likely be seen as a boost for the party's left wing as it seeks greater influence ahead of the 2028 presidential election.
The margin of any victory will matter, said Michigan State University political scientist Matt Grossmann.

"If El-Sayed wins by a couple of points but trails Democratic gubernatorial nominee Jocelyn Benson by a wide margin, that won't be a very convincing argument," said Grossmann. "And if El-Sayed were to lose, then it would be a mark against that faction of the party."
With Trump's popularity sagging, Rogers recently called for an end to the war in Iran and the trade dispute with Canada, while avoiding direct criticism of the president.
But portraying El-Sayed as a national security threat has also become a central feature of Rogers' closing message.

Rogers, 63, has based that claim in part on a 2012 group letter signed by El-Sayed and other Egyptian Americans in support of then-newly elected Egyptian president Mohamed Morsi, who was backed by the Muslim Brotherhood.
Earlier this month, Rogers agreed with a social media post calling El-Sayed a terrorist.
He also appeared with Trump at a rally on Sunday where the president likened El-Sayed to the Sept 11 attackers and said his goal was to keep a "jihadist" out of the Senate.
The rhetoric prompted a rare rebuke from the NAACP, the nonpartisan civil rights organisation, which does not typically intervene in political races.
"The blatantly racist attacks surrounding the Michigan Senate race are unacceptable and disgusting," said NAACP president Derrick Johnson.

John Clark, a political science professor at Western Michigan University, said the attacks on El-Sayed were aimed in part at depressing Democratic turnout but could work against Rogers by angering and boosting turnout among Michigan's sizable Arab American communities in Dearborn and elsewhere.
"Maybe this helps with some voters, but it has the potential of backfiring with others," said Clark.

ac42675551a6ae23: Oracle expects to earn more from existing application customers as it embeds AI in its enterprise software suite.
Speaking at Big Red's investor day on Wednesday, Chris Leone, executive veep of application development, said Oracle will layer usage-based revenue on top of its subscription model.

“The more work that gets done by AI in our system, the more revenue we will see because they're consuming AI units as that work is getting done. We don't have to add more seats in order for us to now generate more revenue,” he said.

Earlier this month, Oracle revealed its Fusion Claw runtime, designed to help customers control AI agents that automate business processes. It targets ERP, finance, and supply chain management in cloud-based Fusion applications running on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure (OCI).
Customers will pay for more work done inside Oracle applications, and Leone said Fusion Claw will also automate work done outside of Fusion.

The promise of more revenue for Oracle, and higher bills for customers, came as the company sought to reassure investors about its spending, borrowing and revenue as it chases a share of the AI market.

Oracle is funding a datacenter spending spree with negative cashflow and borrowing. OCI is set to host large language model builders, notably OpenAI, alongside its own customers' workloads. Oracle spent $55.7 billion on datacenters and cloud infrastructure in fiscal year 2026, which ended in May, and plans to spend between $90 billion and $95 billion in fiscal 2027.
That will require more debt. In 2027, Oracle hopes to raise around $40 billion in debt and equity, on top of the $18 billion in debt it raised in September 2025.

In a notice to investors this week, Oracle said it expects fiscal 2030 revenue of $225 billion, a compound annual growth rate of 35 percent from 2026. It expects positive cash flow by the second half of fiscal 2028, with capital spending falling the following financial year. Investors reacted positively.

Oracle co-CEO Mike Sicilia also told shareholders the company will use AI to help implement its software, a plan he called as important as putting AI in the software itself. He argued AI will cut implementation time, bringing existing and new customers to OCI faster and boosting revenue.

"On-premises customers can now move far more easily to the cloud by leveraging the AI tool sets to automate migrations and decrease the cost and time to implement. They don't have to be Oracle customers; they can be competitive customers."
Sicilia said enterprise application software users' reluctance to change had been a major "headwind" for Oracle, one he hopes AI will ease.

"Our large remaining base of on-premises customers are going to start to adopt this technology quite quickly. When we move customers from on-premises to cloud, we see a multiple increase in revenue," he said. ®
f9be373016982113: SINGAPORE: Climate change is projected to reduce production of key crops across Southeast Asia, with rice, maize and sugarcane facing declines, according to a study released on Thursday by the Singapore Food Agency and the National University of Singapore, Xinhua reported.

The Asean Agri Climate Impact Twenty study projects average rice production to decline by 3 per cent to 5 per cent between 2025 and 2044, while maize output could fall by 5 per cent to 6 per cent and sugarcane production by 1 per cent to 4 per cent.
In contrast, cassava production is projected to increase by 16 per cent, while soybean output could rise by 11 per cent to 13 per cent.

"More favourable average projections for some crops do not mean that they are free from climate-related risks. Production could still be affected by variability in climate conditions in any particular year including extreme heat, heavy rainfall or drought in an unfavourable year," the report said.

Very strong El Nino events could reduce average crop production across the region by up to about 10 per cent, the study found. Rice and rain-fed farming systems are generally more vulnerable to such events.

Overall, Southeast Asia is expected to experience rising temperatures, more frequent and prolonged heat waves, and increasingly variable rainfall, potentially disrupting water availability, planting schedules and crop yields.
TAGS: Singapore, study, Southeast Asia, climate change, key crops, decline

be23949f8f2e9b8b: THE annual monsoon transition, prompted by wind patterns from China and Vietnam across the South China Sea and daily thunderstorms this week are a welcome respite, floods notwithstanding.
The rough weather neutralised the months-long haze, a combination of peatland fires and Neolithic slash-and-burn land clearance in agrarian Kalimantan and Sumatra.

The toxic cocktail of microscopic solids, liquid droplets and hazardous gases spiked the Air Quality Index (AQI) to a dangerous peak of 200+, but with the monsoon barrelling, the AQI sunk to a breathable 16-40.

Affected Asean nations had implored Indonesia to permit firefighters, but Jakarta stubbornly insisted on self-reliance while defending its sovereignty and internal politicking that prevents "complicated" outside help.

In exasperation, Singapore applied their Transboundary Haze Pollution Act 2014, legal action against local and foreign companies that allegedly triggered the peatland fires, even if outside the island.

Officially, Indonesia cannot be charged in the International Court of Justice because it has not accepted the ICJ's jurisdiction on transboundary haze. Besides, Indonesia enjoys immunity from judicial processes of other countries.
Also, Malaysia is not about to lobby the United Nations for "advisory opinions" against Indonesia, so the only constructive option is the 2002 Asean Agreement on Transboundary Haze Pollution.
But the agreement is devoid of compensation claims or dispute settlement penalties between member states, only for resolutions through consultation and negotiation.
This makes the reaction of Natural Resources and Environmental Sustainability Minister Datuk Seri Arthur Joseph Kurup intriguing.

During a routine Dewan Rakyat question and answer, Arthur stated that the government was "open" to exploring international legal mechanisms. Arthur pointed to the haze's impact on public health, productivity and economic activity as the basis for further action.
Arthur also exonerated Malaysian companies of guilt in the burnings, citing lack of evidence.
The debate now is, should Asean rely on voluntary cooperation or negotiate stronger obligations from Indonesia? Obviously, the 2002 agreement has no leverage.
As a plausible precedent, even the United States–Canada Trail Smelter arbitration (1938–1941) on oil pollution compensation is unadoptable.

To build a solid case, Malaysia may require a Royal Commission of Inquiry to assess losses. The RCI has to investigate healthcare costs, lost working hours, business and tourism losses, environmental damage and public mitigation costs.

It must differentiate peatland fires caused by identifiable companies or individuals and a state's failure to fulfil its regional obligations. Scientific evidence must connect the pollution, the source and the claimed losses.
The RCI may be the only recourse since diplomacy and legal action are practically non-starters.

c1536c694606dca7: Michael Stonebraker introduced Postgres® at Berkeley in 1986. Forty years later, the database he invented is a leading choice for a generation of AI projects, and he is among the sharpest skeptics of how those projects are being built. Bruce Momjian is cofounder and core team member of the PostgreSQL Global Development Group, and he works at EnterpriseDB (EDB). In upcoming episodes of AI & Data Horizons by EnterpriseDB (EDB), the Turing Award winner and MIT professor and the Postgres community advocate both make the case that the future belongs to systems that bend without breaking, and to communities that no single company controls.
Zero, not 80

Stonebraker’s first exhibit is text-to-SQL, the promise that a business user can ask a question in plain English and get an answer from the warehouse. Public benchmarks such as Spider and BIRD report accuracy above 80 percent. His team tried the same thing on MIT’s own data warehouse—1,400 tables of student, faculty, building, and salary information—using real queries from its SQL log.

“We got zero-percent accuracy. Not 80, not 70, not 40—zero,” he said. Adding agentic AI, retrieval, and prompt engineering lifted that level into the teens. Telling the model every table and join term reached the 30s. “Still not ready for prime time.”

The reasons are the stuff of every enterprise estate. There is no training data, because the warehouse is not on the public internet. The data is idiosyncratic: among other things, MIT buildings have numbers, not names. The schema has rotted into cryptic table and column names and overlapping views. And real queries are harder than benchmark ones. His team has published its own benchmark, Beaver, and says nobody has broken out of accuracy levels in the 30-percent range.
Use the model for what it’s good at

The deeper problem, Stonebraker argues, is architectural. Large language models are good with text, but “what they are no good at is doing joins of structured data,” which is most of what an enterprise holds. Working with the city of Munich’s transport department, Stonebraker’s team found that answering a single citizen complaint about crosswalk timing meant combining regulations, CAD drawings, trolley schedules, and school-zone maps. Orchestrating that with a language model at the center was, he said, “ridiculously expensive.”

The team’s answer, a system called Rubicon, uses models only on text, then casts the results into tables and hands the rest to a tabular engine. The orchestrator “looks like a query optimizer.” Stonebraker says it is cheaper by a factor of 10 and considerably more accurate than agent frameworks built around a model.

He expects agentic AI to slide from the top of the hype cycle into the valley of despair before a more balanced view emerges. Enterprises hate non-determinism: Approve a loan and reverse it on review, and “that’s called a lawsuit.” Organizations also need protection from rogue agents. The guardrails inside the database, he notes, largely exist already: decades of access control, complete logs, and triggers that can stop a transaction in its tracks. Data-heavy agents, he suggests, belong inside the data layer as user-defined functions, if the tooling to debug and version them improves.

Stonebraker is equally blunt about the frontier. The models have already used the real training data on the internet, and he knows of no enterprise that will let a model train on its proprietary data. AGI, he said, is “basically marketing hype” from foundation model vendors justifying their valuations.
Nobody owns it

Why Postgres? “Postgres is the intergalactic answer to open source,” Stonebraker said. Its unique feature is that “it’s not controlled by any one company.” EDB, Microsoft, Google, and others each contribute committers, and nobody steers. He dates its rise to Oracle buying MySQL, when “everybody said: vendor control.” For enterprises, that independence is the foundation of sovereignty: retaining control over how and where their data systems operate.

Momjian describes the same structure from the inside. Postgres has no office, no assets, and no legal entity, yet it produces “software better than billion-dollar companies.” Its forecasting tool is the community itself, which spots needs early from China, Russia, and the United States. “We only need one person in the world to be supersmart, and that person to tell us what they think.”
Built to bend

Both experts describe a design philosophy that favors flexibility over the last few percent of speed. Stonebraker built Postgres to be extended, and that is why it absorbed JSON, full-text search, GIS, and now AI without a rewrite. Momjian adds a second call from the 1990s: Lean on the operating system rather than absorb it, which made Postgres a natural fit for the cloud.

Momjian resists optimizations that buy 5 or 10 percent at the cost of rigidity, since a mistuned system can lose 40 percent. “If you take a Formula One car to the supermarket, there’s no place for the groceries.” The project plans on a horizon few vendors can match. “We’re looking at what would be the impact 5 years from now, 10 years from now.”
What PostgreSQL 19 delivers

The new release puts that discipline on show. Several previewed features, including SQL property graph queries and partition merging and splitting, were reverted, because reliability comes first. AI-assisted review is finding problems quickly; the August 2026 patch release for PostgreSQL 18 addressed 28 CVEs.

What remains is practical: REPACK CONCURRENTLY for busy tables, smarter parallel autovacuum, and sequence synchronization for logical replication. Plan Advice, from PostgreSQL major contributor and committer Robert Haas, is the community’s answer to Oracle-style optimizer hints it rejected for years. “Somebody found a way of doing it that didn’t have the downsides,” Momjian said.
The database as AI’s memory

The two diverge on how fast AI will write SQL. Momjian expects agents to create databases and generate much of the code. Stonebraker says that will not happen inside the enterprise until data is documented, silos are opened, and the politics change. They agree on the destination. AI needs a relational system to give it permanence and memory, and, in Momjian’s words, that is “a game-changer.”
Forty years on, the inventor and the steward are betting on the same database.

b5ccf41f1539ed5f: PUTRAJAYA: The Court of Appeal has set aside a Bolivian's plea of guilt on a charge of trafficking in 3.714kg of cocaine and remitted his case to the High Court for trial.
Rafael Nunez Pax had been convicted and sentenced to 30 years' imprisonment by the High Court in 2025 after he pleaded guilty to the charge.
Yesterday, a three-member bench comprising Justices Datuk Noorin Badaruddin, Datuk Mohd Radzi Abdul Hamid and Datuk Meor Hashimi Abdul Hamid, allowed Pax's appeal on grounds of justice.

Delivering the court's decision, Justice Noorin said the court was of the view that the strict guidelines governing Section 173 of the Criminal Procedure Code laid down by Court of Appeal judge Datuk Mohamed Zaini Mazlan in the Teh Geok Chin v PP case had not been strictly complied with, particularly whether Pax understood the consequences of his plea.
She said the range of punishment must be explained to the appellant (Pax), and it must be put on record by the judge.
"Because of that, we are allowing the appeal. We remit this matter to the High Court for trial," Justice Noorin said.
Paz's lawyer, Hasnan Hamzah, assisted by Qushwa Hasnan, argued that his client's lack of understanding of the procedures at the High Court stage meant his guilty plea was conditional.
"Therefore, it was unsafe for the High Court judge to convict Paz of an offence under Section 39B (1) (a) of the Dangerous Drugs Act 1952," he said.

He said Paz, in his affidavit, stated that he was merely following the advice given by his lawyer at the time and believed he would be given the opportunity to explain his side of the story to the court after the plea.

He said in the grounds of judgment, the High Court judge only indicated that Paz, a taxi driver, understood what was conveyed by the Spanish interpreter, but did not explain or elaborate on the nature of that understanding.

Deputy Public Prosecutor Nur Aqilah Syaza Ariffin argued that throughout the proceedings in the High Court, a Spanish interpreter was present to translate on behalf of the Pax, and the charge was also read out in Spanish.

According to the charge, Paz was accused of committing the offence at the passenger screening branch, Level 3, Domestic Arrival Hall, KLIA 1 Terminal, Kuala Lumpur International Airport, Sepang, Selangor, at 6pm on Aug 1, 2023.
On June 4, 2025, Paz pleaded guilty to the charge, and the High Court convicted him and sentenced him to 30 years in jal, beginning from the date of his arrest on Aug 1, 2023.

<!--kg-card-end: html--> Andy Yen, the CEO of Proton, had a message for an employee in the company’s security Slack channel who urged the company to at least take a few days to pentest newly written code before pushing it live. “That’s bullshit and loser thinking. Of course it’s possible to be fast and secure,” Yen wrote in the channel at the end of August. “Stop thinking always of how to be slower, and focus more on how to be faster.”
In a follow-up message, Yen reiterated his point: “only losers think like that.” His ultimate message for the team was to “stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more.”

That exchange was just one of many that showed how Yen and other company executives are aggressively pushing Proton towards AI. Proton is a Swiss company that famously makes the encrypted email service Proton Mail and a suite of privacy and security-focused products, including an encrypted drive service, an authenticator app, a password manager, and more.

In the last few months, Yen set up an email address for employees to contact if they come across anything blocking adoption of AI at Proton, so leadership can “ruthlessly smash everything that stands in the way of AI velocity;” Proton installed software on workers’ computers that track how much AI code the company is generating; and Yen said this is the last year that Proton will hire engineers at all, and instead only hire people to build things with AI.

That AI push came to head this week when 404 Media reported Proton said it would re-interview staff about their use of AI, with the clear implication that those interviews, and employees’ willingness to embrace AI, could decide whether a worker is fired or not.

404 Media spoke to eight current and one former Proton employees and reviewed Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company’s CTO. Our reporting reveals a culture of fear inside Proton, where many employees are hesitant to even mildly critique Yen’s views or discuss engineering problems. Workers describe an environment where employees have genuine concerns about security or being asked to develop security products with AI, but feel unable to voice them, lest Yen berates them in front of everyone or threatens their employment at the company.
“The CEO is in full AI psychosis and has been for a while now,” one of the sources told 404 Media.

Our reporting also paints a picture of Proton that is likely very different to the public’s perception of a company with a goal of carefully protecting privacy: one that in reality is barreling ahead with AI as quickly as possible so it can achieve the explicit goal of more annual revenue.

“Due to insufficient velocity,” Proton is not on track to achieve its annual recurring revenue target by the end of the year, one internal document obtained by 404 Media reads. Proton’s year-over-year growth is also “far away from what the market today considers to be good,” and, “By all metrics that matter, we’re an underperforming company.”
In response to detailed questions from 404 Media, a Proton spokesperson did not dispute any of our reporting or characterization of what’s happening inside of the company.

“It’s clear that some people at Proton are unhappy with our direction, or misunderstand it, and many people are anxious,” they said. “In our determination to move fast, we have sometimes been too blunt or too slow in explaining ourselves to our people. We will work on that, as their questions are the ones we most need to answer.”
Do you know anything else about Proton? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at joseph.404 or send me an email at joseph@404media.co.

Yen, a former CERN particle physicist, projects a measured approach in public, but internally he acts more like what one employee described as a “petulant child.” In May, Proton announced it was implementing post-quantum cryptography which should protect against future attacks from quantum computers. The work took years of effort, with one caveat that it would not work on older emails, only those written after the feature’s launch, at least for the moment. Yen was not happy that Proton was drawing attention to this limitation.

In a Slack channel dedicated to thanking people for their work, Yen jumped in. “Get it fixed,” he wrote, referring to Proton’s Reddit post announcing the feature. “Now Reddit is pissed and we look worse than Tuta,” he added, referring to a Proton competitor. When employees explained to Yen the nuances of the encryption and why that was not immediately possible, Yen wrote, “I find this whole thing stupid. You cannot announce this in this way.”

“Now we are left with two shitty choices. Deprioritize more important tasks for the business to re-encrypt old emails, or constantly get attacked online for not doing it. So maybe you can enlighten me on which of the two shitty choices we will take,” he wrote. “In the future there are two options. Either you guys are confident enough to not fuck this up, or you get my advice to make sure it is not fucked up,” he added. He then told a member of the team that made it to “go on Reddit.”
“So go on there with your personal account and comment to set the record straight,” he wrote. “Perception is more important than truth, the truth doesn’t matter if you don’t win on perception.”

One employee told 404 Media, “Whatever persona Andy [Yen] has out of Proton, he’s a straight up bully inside. He routinely breaks his little facade in Slack and calls people losers and stupid, often for stuff he’s paying them for.”

Ever since launching Proton Mail in 2014 after the Snowden revelations, Proton has steadily introduced new products that make Proton more of a worksuite than a simple email provider. More recently, those products were focused around AI, with the launch of Lumo, a large language model (LLM) chatbot that the company says doesn’t log conversations or train on user data. In June, Proton launched a 2.0 version of its chatbot.

Up until this point, Yen’s public comments on AI were relatively tame. In an August interview with WIRED, he said Proton is “building AI features and AI tools, because I think if the privacy companies do not find a way to step in to build privacy-first AI, we are essentially ceding the future to tech companies that don’t have the best interests of users at heart,” and that the company was “capitalizing” on the backlash to corporatized, invasive AI from companies like Google. Last year, Yen and Proton were criticized for statements he made suggesting the Republican Party and Donald Trump would be harder on Big Tech than Democrats.
Toward the end of August, Yen’s internal tone on AI shifted to having Proton use it as much as possible, and as quickly as possible, according to the Slack chats and multiple employees.

“The train is coming, get onboard or get crushed. Don’t be the professional fax machine operator in the internet age,” he wrote to the security Slack channel. “I think by the end of this year most developers stop programming and start writing specs for tests that AI will code and run, to validate AI written code that humans will no longer be able to review. This will be the last year that we hire engineers, and starting next year we hire what we used to call product managers, to build things with AI.”

<!--kg-card-end: html--> AI is changing how cybersecurity works, with AI agents hacking into companies, and AI assisting in the discovery of gaping vulnerabilities in important code. Many companies across the privacy and security space are grappling with how to deal with AI, either in the development of their products or how to defend themselves against hackers who are using AI. Some may do this carefully. Others are trying to do it as quickly as possible for profit. This account of Proton’s own reckoning with AI provides an unprecedented insight into what is happening inside one security-focused company users especially trust.

Initially, using AI was banned inside Proton, but the company has since approved AI for all sorts of use cases internally, including processing financial data, drafting customer-facing responses on Reddit and LinkedIn, and writing code “except when that source code contains information that would give immediate advantage to a competitor” or is related to “innovation or R&D [research and development],” according to an internal Proton document seen by 404 Media. Ninety percent of code at Proton in October was written by AI, the company’s CTO Bart Butler said in a meeting, according to audio 404 Media obtained. Much of that code is written with Anthropic’s Claude, multiple employees told 404 Media. And Yen tells employees in Slack chats to use Claude, too.
“We are a tech company against Big Tech who are spending loads on Claude,” one employee told 404 Media.

In the “bullshit and loser thinking” conversation, another employee pushed Yen for specifics on ensuring that AI-generated code was free of security issues. “AI won’t magically solve our problems, because security is low in our prioritization at present,” the engineer said. Yen didn’t respond directly, and went on to insult one of the other employees in front of the entire channel. The employee “is saying his usual bs of we can do it but we will be even slower than we are today and I’m saying only losers think like that,” Yen wrote, adding that workers should prompt “better.”

“You have the models and the time every developer should be doing this and checking their code which they were doing before manually but now they can do faster with AI,” Yen added. (One employee stressed that engineers still strive to build in a secure way.)
The second clear signal that Proton was going deep into AI for many employees happened when Butler, the CTO, published a self-described AI manifesto one Friday afternoon last month.

“Your old job is gone,” the manifesto, posted to Slack, told engineers. It laid out a future for Proton that fully embraced AI, and said if the company did not do so, that posed an “existential threat to the success of the mission itself.”

Butler said that Proton needs to change in three key ways: accept that an engineers’ job is now to help LLMs write better code, faster; that Proton needs to get to the point where most code is not reviewed by humans but by AI; and to more fundamentally change the company as a whole, and “commit, as an organization, to the transformation that the moment requires.”
One Proton employee replied in Slack, “Perhaps scaring people with: We are in a new world. ‘Programming’ is dead [...] your old job is gone wasn’t really necessary on a Friday afternoon.”

Butler replied, “It’s supposed to be provocative, because it needs to be. I suggest you read it, think about it over the weekend, and come with your questions to me on Monday rather than on Slack. Thanks!”

An employee told 404 Media, “​​People were surprised and somewhat cringed out, since the document clearly exaggerates what you can do with LLMs today and doesn't address any of the problems you get in return for giving up your code base to the AI Jesus (e.g. AI cannot really maintain a large code base over time).” Another called it “ethically bankrupt.”

Earlier this week, Proton sent the email to employees saying they would re-interview workers about how they use AI in their jobs. The tone was clear; you may lose your job because of these interviews, current employees told 404 Media. “These re-interviews are consequential,” the email read. Soon after, a senior employee spoke up in Slack to Yen about the re-interviewing process. He suggested instead that Proton detect who is falling behind and support them and enforce high quality training.
Yen’s response was blunt: “Let’s put it this way, we already know more or less who is behind. If we were giving up on them, we would not bother with this process.”

The employee replied, “That messaging is fear-based. Which is probably why I suspect there are dozens of other employees watching us talk about this live and except for [other employee] no one else is chiming in.”

“People shouldn’t be scared to talk about this in public and to push back on you and leadership. A fear based culture feels like a cancer to me. It’s the opposite of engineering, you need to talk about things, even uncomfortable things,” they added. Yen eventually told the employee, in front of everyone: “If you are making the accusation that this is a financially driven decision and you don’t trust me when I tell you it’s not, then I think this might not be the place for you.”

Only one other employee chimed in during that exchange: “It’s about the culture you instil, people don’t want to feel like they’re on a tightrope, and yes we understand you want to move fast but there needs to be a balance, people also need support, not everyone is the same.”
“It was also faster for my parents to beat me until I ate my vegetables but I’m not sure it was healthy,” they added.

The exchange with Yen was unusual not only in that someone was debating some of Yen’s ideas, but also that it directly referenced the culture of fear at Proton. “Whenever someone talks back to Andy it tends to be highlighted since very few people talk back to him,” one employee told 404 Media.
