01b61253f2f19e4c: Today on Decoder, I’m joined by Joey Brookhart, an analyst at the chip and AI research firm SemiAnalysis, to help me dig into the story inside the numbers of the Anthropic IPO filing — a document known as an S-1.

Anthropic just filed its S-1 to go public on the Nasdaq, and it could start trading as soon as next month at a valuation of anywhere between $1.5 trillion and $2 trillion. That would immediately make it one of the most valuable companies on the planet.

But the price tag really isn’t the whole story here. The S-1 document published earlier this week is hundreds upon hundreds of pages filled with details that finally paint a picture of the economics of a frontier AI lab. As you might imagine, that picture is both really complicated and built on a series of very, very ambitious assumptions about the future and what AI will do to it.

So I wanted to have Joey on the show to help break down what this document tells us, both about Anthropic’s finances and the broader AI economy. Joey and his colleagues at SemiAnalysis actually built a model of Anthropic’s finances from the outside back in July, so he’s been waiting for this filing about as eagerly as anyone, and I was excited to hear his take on what we’ve learned and, importantly, what we still don’t know.
Okay: SemiAnalysis’ Joey Brookhart on the Anthropic S-1 and the costs and risks of building frontier AI. Here we go.
This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity.
Joey Brookhart, you are an analyst at SemiAnalysis. You’re also co-lead on SemiAnalysis’ Tokenomics model, which is going to come up a lot in this episode. Welcome to Decoder.
Yeah, thanks so much, Nilay.

I am very excited to talk to you. We’re talking just a couple days after the big Anthropic S-1 was filed. It’s our first look inside of the finances of one of the leading frontier models. What’s your take? What’s your read into it?

It was an awesome S-1. It’s been a rough three weeks since the investor day. Some people were somewhat disappointed in the September [annualized recurring revenue] numbers, but what we saw here was a company that has efficiently scaled to an amazing level, with a $1 trillion-plus valuation, $70 billion-plus of ARR in a very short amount of time.

In gross margins, compute margins, and free cash flow, everything is what you’d want to see. So I don’t think there was much to nitpick in this filing. It’s the reason you’ve seen a lot of the semiconductor complex, and the neoclouds and compute stocks, really rally again in the last two days.

It’s funny, I don’t think I can nitpick the S-1 itself. I want to get into some of the details because there are a lot of numbers in there that are worth thinking about. I actually just want to start at the really big picture. You run a thing called Tokenomics. I’m going to explain what Tokenomics is to people.

I look at Anthropic and where it could go. I look at Dario Amodei saying that he can see his way to $1 trillion in revenue. Where does that money come from? Because so much of these businesses are about eating every other business and it feels like someone else has to make some money to pay Anthropic to generate these revenues. I haven’t actually seen that laid out very clearly.
Verge subscribers, don’t forget you get exclusive access to ad-free Decoder wherever you get your podcasts. Head here. Not a subscriber? You can sign up here.

It’s so interesting. Today, because even the scale we’re at is $120 billion of ARR between the two leading labs, it’s still an extremely narrow market. The top 1 percent of customers are the ones that are spending $50,000 to $100,000 per employee. Your broader Fortune 500 or Global 2000, which typically do a lot of IT spend, isn’t spending much.

A lot of the spending, especially at Anthropic, is coding-specific. It’s almost a single vertical company. We look in the future to 2027, you think to this broader adoption and white collar work. This typical enterprise Q4 budgeting season, we actually haven’t gone through with one of these labs yet in any meaningful way because their ARR did really start to accelerate until the beginning of the year. We think of other cases like cyber, which can be similar to coding, where these are eight-figure-plus contracts with leading enterprises that can scale very quickly due to all the cybersecurity incidents we’re seeing. You get to other verticals like bio.

To get to $1 trillion, we do have to move to some of that white collar work, where it goes from AI augmentation to labor saving or replacement in some areas. You look at things like Microsoft’s buyout offers to employees as an example of this, but there’s no wealth of other verticals that they can get into and really start to move the needle.

This is the single biggest question I have, not just about the S-1, but the entire industry. I would understand that if there are one or two leading labs. There are two big companies that have a technology that can automate a whole bunch of things. We will see how well that automation goes sector by sector, but there are not just two leading labs. There are quite a few of them. There are open weight models.

I’ve heard from a lot of CEOs who are very nervous about giving all their data to an OpenAI or Anthropic and they would like to run some things on-prem. There are law firms running on-prem AI now, which is the funniest turn in maybe all of history.

How do you see that playing out? Because so much of the pressure on this S-1 was the numbers themselves, which I want to talk about, but then there’s the external pressure of, “You’ve got to grow and growth is not as short.” So how do you see all of that playing out?

It’s very interesting because when we look at coding today, for example — and I think we saw this in Q3 with OpenAI kind of catching up — there are areas of coding where there are very low switching costs, and I can just move between that. What we hear from enterprises and maybe, too, on the OpenAI side — obviously I think they somewhat botched the Fable release, and the lack of zero data retention is why we saw some of the slowdown. That’s something they can fix with Fable 5.5 and maybe drive more enterprise adoption there.

That’s a huge thing for enterprises when we talk with them. We definitely see enterprises now, and more so, too, a lot of the AI natives, doing custom training and post-training on open weight models, and then running either their inference off of that or even their products for internal or external use cases.

Obviously, DeepMind at Google and [Meta Superintelligence Labs] are very well-funded labs that have pretty similar training compute capacity, and they’re bringing on a ton of it. Not even to mention SpaceX as well, with what Elon said on [about] 10 net new gigawatts next year and half of that is the long-term internal use case.

In the first half of the year, Anthropic ran away with it. They were 90 percent of the industry’s net new ARR. We saw in Q3 that OpenAI was probably actually the majority of industry net new ARR. Open-source has grown from probably $1 billion of token inference costs, ARR, in Q1 to $10 billion-plus here in Q3.

So yes, the industry’s gotten much more competitive, but there are all these new use cases, too, and some of these verticalized use cases are really where we’re going to see the growth going forward. Because it’s obvious coding isn’t going to power us to even triple from here.

It’s interesting. The concept is called Tokenomics. You run that practice alongside another co-lead at SemiAnalysis. Explain what it is because to me it’s such a smart way of thinking about, “We’re going to put some money in and maybe we’ll get some money out.”

I think of it as the unit economics [of AI], or even just the broader idea — everything from a macro- to microeconomics of running an AI business or even looking at AI demand. So we cover the hyperscalers, now some of the neoclouds as well in a separate product.

But then just the AI labs, too. For investors, or just people that are interested in the business, Anthropic had negative 94 percent gross margins on inference two years ago. Now they have a positive 85 percent margin, and people don’t understand how they allocate compute. How do we think about the inference business model?

Part of that gross margin conversation is the revenue per megawatt in inference. Why are all companies that are running inference seeing massive gains in inference and compute efficiency? So we try to model out these businesses and obviously when Anthropic was private, we’re dealing with information we can get from the press and things like that.

But now that we have concrete audited numbers, it’s easy to explain the unit economics of this. And also how the businesses differ. OpenAI is a much different business than Anthropic just in both their consumption versus subscription and then historical weight versus consumer versus enterprise. [We are] trying to understand across the demand level the economics of these businesses.

Several years ago when I talked to Google CEO Sundar Pichai about the cost of inference, I said, “How are you ever going to make money?” He was just very clear. He said, “If there’s one thing Google’s good at, it’s bringing this stuff down the cost curve.”

It was a very blunt answer. I understand how Google can do it. They make their own chips. Anthropic is running on everyone else’s clouds. The core part of the S-1 is how much they’ve committed to spend on other people’s clouds: SpaceXAI, Google, Amazon. Where does their efficiency come from?

There’s really token throughput. They have a very diverse chip fleet. Between Trainiums, TPUs, and GPUs, across all of those, we see a ton of token efficiencies. Token throughput, for example, on Trainium chips is up 5x to 10x year-over-year right now.

Dealing with both the hardware level efficiencies and the software — and how the model interacts with the hardware — there are a lot of token throughput gains where if you’re doing X tokens per second, now you’re doing five or 10 times that just a year later. What they’ll tell you is they see continued compute efficiencies as well going forward.

Max Kan, who co-leads Tokenomics model with me at SemiAnalysis, and I have even published some research on this. Right now, if Anthropic’s at $65 million of revenue per inference megawatt, this was mid-teens last year at this time. What we’ve said on maybe Opus 5.5 on a [Nvidia] Blackwell, you can get to $100 to $120 million of revenue per megawatt.

The big thing here is they’re paying on average now just a little over $10 million per megawatt in [cost of goods sold], or just in compute costs. What you can do with those margins is then reinvest in training.

People don’t realize this, but only about 30 percent of the compute is actually in inference-serving revenue. The rest is for experimentation and research, training models, and post-training models. So there’s a lot of compute that is building the next model and that’s more of the R&D side and where you actually get your returns and defensibility in this business.

Actually, what I was expecting to see in the S-1 was that dynamic play out much more strongly — that Anthropic makes a bunch of money selling the models they have now and there are more customers in the future for the models they have now. That’s going to throw off a whole bunch of margin. And then, because it is Anthropic and they think they’re building a digital god, they’re going to train the next models as much as they can.

That is a very particular Anthropic story. The company is chasing AGI. The people who work there will happily tell you that in the S-1 that Claude might be conscious and this could all go to hell. Anthropic is a very unique company in its conception of itself. But you don’t really see that dynamic playing out in the S-1. They’re managing their training costs against their inference margin pretty well. Do you see that going up or changing in any way?

I agree. Long term, and we’ve even said this internally, they want to actually increase the percentage of training. If you believe you’re building a digital god or going towards AGI, and as long as you have the gross margins of 85 percent-plus on inference to do so, you can.

They’ve grown a lot faster than they thought, and they didn’t expect to be at 11 percent non-gap EBITA margins. They’d love to be closer to zero, or even below that if they could get that compute and allocate it towards training and continue to see these compute efficiencies.

They’ve messaged that, too, to investors in the roadshow. You can look at this S-1 and just the curve of profitability over the last few years and how little cash they burned to get to this point and you can say, “This is a good business model, but we’re going towards AGI. Don’t expect the margin leverage we’re seeing to continue to this level, even though long-term margins can be quite a bit higher.”

There are some real shades of Amazon there. Jeff Bezos famously told investors he wasn’t going to make money until he could make a lot of money. Obviously, Amazon and Anthropic have a lot of back and forth. Maybe there’s some family resemblance there.

But I’m curious, there’s a point of model capability that would allow you to go into more verticals than just coding, right? We might be at it now. The idea of capability overhang exists, the idea that the models we have today could go and take over bio research. They’re taking over mathematics today. There’s a point at which the smartest business decision is to stop training and to just sell your profitable model into more and more companies. Anthropic as a public company will face that pressure.
Do you think they’re organized or structured to fend it off?

Yeah, I think they’re structured well. With some of the voting stock in areas like that, they definitely are. We’ve seen this in tech before and even publicly when Mark Zuckerberg has made these decisions before to invest heavily.
It didn’t always pay off. I just want to point out, it didn’t always pay off.
Yeah, it did not always pay off.
Although you and I technically are in the metaverse right now, by some definition.
[Laughs] Right. But I think that’s something, and there’s an interesting number in the S-1 that 80 percent of revenue in the last three months comes from models released in the last six months.

So then you say, “Okay, 20 percent of the models are like Opus 4.5 in earlier versions.” One thing going forward is that if you’re a frontier model company, you always need to be at the frontier and it’s incredibly competitive.
Wait, can I ask a really dumb question about that?
Yeah.

Why? I think the heart of my curiosity about the industry right now is if you enabled some bleeding-edge technology that could revolutionize the entire world, at some point, the most profitable thing to do is to just go play it out in all the different verticals, right? It’s not to go make the next one. It’s actually to run an efficient model in legal services and medicine and wherever else that there hasn’t been diffusion of AI yet.

This idea that you always have to be at the frontier, that Anthropic always has to be competing with Google and OpenAI and whoever else, I get it from their self-conception. But from a business point of view, an AI-enabled business is going to throw out more money and spend more money with me, the AI provider, and that isn’t necessarily related to being at the frontier.
There are a few portions of that. For new verticals, and this is very cyber specific, if an adversary is using a frontier model, you need to be defending with a frontier model.
Fair enough.

When we talk to some enterprises, it’s not like an email summary where I can run that on open source or Sonnet. There are just certain verticals where having… [For example,] if you were in a legal case as a defendant, would you be okay if your lawyer was using a non-frontier model if the prosecution—
[Laughs] I got bad news for you about what’s going on in the legal market right now.

The competitive dynamics do dictate that. I think from a go-forward perspective, we’ve seen this with open source too catching up in one point, but the demand will be there. [SemiAnalysis CEO] Dylan [Patel] says this a lot. The demand will always be there for frontier intelligence, especially in competitive industries. And there are certain tasks, as you go towards more labor replacement versus labor augmentation, where that also is the case.

At the same time, they are getting more vertical. If you go look at job postings or what they’re hiring for, they’re putting out more of these SKUs and areas, and there’s a lot of beta testing going on like Claude for financial services, Claude for legal, their cyber program. They’re giving away 25,000 of credits per month for people in their cyber program.

That’ll be a huge SKU for them in 2027. Those verticalized areas and then ones that are specifically where you need to be… It’s more adversarial, I should say, or competitive, are the main reasons why. But we can both agree there are areas like email summary and work that definitely doesn’t need to happen [at the frontier].

I’ll just make a dumb comparison to the iPhone. It’s iPhone season. I just reviewed the iPhone Duo. Apple kept the iPhone looking the same for several years now. They build all of the tooling for the new iPhone and then they just reuse it for two or three or four models to get all the value out of that investment back before they move on to the next thing. Apple puts out a new iPhone, and it keeps selling the old iPhone for a while to get more value out of that investment and that development program.

The AI industry does not seem to be doing that. All of their emphasis is on developing the next new thing, deprecating the old thing pretty fast, and moving you onto the new expensive product, while at the same time they’re building the next new expensive product.

At some point it feels like that will rationalize, that there will be something that is worth just collecting margin from while they go invest in the new thing. I just can’t figure out where Anthropic sits in that cycle.

I mean, we do see this. Open source token volumes are picking up and there’s a lot of areas, yes, where the open source models have become good enough. I think on a go-forward basis, you’re like, “Okay, was that because of distillation?” And then the frontier labs have some defensibility actually going forward. I think when we talk to clients, it’s also about how we actually think about frontier versus open source. So something like a Sonnet type model, if you want to do the iPhone 18 versus the SE type analogy.

We do see that dynamic, and obviously with open source, it’s a question of how much that can take. Two, because we’re so early in these verticals, we don’t know what’s going to be fully agentic. There’s no human in the loop where the harness actually has, I should say, some value and defensibility to it.

The big area I’d look at here, especially when we talk to enterprises today, is only the coders are allowed to use the frontier models at a lot of these enterprises. If you’re a non-coder, some of these companies just limit you to Sonnet, if you’re an Anthropic customer. That’s reflective of how management views and wants to budget for this, what frontier intelligence is actually worth to them in certain areas.

In my financial analyst brain, Claude could not build a good financial model six months ago. It’s getting better if you connect it to the right areas, but we’ve gone from something like, “I needed a junior analyst six months ago,” to, “Maybe I don’t as much anymore,” and then, “Will I have a full junior analyst at my disposal anytime or multiple pretty quickly, if I have unlimited token budget?” We just look at that across every vertical and major job category.
The time horizon in each of those categories is going to be different. That’s just one of the bigger questions I have: How quickly do they get to where they think they can go?
705e4fe02b52f2f6: Everyone's favorite Unix init system is adding support for the Unix world's favorite new programming language. What's the worst that could happen?

Don't worry, this isn't here just yet. Agent P and his trusty team released systemd version 262 about a month ago. That means that systemd 263 is now under construction, and developer Christian Brauner announced on Mastodon that his new feature has been merged.

The previous effort, which was pull request #44144, has now been split into five separate parts. Part 1 contains keyring-util and voa-util, described as "helpers for enrolling certificates into kernel keyrings." Part 2, support programs written in Rust, is the banner item. Then come a few more: bind only the headers Rust code uses, wrap the libsystemd-shared helpers systemd-keyring-setup needs, and finally, add systemd-keyring-setup.
There are several important riders to the announcement, and these are spelled out in the second PR:
"Rust is only used for new leaf components. Existing C code isn't ported and nothing that other components depend on is written in Rust."
In other words, before anyone gets too excited, this does not indicate the start of an effort to rewrite systemd in Rust. All it means is that new systemd modules can be written in Rust.
The second bullet point will be more significant for existing Rust developers: "No cargo. Everything is built with meson."

Cargo is the Rust language’s package manager and build system. It's the normal way to build Rust applications, as well as to distribute modules of Rust code for other Rust developers to use. However, systemd already has a modern build system. It's called Meson and it's not unique to systemd – it is also used extensively by the GNOME project and the Mesa 3D graphics library. Meson itself is written in Python and uses Ninja to manage the compilation process. Ninja was designed to build Chrome faster, and it's also used for Android.
The third stipulation is that any Rust code must not use the standard library. For those more familiar with C, this may sound extreme, but it's normal for embedded Rust programming.

The project documents the system requirements. It needs Rust version 1.85 or later. That's modest: that version was released in February 2025, and version 1.99.1 appeared earlier this month. It also calls for bindgen version 0.71.1 (from December 2024) or newer, and Meson 1.4.0 (from March 2024). These are relatively old versions – for instance, it's the Meson version included in Debian 13).

Brauner added an interesting little coda in a second Masto post: saying that the team would have liked to support Rust in the core of systemd, but currently, Rust’s support for dynamic libraries isn't quite there yet.

It's perhaps worth noting that writing systemd modules in Rust isn't the same thing at all as calling systemd from Rust code. There are several tools for doing that, and they have been around for years: for example, the systemd crate first appeared in 2015. ®

05e64d90fcbc7502: Their petition to the authorities has already gathered over 500 signatures
Originally published on Global Voices
DigiAction picnic held in Lozhan village, Albania. Photo by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.

This interview is part of a series of spotlights on the work of some of the grantees of the Digital Spark granting scheme, as part of the Regional Support Mechanism EECA project, implemented by the Metamorphosis Foundation and TechSoup, in partnership with CIVICUS and under the Digital Democracy Initiative (DDI) that covers the Global South. It is being published on Global Voices as part of a content-sharing agreement.

In rural parts of Albania, youth are seldom mobilized to help solve local environmental and other problems in their communities, although they, too, are affected by them. This has been the case in the eastern Korce region as well, which was hit by heavy rainfall and subsequent devastating floods in November 2025.

In the Maliq municipality, one of the affected areas, the situation was worsened by improper disposal of waste that blocked drainage channels, including the Devoll River, which flows through the area. Illegal waste disposal has obstructed the river’s infrastructure and contributed to widespread flooding. Despite efforts by the authorities to improve waste management and clean up the river, the situation has remained dire.
Waste accumulated at the Devoll River Bridge in Maliq, Albania. Photo from November 21, 2025 by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.

In 2026, a local non-governmental organization (NGO), Qendra KAZUS, recruited and trained local youth to help solve this long-standing issue by turning them into environmental advocates. Global Voices conducted an email interview with Dhorjela Cela, the group’s executive director, to learn about how Qendra KAZUS implemented a project that brought together youth, digital democracy, environmental challenges, and advocacy. The interview has been edited for clarity and brevity.
Global Voices (GV): Please tell us about your organization and why you chose to get involved with the Digital Sparks project.

Dhorjela Cule (DC): Qendra KAZUS was founded in 2024 and focuses on young people’s activism and engagement. Our team brings together journalists, photojournalists, and education specialists with years of experience in media, law, and mentoring.

Our mission is to strengthen democracy and the rule of law through youth advocacy and to raise awareness around preserving cultural heritage, protecting the environment, and building capacity in ICT and media. As a young organization, our work relied mainly on small activities and projects.

Digital Sparks gave us the opportunity to prioritize digital advocacy. We saw a chance to give young people in rural areas and cities tools they use every day — their phones and social media — and turn them into instruments of civic participation and accountability.
GV: What issue/challenge in your community prompted you to undertake this project?

DC: The Devoll River in the eastern Korça region is facing a serious environmental situation. Plastic pollution, inert waste, agricultural waste, and other debris accumulate along the riverbanks. During winter floods, high river flows expose and spread this waste, blocking drainage canals, and water overflows from the riverbed into agricultural land and residential areas, damaging soil health, livelihoods, and the local ecosystem.
In the villages of Lozhan and Pojan, the waste is considerable, and local authorities seem to have their hands tied in finding a solution.

What worried us most was that young people from rural areas, whose families depend on agriculture and are directly affected, were excluded from the search for solutions. They had phones and strong opinions, but no channel to turn them into public pressure.
We wanted to show that the right to a clean environment is something young people can demand with evidence and a collective voice.
Waste on the banks of the Devoll River in Pojan from May 2026. Photo by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.
GV: What are the key changes/activities that your organization implemented during your participation in the project?

DC: We implemented three phases of the project. First, we recruited and trained 44 young people from Maliq municipality in MoJo, aiming to turn mobile storytelling, video editing for reels, and graphic design in Canva into a powerful advocacy tool.

Second, we organized two Digital Picnics along the Devoll River and the affected farmland, piloting two locations in the villages of Pojan and Lozhan, where participants filmed and photographed the accumulation of waste, creating a “visual pollution map”. Thirty materials produced by the young people were published on social media to raise public awareness.

Finally, we launched an online petition, through which we will ask the Maliq municipality to step up cleaning actions, with the joint commitment of the municipality and the community, as well as community education and awareness.
The petition was hosted on Change.org to reach a wider audience and has collected 506 signatures so far, exceeding our target.
Participants of the DigiAction Picnic in Pojan, Albania. Photo by Qendra KAZUS. Used with permission.
GV: How did your participation in the project impact your organization’s beneficiaries and the community that you serve? Please provide examples.

DC: For the young participants, the project turned social media from an entertainment tool into a tool for action. Forty-four young people learned to document environmental problems and communicate them publicly.

“I had never seen the use of social media from this perspective. Now, I have a different approach to the posts I can make,” said Igli, one of the young people who joined the training and field activity.

For the community, the Digital Picnics made the pollution visible: everyone had the chance to see the waste accumulated along the river in videos and posts, and hundreds of people engaged with our content online.

The petition gave residents and supporters a simple way to take a stand, and 506 people signed it online. The materials now form a public archive of evidence that the community can use in future discussions with local authorities.
GV: How has your own knowledge, awareness, and experience with digital democracy and civic space changed, thanks to your participation in the project?
DC: Through Digital Sparks, we came to understand digital democracy more broadly: using technology to document facts, mobilize people, and demand accountability from institutions.
We learned how evidence, whether a video, a poster, or a signature, gives citizens credibility when they address public authorities.

We also gained practical experience in campaign planning, content strategy, moderating online comments, using Instagram and TikTok analytics, and digital safety and ethics, including the protection of young participants and personal data.
As a team, this project taught us how to turn this knowledge into youth-led digital civic action.
GV: What are the most valuable lessons and experiences you are taking away from this project?

DC: One of the most valuable lessons is that in the digital era, young people need little technical equipment, but much more mentoring and guidance to lead them towards becoming responsible citizens who make demands and engage in concrete action to be part of decision-making. Their phones and creativity are enough when they have a clear purpose and guidance.
Second, an informal and enjoyable format like the Digital Picnic lowers barriers to participation and attracts young people, including girls and those from marginalized groups or low-income families.

Images and facts are more persuasive to institutions than complaints, but this experience taught us that flexibility is essential. Choosing Change.org instead of Google Forms for the petition taught us to adapt tools to the audience.
Finally, institutional change and engagement take time, and follow-up is as important as mobilization.
GV: What comes next? How will you apply the learning and digital capacity you have built in your future work and within your community?

DC: Qendra KAZUS has started implementing another project in which part of the knowledge gained is being applied. The use of social media by young people as a powerful mechanism to raise their voice and demand more engagement and responsibility from institutions is this time focused on cultural heritage.

What remains essential for us is identifying a completely different approach to young people, through the channels and platforms where they spend a considerable part of their time and focus their communication.

It is worth stressing that finding a meeting point with young people, through a method that is interesting to them, is of particular importance. We have managed to involve them by showing that social media can also be used as a healthy mechanism that achieves results for their demands.

d53f11c65001743d: JOHOR BAHRU, Oct 29 — The Johor Department of Environment (DOE) is investigating allegations that Sungai Kim Kim in Pasir Gudang has become polluted again, turning white yesterday.
Johor DOE director Dr Mohd Famey Yusoff said enforcement officers inspected the site at about 6pm following a complaint about the incident.
However, he said preliminary inspections yesterday found that the river water had returned to normal and was no longer visibly white.
Mohd Famey said preliminary investigations suggested that the incident could have been caused by a one-off waste discharge into the river.
“Nevertheless, the DOE, together with the Pasir Gudang City Council (MBPG), will examine closed-circuit television (CCTV) footage in the vicinity of the suspected dumping site,” he told Bernama.
Mohd Famey said the CCTV footage would be examined to identify the source of the pollution and those responsible.
He said strict legal action would be taken against any party or individual found to be involved in the waste dumping incident.
Yesterday, a social media post went viral alleging that Sungai Kim Kim had been polluted again, accompanied by several photographs showing the river water turning white.
The chemical pollution incident at Sungai Kim Kim in March 2019 shocked the nation, affecting more than 2,000 people and resulting in the closure of 111 schools in Pasir Gudang.

Meanwhile, State Health and Environment Committee chairman Ling Tian Soon said that the pollution was believed to have been caused by excavation work to a depth of about five metres for cable installation.
He said the information was based on further investigations conducted by the DOE today.
“The cable installation work was carried out yesterday at about 3pm,” he said in a Facebook post today.

Ling said the state government understood the public’s concerns and stressed that it took all reports involving environmental quality seriously, adding that it would ensure the relevant agencies carried out appropriate monitoring and follow-up action.

4414299774d10e7f: United Launch Alliance (ULA) has set a target date for its return to flight: Friday, November 13, for a Vulcan launch.

The mission will send 40 Amazon Leo satellites into orbit. A pair of BE-4 engines will power the booster, along with six Solid Rocket Boosters (SRBs). A Centaur V second stage, propelled by two RL10C-1 engines, will complete the journey to orbit and deploy the payload.

The launch is the first Vulcan launch for Amazon after eight deployments with ULA's Atlas V. It is also the first since the launch earlier this year for the US Space Force in which an SRB burned through its nozzle during the ascent, treating viewers to some impressive fireworks and controllers to some likely clenched sphincters thanks to a "significant performance anomaly."

In the event, the US Space Force payload successfully reached orbit, but the Vulcan was stood down while ULA conducted an investigation. This wasn't the first time a Vulcan had had issues with its SRBs. A nozzle was shed during the second launch of the rocket in 2024. Things went OK with the third launch. But another problem on the fourth trek to orbit meant a stand-down was unavoidable.

The workhorse Atlas V has continued deploying Amazon Leo satellites during the Vulcan's hiatus. Another 29 were added on a July 2 launch from Space Launch Complex-41 at the Cape Canaveral Space Force station. However, Amazon booked 38 Vulcan rocket launches – quite an increase from the eight Atlas V launches ULA has already performed for Leo. It is obviously keen to add more satellites to its growing constellation.

The SRBs are Northrop Grumman units, and the six Graphite Epoxy Motor (GEM) 63XL units will each provide an additional 459,600 lbs (2,044 kN) of thrust at liftoff. That's assuming nothing unexpected burns through or falls off. ULA has not detailed the results of its investigation or any changes it had to make.

ULA said: "The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the solid rocket booster (SRB) anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle. To support our customers, this upcoming launch will utilize the improved nozzle design, and additional testing and analysis will continue in parallel with the mission. By flying the improved design, ULA gains valuable flight data that validates these improvements and is the most beneficial path in support of all our customers."
US Space Force and Amazon are ULA's biggest customers - and Space Force will be watching. ULA came second to SpaceX in contracts awarded by Space Force for FY25 to FY29. ®

cfa660a4eeb9d23a: RAJSHAHI (Bangladesh), Oct 29 — In Bangladesh’s parched Barind region, 72-year-old Bikash Soren remembers when the Ganges river flowing in from neighbouring India carried large boats past his village year-round.

But the South Asian country is now blighted by persistent water shortages — and the expiration of a long-term water-sharing deal with Delhi in just a few weeks’ time threatens tens of millions of livelihoods.
“For almost three months a year, you hardly see the river flowing,” the Protestant priest said.
Two farmers killed themselves last season, he added, after dwindling water levels left their rice and wheat crops in tatters.
Shrinking flows in the Ganges have also slashed fish catches in the river, known in Bangladesh as the Padma.
“Where will we find fish now?” said Abu Bakar Siddique, 55, who has switched to fish farming in ponds.
“I used to catch many kinds.”
The 2,525-kilometre Ganges flows through the world’s most populous river basin, home to 655 million people including more than 50 million in Bangladesh, according to the World Bank.
The 1996 treaty, which expires on December 12, governs dry-season water sharing at India’s Farakka Barrage, 20 kilometres upstream of Bangladesh.
But Bangladesh needs a new deal based on “mutual benefit and respect”, Rashed Al Mahmud Titumir, a prime ministerial adviser who heads a technical committee on water-sharing, told AFP.
Water arguments over 54 cross-border rivers between India and Bangladesh stretch back decades, and the Ganges is among the most important.
Malik Fida A. Khan, a former Bangladeshi member of the Joint Rivers Commission (JRC), the body overseeing water-sharing, said India had built “additional dams” upstream.
“This time, the agreement must include provisions on climate change — and take the entire river basin into account,” he said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This aerial photograph taken on October 13, 2026 shows a water intake tower built close to a dam along the Padma river at Ujirpur, near the Bangladesh-India frontier in Bangladesh’s Rajshahi division. Bangladesh said India had not responded to its request to negotiate a treaty renewal. — AFP pic
Soured relations
Bangladesh said India had not responded to its request to negotiate a treaty renewal.
New Delhi’s foreign ministry said that “discussions regarding river-related matters” are a matter for the JRC commission, which held its last technical talks back in May.
The last officially confirmed ministerial-level JRC meeting was in 2022 — after a 12-year gap.
And a proposed water-sharing deal for the cross-border Teesta river has been stalled since 2011.
Relations between New Delhi and Dhaka have soured since Bangladesh’s ex-leader Sheikh Hasina fled to old ally India, where she remains, following a 2024 uprising.
Hasina, sentenced to death in absentia for crimes against humanity, has vowed to return to Bangladesh from India in December, the month the treaty she signed expires.
Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman may also reportedly visit India before the treaty expires, but no visit has been confirmed.
Arguments over water-sharing date back to 1975, when India opened the 2.2-kilometre Farakka Barrage — which Bangladesh accuses Delhi of using to divert most of the water.
The United Nations intervened in the dispute and a deal was agreed in 1977.
But water-sharing arrangements lapsed a decade later, bringing severe consequences, said Sheikh Rokon of Dhaka-based environmental group Riverine People.
“The Ganges suffered during the years without a treaty, and at least three rivers almost dried up,” Rokon said.
One was the Gorai, which carries freshwater into the Sundarbans, the world’s largest mangrove forest and a World Heritage site, helping limit saltwater intrusion as sea levels rise.
Bangladesh’s Ganges-Kobadak Irrigation Project, designed to water a vast area of farmland bigger than the size of Berlin, “became inoperative because of water scarcity”, Rokon said.
In May, Dhaka approved the Padma Barrage, a US$2.8-billion (RM11.3 billion) project intended to ease shortages and include a 113-megawatt hydropower plant.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

This aerial photograph taken on October 12, 2026 shows a settlement of climate-displaced people following the erosion of Padma river at Namo Jagannathpur village, near the Bangladesh-India frontier in Bangladesh’s Rajshahi division. — AFP pic
‘Disastrous’
The 1996 treaty has no automatic extension clause.
“If we fail to reach a deal, I fear the situation will be worse than what we experienced during the years without a treaty,” Rokon added.
“Demand for freshwater on both sides has increased significantly.”
Even with the treaty in place, the Ganges-Kobadak project has shrunk to 550 square kilometres, according to Bangladeshi state news agency BSS.
“If the river does not carry enough water, the consequences could be disastrous,” said Chowdhury Sarwar Jahan, a geology professor at Bangladesh’s University of Rajshahi.

Bangladesh’s agriculture-dependent economy is already reeling from the impact of climate change, which compounds shifting river flows, alternating dry-season shortages and intense monsoon floods washing away farmland and villages.
In Chapainawabganj district, the river has widened by three kilometres in recent years — nearly doubling its size — according to Bangladesh’s Water Development Board.
Rehana Khatun, 50, described the “howling sound” as floods destroyed her home in Fielder Bazar village.
“The river turned wild and started swallowing everything along the bank,” said Khatun, who now lives in a bamboo shelter.
“And the trauma stays with children long after the waters recede.” — AFP
384eda121c3c7730: PARIS, Oct 29 — Airbnb said yesterday it will begin donating a dime for each reservation made on its platform to finance its nonprofit that helps house people in crisis.

The short-term tourism rental platform, which is regularly criticised for reducing housing available for local residents, expects it will thus be able to provide US$500 million (RM2 billion) to Airbnb.org over the next five years.

“It will vastly expand our ability to help people because it’ll bring in a lot more resources to the organisation” which has been financed from donations from Airbnb and its own fundraising, Airbnb.org’s executive director Christoph Gorder told AFP.
The inspiration for the nonprofit came from Airbnb hosts welcoming people displaced by Hurricane Sandy, which lashed the east coast of the United States in 2012.
The movement developed informally and then Airbnb.org was launched in 2020.

7e2c36f7c6650f71: KHAN YUNIS, Oct 29 — In war-ravaged Gaza and the occupied West Bank, many Palestinians were less focused on who would win Israel’s election than on whether anything would really change.
Whether Benjamin Netanyahu clings to power with his far-right allies or centrist rival Gadi Eisenkot comes out on top, few see much reason for hope in the Tuesday vote.
“We fear these elections could bring an even worse leader,” said Huda al-Houli, a displaced resident of Khan Yunis in southern Gaza.
Such an outcome, she said, would only bring “more destruction and devastation” to the Palestinian territory.
Still, Houli said she hoped a more “human voice” would emerge in Israeli society and demand an end to the conflict, regardless of who forms the next government.
In Ramallah, in the West Bank, Ahmed Awad, 67, was equally sceptical.
“Whatever the result, and even if the politicians change, I don’t think there will be any radical or dramatic shift in policies towards the Palestinian-Israeli conflict,” he told AFP.
With 85 per cent of ballots counted from Tuesday’s vote, Netanyahu’s camp remained ahead but without a clear majority, leaving uncertainty over Israel’s next government.
The first election since Hamas’s October 7, 2023 attack comes after years of right-wing and far-right rule marked by the war in Gaza and rising settler violence in the West Bank.
For Netanyahu, fighting for his political survival, several paths remain open: renewing his alliance with the far right, building a broader coalition or facing yet another political deadlock.
Far-right minister Itamar Ben Gvir has already signalled that, if the current coalition survives, he would seek the defence portfolio and push for the expulsion of Gaza’s population.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
People wait to receive meals at a charity kitchen in the Jabalia camp for Palestinian refugees in the northern Gaza Strip on October 24, 2026.
More of the same
Not everyone has given up hope.
“Whatever happens, it will surely be better than what we’ve lived through in recent years,” said Abdallah Abu Rahma, 54, from Ramallah.
But if Netanyahu remains in office, he added, “any coalition he forms, he will continue down the same path”.
A government led by Eisenkot, a former army chief, could rein in the influence of the pro-settlement far right, said researcher Beth Oppenheim of the European Council on Foreign Relations.
It could also ease pressure on the Palestinian Authority and take a more flexible approach on aid and a ceasefire in Gaza.
But she warned against expecting too much.

There would be “nothing transformative”, she said, and certainly no major shift on Palestinian statehood or the peace process, issues that have largely disappeared from Israeli political debate since October 7.
A renewed Netanyahu coalition with far-right partners would likely mean more of the same, including settlement expansion and impunity for settler violence, Oppenheim added.
“I think we need to have quite low expectations when it comes to seeing any major changes in policy from a different government,” she said.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->

Mourners grieve over the bodies of three Palestinians during their funeral at Al Shifa Hospital in Gaza City on October 25, 2026, after they were killed in an Israeli strike on the Islamic University building.
Fears of escalation
Even a Netanyahu defeat could leave Palestinians worse off in the short term, argued Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine-Israel programme at the Arab Center Washington.
“There is every reason for Palestinians to be concerned,” he said.
Eisenkot himself served in Israel’s wartime cabinet during the Gaza offensive, Munayyer noted.
A fragile alternative coalition under constant attack from Netanyahu and the right could try to prove it was tough enough by taking a harder line on Palestinian issues.
In the West Bank, violence could rise if the far right loses power, with settlers potentially acting out against a new government, he explained.
“It’s important to understand that most settler violence in the West Bank is structural. It’s not about the government in charge,” Munayyer said.
“Settlers live in places that surround the Palestinian population. The Palestinian population is vulnerable to the settlers, who are armed, whereas the Palestinians overwhelmingly are not.”
In Gaza, Adnan Al-Assar said he harboured few illusions.
“Netanyahu may win,” he said. “But whatever happens, they all follow the same overarching policy, directed against the Palestinian people.” — AFP
392fadfc78a2877d: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — At a time when Chinese food and beverage brands such as Mixue, Chagee and Haidilao are expanding their presence in Malaysia, one homegrown seafood noodle chain is reportedly heading in the opposite direction.
Hai Kah Lang, a Malaysian restaurant chain with roots in traditional Chinese cuisine, is reportedly expanding into China, with plans for an outlet at The Mixc shopping complex in Hangzhou.
The move would see a Malaysian brand with Chinese culinary roots enter a market where such dishes are already familiar, reversing the more common trend of Chinese F&B chains expanding into Malaysia.

The expansion was featured in an October 27 Instagram post by Malaysian food and lifestyle platform KL Foodie, following earlier posts by Hangzhou locals on Chinese social media platform Xiaohongshu, also known as RedNote, who shared pictures of banners announcing Hai Kah Lang’s arrival in the city.

The planned Hangzhou outlet would mark the brand’s entry into its second overseas market, following the opening of its first international branch at Singapore’s Funan shopping centre in September 2025.
The move comes less than five years after Hai Kah Lang opened its first restaurant in Taman Cheras, Kuala Lumpur, in January 2022.
Founded by Steven Tan, the restaurant began as a new venture after the Covid-19 pandemic forced him to close a seafood steamboat restaurant he had operated in Balakong for seven years.
In a 2024 interview with the Michelin Guide, Tan said he subsequently opened a seafood retail business before deciding to take over a nearby breakfast noodle shop that was closing.
The restaurant’s popularity grew through word of mouth, and its Taman Cheras outlet received a Bib Gourmand distinction in the inaugural Michelin Guide Kuala Lumpur and Penang in 2023.
It has retained the recognition in subsequent editions, including the 2026 guide.
The Bib Gourmand distinction recognises restaurants offering good-quality food at reasonable prices.
Hai Kah Lang’s menu centres on fresh seafood noodles, allowing diners to choose from fish, shellfish and other seafood, alongside eight types of noodles and five soup bases.
In the same Michelin Guide interview, Tan said nearly 99 per cent of the seafood used at the restaurant was wild-caught and brought in daily from Sabah, Indonesia and the Philippines.
The business also draws on Tan’s family heritage as Teochews, whose ancestral roots lie in the Chaoshan region of China’s Guangdong province.
The opening date and other details of the planned outlet at The Mixc in Hangzhou have yet to be announced.

814a544925affa0c: The UK’s comms watchdog has put forward four methods of checking netizens aren't kids – dubbed highly effective age assurance (HEAA) – as it prepares for the proposed under-16 social media ban.

The regulator says some adults may not need to prove their over-16-ness to social media platforms that will make inferences about their age based on previous activity, but confirmed that "many" are likely to have to undergo the same verification process.

Big Brother Watch's (BBW) Director Silkie Carlo said: "This plan for a government 'social media ban' is a national ID system by the back door. Both the government and Ofcom have admitted that children will get around the ban, which means the real effect will be normalizing adults and children alike to handing over their passports just to get online."
Ofcom says four methods remain from the seven it initially outlined when the Online Safety Act (OSA) came into force last year.
The seven were capable of verifying whether a subject was 18 years old, but there are fewer viable options for determining the age of 16-year-olds, it said today.
The methods put forward include:
Photo-ID matching: Checking information displayed on identity documents and analyzing the photo against a live image of the subject taken during the verification process

Banking checks: An estimated 90 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a bank account, which they would have provided their identity documents to open. The information processed by the bank can be used to verify whether someone is aged 16 or older

Digital ID services: An interesting entry, given how quickly these were circumvented once the OSA age-checking requirements came into force. These third-party services analyze a person’s photo once, and if it matches the age they claim to be, let them verify their age across other services

Facial age estimation: A method that even Ofcom admitted isn’t quite reliable enough to be used on its own. The regulator said that online services can use technologies to analyze a subject’s facial features to determine their age. The same technologies also have a margin of error of a few years, so online services may wish to use a second method of HEAA to verify the results of this check.

The three reserved for those aged 18 and above include credit card checks (only adults can have a credit card), mobile network checks (MNOs require proof of adulthood to remove content blocks), and email checks – using a subject’s email address to make educated guesses about their age based on the other types of services with which it is registered.
Ofcom acknowledged that not every 16-year-old will have a form of photo ID, which is required for all four of its HEAA methods, so they will need to acquire one in order to access online services.

It estimates that around 94 percent of 16-17-year-olds in the UK have a form of photo ID, such as a passport, driving licence, or an ID card certified by the Proof of Age Standards Scheme, and that around 150,000 have neither.

BBW's Carlo added: "Hundreds of thousands of people without ID, who tend to be poorer people, and many more who don’t want to risk handing their passports over to foreign tech companies will be locked out of huge parts of the internet.

"The plan will kill anonymity online, whilst the UK’s culture of speech policing is reaching a crisis point. The policy is painfully misguided, an Orwellian assault on free speech and privacy, and will make children no safer at all."
'Circumvention inevitable'
Ofcom admitted that "the risk of circumvention cannot be entirely eliminated," as some children will find ways to bypass these age checks, no matter how fully they are implemented.

It cited Australia sporadically in its announcement, a country that introduced an under-16 social media ban in December 2025, but has struggled with a large proportion of children devising ways to circumvent these checks.
Ofcom said the UK government intends to adopt, but learn lessons from, Australia’s rollout, committing to implementing more robust measures that promote the ban’s aims.

It said it has identified some mitigations that could be taken to counter circumvention, such as making it easier for users to report suspected underage social media users, and “using age inference models.”
The regulator said it will closely monitor circumvention for the first 12 months after the ban is enforced to understand possible methods to prevent children from finding ways around the age checks.

In May, nearly a year after the OSA’s age verification requirements kicked in, researchers found that the existing age checks proved largely ineffective at keeping under-18s away from adult content online.
Some reported beating age checks with just a drawn-on moustache.
England's Children's Commissioner, Dame Rachel de Souza, said recently that the OSA "has made absolutely no difference" to children’s ability to access potentially harmful online content.
Commenting on today’s announcement, Ofcom chief exec Dame Melanie Dawes said that when the social media ban takes effect, it will take a whole-of-society approach to ensure the ban is upheld.

?This ban will shape the future of children’s lives online, so it’s important to get it right," she said. "It can work if social media firms do highly effective age checks properly, and we’ve set out ways that could be achieved. When it comes into force next year, we’ll be ready to take swift and firm action against any company that fails to comply.

"We should expect that motivated children will seek to bypass the restrictions – just like alcohol laws can’t completely eradicate underage drinking – but there’ll be ways for platforms to mitigate this risk. This will be a huge cultural shift for our society, so it’ll take time to adjust, and everyone will have a part to play."

The UK government is expected to outline the first set of regulations related to the under-16 social media ban by the end of the year, and Ofcom is in the process of developing draft guidance for platforms. ®
e5d6004b39bc62dd: Some local papers that were on the verge of extinction, like the Solon Economist in Iowa, have teamed up with universities as a way to get staffing and support. Photo from Teri Finneman, CC BYCatherine Bilskie, the advertising and office manager for the newspaper in Solon, Iowa, had seen many local news outlets close. So she was sure her job at the Solon Economist was about to go one Friday morning in February 2024. But to her surprise, a new owner, Jason Brummond, appeared. He not only promised to keep her and her co-worker employed at the weekly paper but assured them raises if they agreed to an unusual new venture. And he wasn’t a wealthy benefactor or a representative from a private equity firm – he came from the University of Iowa. It’s just one example of academic institutions stepping up to address the “news desert” crisis: Thousands of communities across the U.S. have lost local newspapers over the past two decades. And journalism faculty, staff and students are increasingly working together to either rescue legacy newspapers or start new publications for communities lacking local news outlets. These partnerships have ranged from the Spanish-language news site Noticiero Móvil at the University of Nevada, Reno, to “Good Morning Indian Country” at the University of Kansas, to The Scope at Northeastern in Boston. We’re journalism professors who have studied and experienced the opportunities and challenges of running community news through higher education. Our new book, “News Desert U,” asks whether this approach is one solution to saving local news. We believe the need is urgent given the stakes and the scope of the crisis. Knowing your community These experiments come against a grim backdrop. Over 3,000 newspapers have closed in the U.S. in the past 20 years, including about 170 in 2025, according to Northwestern’s 2026 State of Local News report. Causes include an antiquated business model, declining advertising revenue and hedge-fund buyouts that have gutted papers. Northwestern’s 2025 report estimated that total print newspaper circulation has declined 70% in the past 20 years. But university partnerships can show promise, we found, with the help of the next generation of journalists. How the University of Iowa stepped in to save the Solon Economist. Iowa’s Solon Economist is one example. The University of Iowa doesn’t actually own the paper, or its sister paper, the Mount Vernon-Lisbon Sun. Still, the relationship is key to making the new venture work. Its owner, Brummond, is also the publisher of the University of Iowa’s student newspaper, the Daily Iowan, which is owned and operated by the nonprofit Student Publications. While the student newspaper office is inside the journalism school’s building, it operates independently. In August 2023, Student Publications began talks about buying the Sun and the Economist after the weeklies’ then owner reached out about selling the publications. With both newspapers 20-30 minutes from campus, discussions included how the faculty and students could help the papers. The Journalism School’s director, Melissa Tully, was immediately in favor – provided that the newspapers’ existing professional staff stay and not be replaced with students. In addition to the editors, this included keeping the advertising and circulation staff. “They know these communities. So that was really important just from a moral and ethical imperative, but also from a news perspective,” she said. “They’re trusted in their communities. They know what’s going on.” Student Publications bought both newspapers for US$10,000 in 2024. Since then, circulation has remained stable at both, Brummond said, even as many other publications across the country have suffered declines. Meanwhile, students in classes such as community news, high school sports, social media marketing and photography contribute for academic credit while other students do paid internships. Solon Economist Editor Chris Umscheid said he welcomes a revolving door of student interns because it means he’s “actually going to have staff for once.” “People thought we were going to be the university’s paper, and we’re not,” he said. “I don’t anticipate anything changing there. We’re still going to focus on everything Solon that we can.” Chris Umscheid, editor of the Solon Economist, says the paper’s mission remains serving the community by reporting local news, but now with more staff. Teri Finneman, CC BY The success has led to Student Publications getting requests to buy other newspapers, Tully said, and it’s working on a list of criteria to consider future partnerships. Brummond cautions these arrangements aren’t easy to pull off, as they require a careful review of finances, workflow and logistical complications that come with a merger. Liz King, who served as Solon Public Library director, said many locals were afraid the newspaper would close, which would have been a hard blow for the town of about 3,000. Some readers only get their news through the newspaper, she said. “They’re not comfortable with online sources.” A $10 deal Dink NeSmith had a similar close scare in Georgia with the The Oglethorpe Echo. Owner Ralph Maxwell had decided in September 2021 that he had no choice but to shutter the paper due to his own health issues, revenue declines and lack of interest from prospective buyers. He gave NeSmith, an old friend and retired newspaper owner, an early heads-up. How the Oglethorpe Echo found a new owner. “I don’t know that I want to live in a town that doesn’t have its newspaper,” was NeSmith’s response. He told Maxwell: “You can’t close the Echo.” NeSmith immediately reached out to the University of Georgia’s journalism school to suggest a partnership. In the meantime, NeSmith worked to set up a separate nonprofit, Oglethorpe Echo Legacy, for the paper’s new ownership structure. Keeping the newspaper’s finances independent of the university was an important step to ensure the paper would not be subject to any possible “whims” of future administrations, as Charles Davis, the journalism school’s dean, put it. That status was also a signal to Oglethorpe County that the paper’s goal was to serve the community, not make money, he added. The new nonprofit bought the paper from Maxwell in October 2021 for $10 – a check that Maxwell never cashed and has since been framed. Davis asked Andy Johnston, an adjunct professor with decades of journalism experience, to serve as the newspaper’s full-time editor. Since November 2021, Johnston has led a team of journalism faculty and students, with the help of several adult staff and volunteers from the county. The paper covers a wide terrain. Oglethorpe County has over 16,000 people stretching over 442 square miles, and Lexington, where the Echo has its office, is 18 miles (29 kilometers) from the campus in Athens. The reporting staff is provided by journalism professor Amanda Bright’s capstone class – 20 students each semester. Supplementary funding comes from the journalism school, various grants and Echo subscription and advertising funds. She pairs two students to each beat, with one in charge of a story and the other in charge of editing and producing, with a rotation each week. Students need to turn in eight stories a semester – with corresponding editing and producing assignments that include video, an email newsletter and social media – to get class credit. When the journalism school took over, the weekly had only a printed newspaper, with no website, social media presence or other digital products, she said. So in their first print edition, the editors outlined their plan for the newspaper to readers and then introduced the student reporters, which they still do every semester. Amanda Bright’s journalism students at The University of Georgia rotate across different roles to develop writing, editing and multimedia skills. Teri Finneman, CC BY The partnership has paid off. Print subscriptions to The Echo have doubled and overall digital audience has quadrupled thanks to the launch of new digital products, Bright said. Advertising revenue, meanwhile, has tripled, she said. However, it took some time for local businesses to get used to advertising again, NeSmith said. But many challenges remain. Johnston has to handle student turnover every semester while students covering events such as government meetings face a steep learning curve and need support. The additional time it takes to edit student copy means content doesn’t appear as quickly. Many faculty members have to work long hours to keep the paper afloat. But the broader impact is clear: More than two dozen students have gone into local news as a career following their time at the Echo, Bright said. Should other universities want to follow this model, they need at least two key people in leadership, whether that’s two faculty members or one from faculty and a professional editor, Bright said. “That’s a bottom-line necessity for sanity,” she added. Service over profits One common theme from our research is that a service-oriented approach to news that addresses the community’s needs takes priority over profit at these partnerships. The built-in advantages for these initiatives is that the faculty and staff who tend to manage them get their paychecks and health insurance from their university work. They don’t need to draw a living wage from the news outlet’s finances. These partnerships are also ideal for students seeking real-world experience while earning class credit or internship wages. And journalism schools are already stocked with multimedia equipment that students can use for their reporting. Still, they can look deceptively simple on the surface, Brummond said. Tully, at the University of Iowa, recommends other interested universities should go slowly. Building a successful project takes patient experimentation and a willingness to regroup when needed, in her view. “Doing this slowly is OK,” she said. “In the end, it’s going to be better. So far, that’s been a good recipe for us.” Teri Finneman and Pamela Walck are co-authors of the book "News Desert U." Pamela E. Walck does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
76b1fc93db730851: A frequent complaint about the U.S. healthcare system is that predicting how much your care will cost is notoriously difficult. The Good Brigade/DigitalVision via Getty ImagesImagine you get hit by a car. An ambulance brings you to the nearest hospital. Your private health insurance covers emergency care, but the hospital isn’t in your plan’s network. Before 2022, if you received emergency care from an out-of-network provider or hospital, you could get hit with an extra, often huge bill on top of what you owe as a copay, coinsurance or deductible. A law called the No Surprises Act, which took effect in 2022, was designed to protect people with private health insurance from just these situations. It limits your costs to what you would have paid if the ambulance had brought you to an in-network hospital or you were treated by an in-network provider instead. As a health policy researcher and a former federal employee who helped draft the rules to implement the No Surprises Act, I applaud the law’s success in preventing patients from being hit with surprise medical bills in most cases. However, a small number of out-of-network providers are using the law to extract enormous payments from health plans. This behavior is starting to drive up the cost of coverage for both employers and individuals. In my view, if left unaddressed, these increases will only get steeper. Medical bill concerns The No Surprises Act was designed to address a troublesome feature of the U.S. healthcare system: It is notoriously difficult to predict how much your healthcare will cost. This is especially true when someone receives out-of-network care. Before the law went into effect, roughly 20% of inpatient emergency department visits resulted in a surprise bill from an out-of-network provider. Surprise bills are common for other types of care too. One study found roughly 40% of air ambulance rides resulted in a surprise bill, costing an average of almost US$20,000. The threat of these bills exacted an enormous emotional and financial toll. Roughly two-thirds of Americans reported being very or somewhat worried about unexpected medical bills, according to a 2020 poll conducted by KFF, a national health policy nonprofit. In some situations, you really can’t check whether your doctor is in-network. Security from surprises The No Surprises Act protects Americans from certain instances of a practice called balance billing, in which an out-of-network hospital or doctor asks you to pay the difference between what they billed for a service and what your insurance agreed to pay for it. When a provider joins your plan’s network, they agree to accept a specific payment for a given service or procedure. They agree to charge you only for cost sharing, such as a copayment, coinsurance or deductible, and they aren’t allowed to balance bill you. However, plans can’t prevent out-of-network providers or facilities from balance billing. On top of that, your own plan may also charge you a higher copayment, coinsurance or deductible when you go out of network. That’s why out-of-network care can be much more expensive than in-network care. The No Surprises Act protects consumers from these extra costs in cases where they have little or no control over whether they see an in- or out-of-network doctor. The law prohibits balance billing and requires cost sharing to be at approximately in-network levels in three cases where surprise medical bills were common: If you receive out-of-network emergency care at a hospital or independent freestanding emergency facility. In a medical emergency, you’re not expected to figure out whether the closest hospital is in-network. You can’t be balance billed. If an out-of-network provider treats you during a visit to an in-network hospital or ambulatory surgical center. For example, if an out-of-network anesthesiologist cares for you during a surgery at an in-network hospital, that anesthesiologist cannot balance bill you. If you receive out-of-network air ambulance services. The No Surprises Act doesn’t prevent big, unexpected medical bills in all cases. For example, you can still get balance billed for ground ambulance services or if you see an out-of-network doctor outside of a hospital or ambulatory surgical center. Providers win big The No Surprises Act is working as promised for patients – as of September 2026, it has prevented approximately 50 million surprise medical bills. But there’s a downside: Employers and unions are raising the alarm that the No Surprises Act is increasing the cost of providing health insurance. What’s driving up costs is an arbitration process run amok. Rather than specifying how much insurance plans should pay out-of-network providers, the law allows providers who are dissatisfied with the plan’s payment to bring disputes to arbitration. Each side submits an offer. The arbitrator must select one party’s offer as the out-of-network payment. To choose an offer, the arbitrator considers information submitted by both parties. Information can vary by case. But the law requires the arbitrator to always consider an amount that is basically the middle amount the health plan pays in-network providers for the same service. Health policy experts like me anticipated most disputes would be settled close to this amount. Over time, experts expected this would put downward pressure on the cost of healthcare and result in payments to both in- and out-of-network providers going down. The Congressional Budget Office predicted these lower payments would reduce premiums for consumers by 1% and reduce federal deficits by $17 billion. If insurers are charged big bucks by out-of-network providers, they will likely pass on the cost to consumers in the form of higher premiums. krisanapong detraphiphat/Moment via Getty Images As a federal employee, I worked on rules that would have required the arbitrators to treat the middle amount as a strong benchmark. I expected those rules to achieve savings like those predicted by the Congressional Budget Office. But lawsuits from providers blocked those rules from going into effect. Without those rules, arbitrators are selecting offers that are far above what plans would pay in-network. The winning offers are also much larger than what Medicare would pay for the same service. Providers are winning the vast majority – roughly 85% – of these disputes. They are also using arbitration more than expected. The federal government estimated there would be 17,000 disputes annually. Last year, there were more than 2 million disputes, many brought by providers with private equity investment. And the volume of disputes has grown every year. Frequent and big provider wins at arbitration will not put downward pressure on healthcare prices. They will likely do the opposite. Consumers bear the cost When a provider wins an arbitration dispute, an individual patient’s cost sharing doesn’t change. It is capped at what the in-network amount would have been. However, consumers as a group are the ones who ultimately will pay for the cost of arbitration. Researchers estimate the arbitration process alone cost health plans $22.4 billion in the law’s first four years. This doesn’t include the increases in in-network rates that are likely to occur if arbitration trends continue on pace. I’m concerned that to pay for this, insurance companies will increase rates. Employers will need to budget more to pay for health insurance or increase the amount their employees pay. We’re already seeing the costs of arbitration affect the price of health insurance. The New York state employee plan reported that the No Surprises Act was a key driver behind the plan’s 10% rate hike for 2027. A Texas city reported the No Surprises Act caused its employee plan to exceed its 2026 budget by $40 million. Right now, only a small portion of providers use arbitration. If volume continues to grow and providers continue to win big, the cost of arbitration will grow as well – and so too will costs for consumers. Looking forward With healthcare costs a huge concern for Americans and a major issue in the 2026 midterm elections, the No Surprises Act is under scrutiny. Congress appears interested in addressing this threat to affordability. In September 2026, the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee hosted a roundtable to discuss options to fix the law. In October, U.S. Rep. Frank Pallone, a New Jersey Democrat, introduced legislation to scuttle the arbitration system entirely. Absent action by Congress, I fear that the protection the No Surprises Act offers Americans will come at a cost that ultimately limits consumers’ access to health insurance. Lindsey Murtagh receives funding from Arnold Ventures

28d1a96b6b9d8fe1: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.
Opinion: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
—Madhulika Srikumar and Claire Leibowicz from the Partnership on AI, a nonprofit advancing best practices in AI governance.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, from hacking websites to accessing private government files. In many cases, they’ve eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability.
​​In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. Because right now, we’re effectively flying blind when deploying these tools.
Here’s what needs to change.
Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot

Climate change itself increasingly fuels climate change. Rising greenhouse gas concentrations are driving up global temperatures, creating dangerous feedback loops that aren’t fully represented in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming. Now, a growing number of observations and studies are indicating how powerful these cascading effects could be. By extension, they’re also showing how much faster the planet may warm this century.
—James Temple
This article is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
Are we there yet? Solid-state batteries

Lithium-ion batteries power everything from personal electronics to grid-scale energy storage, but their liquid electrolytes have drawbacks, not least a troubling tendency to catch fire. Enter the solid-state battery, which swaps liquid for a solid ceramic or polymer.

The technology promises faster charging, longer life, greater energy density and improved safety, and a new generation of companies aims to bring it to market. If their bets pan out, the tech could ease the shift away from fossil fuels.
Find out how close solid-state batteries are to delivering on their promise.
—Alexander C. Kaufman

This story is part of “Are we there yet?”, our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter.
