5245ed50c1d5b9dd: LONDON, Oct 29 — Oil and gas giants Shell and TotalEnergies today reported soaring quarterly net profits as the Middle East war pushed up hydrocarbon prices — and the cost of living around the world.
Britain’s Shell said profit after tax more than doubled year-on-year to US$12.1 billion (RM49.1 billion) in the third quarter.
France’s TotalEnergies net profit hit a new record of US$8.3 billion in the July-September period.
Rising fossil fuel prices also saw Spanish oil group Repsol quadruple its net profit over the first nine months of the year, to €5 billion (RM22.7 billion).
Energy majors are reaping bumper profits from disruptions to oil and gas supplies in the Middle East, pushing up refining margins and prices.
British energy giant BP and US majors Chevron and ExxonMobil will report their third-quarter earnings on Friday.
Shell and TotalEnergies used the surge in profits to lift payouts to shareholders.

Both companies had already reported strong profit increases in the first two quarters of 2026, benefiting also from trading operations as oil and gas futures swung between big gains and losses on the Ukraine war’s latest headlines.
Shell’s chief executive Wael Sawan today praised “very strong results in a quarter with continued severe disruption to the global energy system”.
But the companies have also been targeted by critics who say rising energy bills and higher fuel prices at the pump are driving up global inflation, heaping pressure on households and businesses.
Countries across Europe are grappling with a wave of rising discontent over the cost of living, with weeks of protests breaking out across France this month.
‘Set an example’
The French government today called on TotalEnergies to “set an example” by passing on savings from the release of strategic diesel reserves to consumers.

“We are asking Total to pass on the benefits of these released barrels — by lowering prices — and to continue capping prices for as long as necessary,” government spokesperson Maud Bregeon told BFM television.
The French government hoped its decision this month to release 10 million barrels of diesel to distributors would reduce prices at the pump by 12 to 18 cents per litre.
Instead, TotalEnergies CEO Patrick Pouyanne estimated the price reduction passed on to consumers would be just eight to 12 cents per litre.
But while TotalEnergies has been accused of profiting from the conflict in the Middle East, Bregeon said it “would be a mistake to fall into ‘Total-bashing’”.
In Britain meanwhile, senior climate campaigner Philip Evans of Greenpeace called on the UK government to “tax these companies for the untold damage they’re inflicting”.
“Against a backdrop of near-constant climate disaster both in the UK and worldwide, these profits go beyond mere greed — they are openly villainous,” he said.

The price per litre of unleaded petrol and diesel fuels, with diesel at just under two GBP pounds sterling per litre, is displayed on sign outside a Shell petrol station in London October 2, 2026. Shell’s third quarter was boosted by record refining margins, which reflect the spread between the price of crude oil and the fuels derived from it. — AFP pic
Record margins
Shell’s third quarter was boosted by record refining margins, which reflect the spread between the price of crude oil and the fuels derived from it.
Production and exports of refined products in the Middle East remain heavily disrupted, meaning refineries unaffected by the conflict can benefit from tighter global supplies.

Profit margins reached US$42 a barrel in the third quarter, up from US$24 a barrel between April and June, surpassing the previous record set after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, according to Bloomberg.
Logistical constraints have complicated re-routing of fuel supplies, widening the gap between crude oil prices and refined products.
At the same time, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have prompted Russia, a major player in the oil market, to ban the export of certain products, notably petrol and diesel.
“The last time profits were at these levels was in 2022 when Russia’s invasion of Ukraine created its own energy shock,” said AJ Bell investment director Russ Mould.
“The current extremely favourable market conditions may not last forever, but Shell looked to share the benefits with shareholders,” he added.
TotalEnergies benefited from “a high-price environment characterised by historic refining margin levels and a bull gas market”, Pouyanne said in a statement.
Shell, whose revenue rose sharply to US$92.8 billion, said high natural gas prices also boosted its third quarter. — AFP
2708f11b67fca1d6: EXCLUSIVE Researchers identified at least 83 attacks against 61 public GitHub repositories, including popular open source projects such as Google LangExtract, Trivy, Brave browser, and MLflow, in what they suspect is a coordinated campaign to execute commands in CI/CD environments and steal credentials and access tokens.

It all happened very quickly, the Radware threat hunters said in an exclusive interview with The Register. Most (77) of the malicious items were published during a 43-minute time span on September 1, with the remaining six occurring within the next two minutes.

“Our guess is that the final aim was a supply-chain attack in which the attacker gains credentials for the repo, and then he has the power to change the contents – the code – as he wishes” and then push the malicious changes to others, Radware VP and researcher Gabi Nakibly told The Register.

Nakibly and fellow Radware researcher Zvika Babo say they suspect a single individual is behind this supply chain campaign. This attacker used 74 different GitHub accounts, many of which had legitimate development histories, meaning they were likely compromised.

"Considering that dozens of accounts posted the same type of payload, on the same day, within a narrow time window, and to the same infrastructure, it is reasonable to assess that the activity was coordinated,” the team wrote in research shared ahead of publication with The Register.
A novel attack chain
They discovered the campaign while investigating prompt injection in GitHub – and they told us the attack chain is part of what makes this supply-chain campaign novel, and extremely stealthy.

First, the attacker publishes an issue, pull request, or comment containing malicious commands hidden in HTML comments. This ensures the content is not visible in the rendered page. Plus, a GitHub event – like a pull request or issue – can automatically trigger a workflow if the repository is configured to respond to that event, meaning the attacker can be pretty hands-off at this point.
“The workflow automatically is triggered within a second, and if the workflow is indeed vulnerable, then the attack is executed successfully,” Nakibly said.

The workflow incorporates attacker-controlled content directly into shell source code, and the shell executes the hidden, malicious command, which hoovers up environment variables and attempts to exfiltrate those to an attacker-controlled server.

While the researchers examined logs from actual runs, and told us they found two cases containing evidence that the malicious command ran inside the automation environment, they can’t definitively say whether the attacker successfully obtained repository write permissions, modified source code, or compromised downstream software. But they're trying.
“The big picture is that the attackers are trying to find every possible way to get inside the repos to get credentials,” Nakibly said.

Plus, “the attacker doesn't need to compromise the repository or to have access to its codebase” to do this, Babo added. “Basically, every user with a GitHub account can try to run this attack – it's very easy to start this attack.”
Which repos were affected?

As of October 13, the threat hunters identified 83 GitHub items with a verified payload across 61 different repositories. The repos span AI frameworks, security tools, development infrastructure, databases, and other widely used open source software projects.

The Radware report lists agno-agi/agno (42.7K stars), ToolJet/ToolJet (41.1K), google/langextract (38.9K), aquasecurity/trivy (38.4K), CopilotKit/CopilotKit (38K), and podman-container-tools/podman (33K), among the most popular.

Other notable targets included QwenLM/qwen-code (28.5K), mlflow/mlflow (28.4K), discordjs/discord.js (26.8K), cilium/cilium (25.6K), brave/brave-browser (23.9K), dotnet/maui (23.3K), Homebrew/homebrew-cask (22.2K), github/docs (21K), apache/doris (16K), and PX4/PX4-Autopilot (12.8K).
“These projects are used by thousands of organizations," Babo said.
The researchers disclosed their findings to all of the projects’ maintainers, and most of the repositories were closed or fixed, but they can’t confirm that all of them were.
This campaign follows several earlier supply chain attacks against open source security and dev tools as attackers increasingly look for new methods to steal credentials and other secrets.
“There is no way to stop the attackers from attempting,” Nakibly said. “The only way is to make sure that the workflow code is resilient, and not vulnerable to such attacks."
The researchers recommend applying least-privilege access to CI/CD workflows, and separating as much as possible workflows triggered by external events from jobs with elevated permissions.
“Developers should treat external content as untrusted, and also limit the secrets and environment variables that are available to the workflow,” Babo said. ®

e8f7dfb3b666ca1d: BEIJING, Oct 29 — Top officials from China’s ruling Communist Party adopted measures to tighten discipline within their ranks at a key meeting in Beijing that concluded today, state media said.

The fifth plenum of the Central Committee, led by President Xi Jinping, adopted a decision on “advancing full and rigorous governance of the party”, which includes reducing corruption among cadres, state news agency Xinhua said.
Roughly 300 officials make up the Central Committee, whose plenums have previously represented key moments for Xi to cement his authority.
However, despite speculation, Xi was not described in the readout as the “People’s Leader”, a designation that would have signalled a further elevation of his political stature.
The Chinese leader has waged a 14-year campaign against corruption that has ousted thousands of officials, including dozens of Central Committee members.
As a result of his expansive purges, this year’s plenum had the lowest turnout since former leader Mao Zedong’s death in 1976, with eight Central Committee seats vacant prior to the meeting.
Some positions, however, were filled during the proceedings, which began on Monday.
Anti-corruption chief Zhang Shengmin, who serves as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC), was promoted to the Politburo, the country’s top decision-making body.
With his promotion, the Politburo stands at 22 members.
China’s military has been particularly impacted by Xi’s anti-corruption drive.
In August, China ousted Zhang Youxia, then the highest-ranking general, from his position following a months-long graft investigation.
His removal left the CMC, which is supposed to have seven representatives, with only two: Xi and Zhang.
The plenum came ahead of a major party congress next year, where 73-year-old Xi is almost certain to secure a historic fourth term and oversee a leadership reshuffle. — AFP
6839eee887821541: DHAKA, Oct 29 — A Bangladesh court sentenced a senior leader of the former ruling party to death in absentia today for his role in the killings of six people during the 2024 uprising, while three other party leaders were sentenced to life imprisonment.

The four men, members of ousted leader Sheikh Hasina's Awami League, were convicted of the murders of six people in western Kushtia district during the unrest, which led to the former premier's ouster.
The leader sentenced to death by the three-member tribunal was Md Mahbubul Alam Hanif, the party's joint general secretary, who also served as a minister during Hasina's iron-fisted rule.
“The charges against the convicts were undoubtedly proved,” chief prosecutor Md Aminul Islam told reporters.
The tribunal also ordered the confiscation of half of their immovable properties to be distributed as compensation to the families of people killed or injured during the uprising, Islam said.
State-appointed defence lawyer Md Amir Hossain called the verdict “unacceptable”.
As many as 1,400 people were killed between July and August 2024, according to the United Nations, when Hasina's government attempted to suppress the student-led uprising.
Hasina's 15-year rule ended in August 2024, when she fled by helicopter to neighbouring India, where she remains in hiding.
She was sentenced to death by hanging in absentia in November 2025.
Thursday's sentencing brings the total number of people convicted of crimes related to the 2024 uprising to 72.
Of those, 23 have been sentenced to death, but only four are in custody.
Hasina has refused to accept the authority of the court.
The government of Prime Minister Tarique Rahman, which won a landslide victory in February in the first elections since Hasina was ousted, has requested her extradition.
Hasina, 78, has said she will return to Bangladesh of her own volition in December, despite the death sentence she faces. — AFP
7b6f2f158cca10b1: LONDON: Europe's government bond and stock markets rallied on Thursday as traders waited on the European Central Bank's (ECB) next move and for results from Amazon and Intel after Alphabet's shares became the latest to be hammered by AI spending worries.
Europe's STOXX 600 was up 0.5% despite a 1% slide in Nasdaq futures and some erratic trading in Asia after Alphabet's hefty cash burn looked set to wipe nearly US$400 billion off its shares later.

Both the euro and euro zone government bond market yields were edging lower, meanwhile, as oil and natural gas prices dipped ahead of what is widely expected to be a pause in the ECB's rate hike cycle.
There was also breaking news that ECB president Christine Lagarde had confirmed, after months of speculation, that she was to step down early and leave her post in February.
Wednesday had also seen a rally in US Treasuries after the Federal Reserve chair Kevin Warsh had struck a more confident tone on the inflation outlook after it had also kept rates steady.

RBC's European Macro Strategist George Moran said his bank expects the ECB to hold rates at 2.50%, with a further final hike to 2.75% in December, although money markets are pricing as many as three additional increases.
"Widening sovereign spreads — particularly for France — give the ECB cover to avoid further aggressive tightening," Moran said, despite the recent surge in energy prices.

The main gauge of French concerns - the yield gap between Paris' government bonds and triple A-rated German Bunds was at 153.50 basis points on Thursday, having hit a near 15-year high of almost 178 basis points last week.

Lagarde's February departure from the ECB meanwhile, means French president Emmanuel Macron and other EU leaders will be able to fill one of the bloc's most powerful economic positions before France's presidential elections in the spring.
It is a vote that opinion polls suggest could be won by the country's far right.
Big spenders, big falls
Overnight, MSCI's broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan dropped nearly 0.5%, while Japan's Nikkei ended up more than 1% after another day of swings.

However, the region's bigger test came from earnings. Samsung reported another set of record results thanks to booming demand for its memory chips, but it was silent on plans to boost returns, which sent its shares down 4%.
That weighed on South Korea's KOSPI index, which fell 1.2% after a nearly 7% surge a day earlier.
Another AI darling, SK Hynix, continued to surge though as its plans to return about US$75 billion to shareholders this year took its two-day gain past 15%.
Nasdaq futures were pointing to a fall for US markets later.

Alphabet was down 10.5% in premarket trading after the company reported disappointing results in the firm's core search business and a massive acceleration in cash burn as it poured resources into building out AI.
That focus on AI spending will continue on Thursday too with both Intel and Amazon due to report their earnings after US markets close.
"Investors are starting to scrutinise monetisation timelines versus the capital expenditure burn rates.
"Some investors are no longer giving all hyperscalers a 'free pass' to spend without limit," said Jeremy Saltzberg, VP and senior investment officer at Check Capital Management.
Oil dips
Macro data will continue to flow too, with both US personal consumption expenditures figures - the Fed's preferred gauge of inflation - and US Q3 GDP data due to be released.
Forecasts are centred on a 0.3% monthly rise in the core measure of PCE inflation, picking up from a 0.2% gain the previous month.
Markets are still 80% priced for a rate rise in December despite Wednesday's dovish comments from Warsh, which led to a steepening of the Treasury yield curve.
The 2-year Treasury yield fell about 5 basis points overnight and was last at 4.68%.
The US dollar was fractionally higher against its major peers at 102.23 after a 0.2% dip on Wednesday following the Fed decision.
Ahead of the ECB, the euro was hovering around US$1.1137, having fallen almost 2% this month against the dollar and 2.5% against sterling.
Data shows investors are betting heavily against the euro and have built up their biggest short position in a decade that is currently worth almost US$19 billion.

In the commodity markets, Brent futures fell 1.2% to just under US$114 a barrel after the Wall Street Journal reported US vice-president JD Vance had sent a letter to Iranian Security Council chief Mohsen Rezaei in an effort to revive peace negotiations.

Qatari mediators have also presented Iran with a new draft deal to end the war, an official briefed on the negotiations told Reuters, although a senior Iranian official dismissed it as unacceptable ideas that did not amount to an offer.
b0b6dfae09899f15: The Document Foundation (TDF) says LibreOffice has no built-in AI features and that its core developers do not use LLMs - but community contributors face different rules.
In a Fediverse post, someone who goes by the handle of argv[-1] highlights three LibreOffice commits this year that acknowledge the use of LLM coding assistants.

Two of them – Inheritance when setting paragraph style font size to 100% or +0pt and Enable relative font sizes in Calc cell styles – date from April and credit Claude with helping identify the fixes. More recently, September's Add Copy Image button to screenshot dialog acknowledges using GitHub Copilot in VS Code to generate the BitmapTransferable class, while the copyButtonHandler method was written manually with LLM/code-completion assistance.
This is hardly a fatal flaw – after all, it's getting hard to find any major FOSS project with absolutely no LLM-generated code in it these days.

However, The Document Foundation says that the leading FOSS office suite is AI-free. As we noted when it released version 26.8 in August, we interpret this statement as a jab at its former development partner Collabora. Back in June, we noted that increased AI integration was a headline feature in Collabora CODE 26.04. CODE is Collabora's web-based office suite, based on LibreOffice code.

TDF – the primary maintainer and custodian of LibreOffice since its 2010 fork from Oracle-controlled OpenOffice.org – has made the absence of built-in AI a selling point. In September, it published a blog post declaring that no AI is now a feature. Meanwhile, on October 21, TDF announced 9.4 million downloads over eight weeks – excluding Windows updates and downloads of older releases, which are counted separately. The foundation acknowledged that the reasons for the growth are difficult to determine.
TDF's direct response on Mastodon is dismissive:

"Ah, another high-quality Mastodon discussion. Again: No core developers use LLMs. We rely on contributions from the wider community and don't explicitly list tools people can't use – but we do require people disclose when they use LLMs and generally discourage the practice. We carefully review submissions by contributors to make sure the code quality is good and that the patch author understands their own code. LLMs are prohibited for students. That is not 'slop'."

In other words, TDF's approach resembles what some commenters have compared to the Debian approach: LLM coding assistants are permitted for some contributors, subject to disclosure and human review. For AI advocates, this is the only pragmatic response – which could be summarized as the "AI is just a tool" school of thought.

However, since this admission does seem to contradict the very visible public no-AI message, some LibreOffice users are really rather unhappy. Our favorite comment so far is from Argentinian developer Federico Schonborn, who slyly noted:
"When a bakery announces they won't put asbestos in their cake frosting you must not point out they're already putting asbestos in their cake filling, you see."
We asked TDF’s spokesman Italo Vignoli for comment. He pointed us to TDF's Development/AI policy, and added:
"There isn't any departure from the public statements about LO 26.8, as they were about user features and not about development."
"It strikes me as odd to ban all use of LLM for the commit message, but still allow its use for the actual code." ®
81dbb9a23742d815: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — The federal government will continue to implement the Sales and Service Tax (SST), as the Goods and Services Tax (GST) will not be considered due to the ongoing burden of the cost of living.
Finance Minister II Datuk Seri Amir Hamzah Azizan said the government would continue to improve the SST to reduce the impact of cascading taxes and simplify compliance.
He said the SST also provided room for a more progressive and targeted approach.

“The government can choose which goods and services to tax while exempting essential items. Although some of the tax may be passed on through prices, the scope of taxation can be determined with the people’s affordability in mind,” said Amir Hamzah during the Supply Bill (Budget 2027) policy-level winding-up debate for the Ministry of Finance (MoF) in Parliament today.
He explained that the GST tended to be regressive because lower-income groups spent a larger proportion of their income on goods and services.
“In other words, even at the same tax rate, the burden relative to income is heavier for the people, particularly the B40 and M40 groups.
“Therefore, any additional revenue must be assessed alongside the burden borne by the people,” he said.

According to the Fiscal Outlook 2027, SST collections are estimated to rise to RM67 billion in 2026 from RM55.9 billion in 2025. They are projected to reach RM73.3 billion in 2027, an increase of RM17.4 billion over two years.
Amir Hamzah said SST collections currently account for three per cent of gross domestic product (GDP), the same level recorded by the GST in 2017.

This means replacing the SST with the GST would not necessarily generate additional revenue, but would instead shift the tax burden entirely from businesses, including exporters, to the people, he emphasised.
“This increase demonstrates the SST’s ability to generate revenue to finance the country’s needs.
“At the same time, the government has the flexibility to determine which goods and services are taxed on a targeted basis while exempting essential items,” said Amir Hamzah.

He said the government recognised GST’s advantages in collection efficiency, transparency and the input tax credit mechanism. However, the choice of tax system must take into account the people’s ability to pay.

On compliance, he said nearly 700,000 businesses were registered under the GST in 2018, compared with only about 130,000 under the SST in 2026. This means more businesses would have to bear compliance costs under the GST system, said Amir Hamzah. — Bernama
0ee5f2702d5a60f1: FRANKFURT: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced her resignation on Thursday, ending months of speculation about her future just as Europe enters a period of rising economic volatility and divisive electoral politics.

Lagarde will step down on Feb 7, giving current European Union leaders time to pick a successor well before a French presidential election that polls show far-right candidate Marine Le Pen is favoured to win.
The move comes as the ECB battles inflation risks from an Iran-driven oil shock while a sharp rise in bond yields, especially in France, threatens to dampen growth.
"I leave this institution with a sense of good work done and an ECB that is fit for the future," Lagarde said in a short video shared on social media.

A source with direct knowledge of the matter said Lagarde had resigned so she could weigh in on political matters in her native France and globally. As ECB president, she was expected to remain neutral to safeguard the institution's independence.

European Council President Antonio Costa said in a statement the process to find a successor for Lagarde would begin immediately. The former central bank governors of the Netherlands and Spain, Klaas Knot and Pablo Hernandez de Cos, are widely seen as frontrunners.
"The rumoured successors are both very competent, well established central bankers, so for markets, it won’t matter too much," Piet Haines Christiansen, an economist at Danske Bank, said.
Financial markets did not move much after the announcement, with some analysts noting the ECB had by now built a reputation that outlived any of its leaders.

"The ECB is now quite well established, the market is familiar with the way it operates," Goldman Sachs' head of Fixed Income Macro Investing Simon Dangoor said. "Our view is that institutional behaviour is likely to outlast Lagarde, and be quite similar, whoever takes over."
Lagarde's term was scheduled to run until the end of Oct 2027 but speculation about an early departure had been mounting for months, with the World Economic Forum seen as a likely destination.
The ECB is in the middle of a rate-hiking cycle aimed at preventing an oil-price shock linked to the Iran war from feeding into other prices and wages.

But it must also contend with a surge in government bond yields — especially in debt-laden France — that has pushed up borrowing costs for households and businesses and which Lagarde has said will curb growth and inflation.

Caught between persistent inflation fuelled by a renewed surge in energy costs and deteriorating financing conditions, the ECB is widely expected to keep its deposit rate at 2.5% on Thursday while signalling that another increase, potentially as soon as December, remains likely.

"There is likely a low bar to another hike in December, given the likelihood of another upward revision of the ECB's inflation forecast due to higher energy prices," Oliver Rakau at Oxford Economics said.
The ECB is due to announce its interest rate decision at 1315 GMT on Thursday, followed by Lagarde's regular press conference at 1345 GMT.

Money markets are currently pricing another three rate increases from the ECB by the end of next year, which would take the deposit rate to 3.25%, a level that is widely seen as restricting economic growth.
French turmoil in focus but no action
The more immediate challenge for policymakers may be turmoil in bond markets.

A global rise in yields, fuelled by stronger growth expectations, higher debt issuance and massive investment linked to artificial intelligence, is pushing up borrowing costs for governments, households and businesses alike.

In France, investors have become increasingly uneasy about the country's growing debt burden and uncertain fiscal outlook following this year's elections. Concerns have been amplified by suggestions from parts of the political left that debt held by the ECB could be written off.

The result has been a sharp increase in French borrowing costs. France is now paying some of the highest yields in a quarter-century to raise money on bond markets, while the premium investors demand to hold French debt over benchmark German bonds is larger than for any other euro zone country.
That has fuelled speculation that the ECB might be forced to respond, if only verbally for now.
"They've typically come up with a new tool that's customised for that specific set of circumstances," said Dangoor at Goldman Sachs.
The ECB's first line of defence would probably be flexible reinvestment of proceeds from bonds acquired during its vast asset-purchase programmes of the previous decade.
Beyond that, it could activate its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument, a scheme designed to counter what policymakers deem unjustified market pressure.
da82f63c16f69a8c: FRANKFURT, Oct 29 — European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde will step down in February 2027, months before her term expires in October next year, the Frankfurt-based institution said today.

“European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde today informed the Governing Council and the president of the European Council Antonio Costa that she will step down from her position on February 7, 2027,” the ECB said in a statement.

Lagarde’s departure before the end of her term opens the way for European leaders to choose a new ECB chief before French presidential elections scheduled for April, in a race where eurosceptic far-right and far-left candidates are leading in opinion polls.
Lagarde herself has ruled out standing for the presidency, telling French newspaper La Croix last month that it would “not be a good idea”.

Months of speculation have preceded her departure, and Lagarde has been tipped to take the helm of the World Economic Forum, which organises the annual summit of politicians and business leaders in Davos, Switzerland.
Lagarde took the helm at the ECB in November 2019, having previously led the International Monetary Fund and served as French finance minister.
Her tenure took in the Covid-19 pandemic and an inflationary wave that followed Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which prompted a spike in energy prices.
Antonio Costa, head of the European Council, praised Lagarde’s “leadership” and said the process to name a successor would begin immediately.

“Through a global pandemic, a war in Europe, energy crises and inflation shocks, she has provided a steady and determined stewardship, helping to safeguard stability and the resilience of the euro area,” Costa posted on social media.

“To ensure a smooth transition to the next leadership of the ECB, the process for the appointment of her successor will be initiated today and will proceed without delay, with a view to a timely decision,” Costa said. — AFP
5d4f35041c9967f4: CEBU, Oct 29 — Beijing accused Manila today of “erecting multiple obstacles” to its attendance at an Asean meeting in the Philippines this week, a claim rejected by the South-east Asian country’s defence chief.
The war of words is the latest instance of tensions between the two countries — long at loggerheads over competing claims in the South China Sea — threatening to overshadow an Asean event.
The bloc’s July leaders summit in the Philippine capital opened only a day after a clash between sailors in the disputed waterway disrupted months of relative calm.

China has typically sent a senior official to the annual defence meeting, which brings together defence chiefs from the 11-member Association of South-east Asian Nations along with dialogue partners from the United States, Japan, Australia and others.
The decision to send only its Manila embassy defence attaché this year was due to recent Philippine actions, a Chinese defence ministry spokesman told a news conference today.

“The Philippine side has allowed certain politicians to act recklessly and use public office for private ends and erected multiple obstacles to obstruct China’s participation in the Asean Defence Ministers’ Meeting-Plus,” he said.

“This has seriously undermined the Asean principle of consensus, gravely contravened the spirit of openness and inclusiveness” of the summit, the spokesman added, accusing the Philippines of “hijacking Asean and stirring up trouble”.

A number of Philippine senators called in recent weeks for China’s ambassador to be declared persona non grata after he suggested China could “easily win” any confrontation with the archipelago country.
At a press briefing today that wrapped the two-day defence summit in Cebu, Philippine defence minister Gilberto Teodoro said that the bloc’s members did not share China’s viewpoint.
“It is China’s position; it is not Asean’s position,” Teodoro told reporters.
“They were given an opportunity to articulate their position, which is not any different from what they have been articulating before,” he added.

The summit opened yesterday with US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth calling for the creation of an “ambitious” new US-Asean defence framework, as his country aims to build up partnerships in the region.
Teodoro provided no specifics of what that framework might look like as the summit wrapped up on Thursday, telling reporters they would have to wait for the finished reports of Asean working groups.
US ally the Philippines has been engaged in years of confrontations with China over disputed areas of the South China Sea.

Beijing deploys hundreds of coast guard, navy and other vessels to patrol disputed areas of the South China Sea, which it claims almost entirely despite an international ruling that its position has no legal basis. — AFP

a66ffa8c5befe0b3: The wait for a new Raspberry Pi Zero may be nearly over, judging by the raspberrypi/linux repository.
Among the merged pull requests is one titled "Add device tree for Pi Zero 3 W and Pi 4A," suggesting new hardware is on the way, including a successor to the very long-in-the-tooth Pi Zero 2 W.

The board launched five years ago. Its 512 MB of memory was hardly generous, but it offered considerable bang for the buck. At the time, we reckoned performance was closer to the Raspberry Pi 3 than the flagship Pi 4, but perfectly adequate provided you didn't open too many browser tabs at once.

According to the source tree, as reported by Phoronix, the new board could use the Broadcom BCM271, up from the RP3A0 in the current Zero. If so, that would be a significant performance gain, though it's unclear whether the 1.5GHz clock speed of the Pi 4, which uses the same SoC, will be retained.

Heat is a concern as the Pi 4 gained a reputation for running hot under load without active cooling, and it throttles performance when temperatures climb. A board as small as the Zero will have even less room to shed heat.

Assuming that challenge can be met, it would be a worthy upgrade for the venerable Pi Zero 2. There is no word on how much memory it is likely to have – we can't imagine much given the current cost of RAM and the need to keep the price at least close to that of the Zero 2 W, which can still be had for around $18.
The code also hints at eMMC storage is mentioned, but that seems unlikely to reach the finished product, probably because of the cost.

Alongside the Pi Zero 3 W is a Raspberry Pi 4 Model A. Where the Zero 3 W is a clear upgrade, the 4 Model A looks more like a cost-cutting measure amid rising hardware prices. Model A boards typically have less memory, and no Ethernet port, and the 4A appears to have a single HDMI output rather than twp.
Things could change before any hardware ships. We asked Raspberry Pi if anything was in the pipeline, but the company said it had nothing to add.

Enthusiasts will welcome an upgraded Pi Zero after more than half a decade, provided the price is right and it doesn't run too hot. At the same time, a cut-down Pi 4 carries the whiff of inevitability in an era of rising component costs. ®
1ece9282e98a41b1: BEIJING: Sanrio, the Japanese company that owns the popular Hello Kitty character, apologised Thursday over its tie-up with a TV spy drama criticised as anti-China, cancelling a merchandise collaboration with the show.
It comes after Chinese sponsors dropped football superstar Kylian Mbappe over comments calling communist leader Mao Zedong a "dictator", which the Real Madrid forward later apologised for.

"We have recently received feedback from various quarters regarding the collaborative merchandise with the Japanese television drama VIVANT," Sanrio's Chinese unit said on social media platform Weibo.
"We sincerely apologise for any concern this may have caused," the post said.
The project "contains expressions that are inconsistent with the Sanrio Group's corporate philosophy", it said.
Sanrio said it had "decided to cease this collaboration, as well as all subsequent projects and promotional campaigns".

Contacted by AFP, private broadcaster TBS, which created the drama Vivant, could not immediately comment.

ec7745c3df56fc92: PUTRAJAYA, Oct 29 — The Court of Appeal today upheld the three-year jail sentence and RM239,500 fine imposed on a former procurement manager of Pengurusan Air Pahang Berhad after dismissing his appeal to set aside his conviction on 22 charges of receiving RM44,700 in bribes.

A three-member panel led by Justice Datuk Noorin Badaruddin ruled that Sani Khan Ali Khan had failed to show any error of law or material fact in the High Court decision that convicted him on all the charges.
On January 26, the Kuantan High Court set aside a Sessions Court decision that had acquitted and discharged him of all the charges.
The Court of Appeal panel, which also comprised Justices Datuk Mohd Radzi Abdul Hamid and Datuk Meor Hashimi Abdul Hamid, ordered him to begin serving his sentence today.
Sani Khan, 51, had previously been granted a stay of execution and released on RM20,000 bail with one surety pending the outcome of this appeal.

In today’s proceedings, Justice Noorin said the High Court’s intervention was justified and that it had made no material error in setting aside the Sessions Court decision that had acquitted and discharged Sani Khan.
“The statutory presumption under Section 50(1) of the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission (MACC) Act 2009 applies,” she said.
She said banking records proved that the money had been received into the appellant’s bank account, and that his claim that the payments were house rental was unconvincing.

Justice Noorin said that although the appellant relied on tenancy agreements and bank transactions labelled as house rent, the court found that the documents did not prove the payments were genuine rent.
She added that the appellant had also failed to show that the alleged defects in the charges had caused him to misunderstand the case or suffer material prejudice in preparing his defence.

Justice Noorin said the evidence was assessed cumulatively, with the banking records, witness testimony, tenancy documents and surrounding circumstances weighed together for each charge. The court found no material error warranting the overturning of any of the 22 convictions.
On December 26, 2024, the Sessions Court ruled that the prosecution had failed to prove its case beyond a reasonable doubt, and acquitted and discharged Sani Khan on all the charges.
However, the High Court allowed the prosecution’s appeal to set aside his acquittal and found him guilty on all 22 charges.
The High Court imposed three years’ jail for each charge and ordered Sani Khan to pay a RM239,500 fine, or 12 months’ jail in default. The sentences were ordered to run concurrently.
At the Court of Appeal today, MACC deputy public prosecutors Law Chin How, Haresh Prakash Somiah and Hazel Tan Jia Qi appeared for the prosecution.
Sani Khan was represented by lawyers Mohd Baharuddin Ahmad Kassim, Datuk Mohd Najid Husain and Nornajihah Ahmad Nadjemudin. — Bernama

13381c3769243f0b: PALANGKARAYA (Indonesia), Oct 29 — Residents and firefighters in an Indonesian city long shrouded in a toxic haze brought on by months of wildfires rushed outside dancing and chanting as rain this week brought a welcome respite.
Intermittent rains have been falling in Palangkaraya, the capital of Central Kalimantan province on Indonesian Borneo, where devastating wildfires have raged since August.
Last night, exhausted volunteer firefighters jumped around in the puddles and kissed the ground in gratitude as another burst came down.
“We were overjoyed; every one of us volunteers was so happy that we prostrated ourselves in gratitude. Praise be to God that there was finally rain,” firefighter Lukman El Hakim told AFP.
More than 11,000 people have been treated for respiratory infections in Palangkaraya during the months-long crisis that has also affected Indonesia’s neighbours with haze pollution.
The city’s air quality index hit 4,000 this month, its worst ever measurement and more than 13 times the environment ministry’s threshold for pollution deemed “hazardous” to health.
The World Health Organisation has linked exposure to air pollution, including high levels of tiny, airborne PM2.5 particles, to increased risk of illness and premature death.
Palangkaraya resident Muhammad Jihan Alwi used the reprieve to jog outdoors for the first time in months.
“Of course I’m happy to be out jogging again, breathing in fresh air that’s better than yesterday, just feeling grateful,” the 23-year-old said, smiling.

Tri said the short-term prediction was for rain clouds in affected provinces.

But he said vigilance was necessary “bearing in mind that there is still the possibility of another dry period before we fully enter the peak of the rainy season”.

At least 11 people have died fighting Indonesia’s wildfires, most recently a 45-year-old forest ranger who was killed by a falling tree while battling flames in North Toraja, South Sulawesi, yesterday.

The national police’s top detective, Asep Safrudin, said 245 individuals and 20 corporations have been named as suspects and could face jail time and heavy fines.
Deforestation monitor Nusantara Atlas says the fires consumed more than 1.9 million hectares in the nine months to September.
The haze has sent pollution levels soaring as far afield as Malaysia, Singapore, the Philippines and East Timor, clouding Indonesia’s ties with its neighbours.
Experts say the wildfires can be blamed in large part on slash-and-burn land-clearing practices, often by timber, palm oil or mining companies. — AFP

e13642b88152f6db: BENGALURU: Wall Street rewarded Microsoft and Oracle on Wednesday for showing that they could fund their enormous AI ambitions without endlessly tapping investors.
Alphabet, by contrast, was punished for burning through cash, while Google Search's slower growth fanned fears that competition was hurting the business that bankrolls its AI expansion.

Microsoft shares jumped more than 3% in after-hours trading, while Alphabet plunged nearly 10%, as investors drew a sharper distinction between companies making money from AI and those struggling to contain its costs.

The divergence shows that after rewarding companies for spending aggressively to secure computing capacity — often through debt — investors are demanding more evidence that the resulting growth can finance the next round of outlays.

Meta offered an early warning last week, when better-than-expected revenue growth and an upbeat outlook were eclipsed by its cash burn. Oracle, on the other hand, ended regular trading nearly 11% higher on Wednesday after Larry Ellison's company said it was planning to put a ceiling on external financing and expected to turn its cash flow positive in the second half of fiscal 2028.
"Alphabet and Microsoft were night and day," said Melissa Otto, head of research at S&P Global Visible Alpha.

"Microsoft's quarter demonstrated very disciplined growth, whereas Google is burning cash and its core business came in below expectations," she said, adding that it may lead investors to question "is AI taking some share" from Google Search.
Google's search revenue grew 12% in the September quarter but fell short of expectations for a 14.7% increase, even as CEO Sundar Pichai said queries were growing at their fastest pace in five years.

The long-lucrative business is under threat from AI chatbots and agents that are changing how people search for information, just as the company pours more money into the technology. Capital expenditure will increase significantly in 2027, CFO Anat Ashkenazi told analysts.
Cloud boom, cash squeeze
Alphabet's eyebrow-raising capital outlay — with as much as US$205 billion expected this year — is, however, driving gains at Google's other major AI business.

Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to US$30.71 billion, but Alphabet's spending overwhelmed that growth. Cash burn hit US$9.07 billion after the company posted its first quarter of negative cash flow in the June period.

"This is definitely a different business, Google. It's a different business today than it was three, five, 10 years ago," said Jeremy Saltzberg, vice president and senior investment officer at Check Capital, which owns Alphabet shares.

Saltzberg pushed back on the concerns about spending, saying Alphabet needed to have big outlays to stay competitive at a time when OpenAI and Anthropic appear to be pulling ahead in Silicon Valley's AI model race.
"We think this is a sport of kings, which is that if you don't have US$150 billion to spend next year on capital expenditure, don't even bother showing up," Saltzberg said.
Microsoft's cash flow advantage

Microsoft offered a stark contrast. The company generated US$18.6 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal first quarter, nearly US$10 billion more than Wall Street expected, even as it poured US$45.2 billion into expanding its computing infrastructure.

Revenue at its Azure cloud business surged a better-than-expected 48% and the company forecast faster-than-expected cloud growth for the current quarter, suggesting corporate demand for AI computing remains strong.

The results also suggested Microsoft was finding a broader market for AI beyond a handful of deep-pocketed customers, including OpenAI, whose heavy computing requirements have fueled the industry's expansion.

"The shiny object stuff is waning" as more businesses move beyond experimenting with the newest or most powerful AI models and commit to long-term contracts, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in a conference call with analysts.

"I want the breadth," he said. "We have large customers who want to buy from us ... As long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient about building the breadth business."

6536d74f4173aecb: Users of New Outlook wondering where the option to open an attachment went have a culprit to blame – an Edge update.

The issue underscores how interconnected things are in the Microsoft ecosystem. According to the vendor, an update to Edge 156 "unintentionally enabled an unnecessary configuration," which means some New Outlook users are unable to open email file attachments.

An error stating the file cannot be opened also appears for some, along with an instruction to restart Outlook. However, the "Open" option goes away after the error is encountered. A workaround is to use "Save As" to save the attachment, and then open the file manually.

Microsoft confirmed the issue yesterday afternoon in the advisory EX1528992, and early this morning began rolling out a fix to disable the "unnecessary" configuration. It expects that it'll take 12 hours for the fix to be rolled out, and users will have to close and reopen New Outlook to feel the benefit.

The problem raises some interesting questions. While we'd understand how something unexpected in Edge might cause rendering issues in New Outlook, losing the ability to open attachments because of something an Edge update did is concerning and may make some administrators reconsider the blast radius of software updates.
We asked Microsoft for more information about the "unnecessary configuration" and will update this piece should it respond.

However, the incident highlights connections within Windows that might surprise users. In addition, it shows that, despite a woeful showing on the desktop market share front – although Edge recently "surged" to almost 15 percent last month, according to Statcounter, up from around 10 percent for much of the year – Microsoft's browser can still capture user attention. It's just not the sort of attention the Windows maker might have hoped for.
It is also worth noting that Outlook Classic does not appear to be affected by the issue (according to Microsoft's EX1528992 advisory for Exchange Online).
Impacted users could therefore temporarily add opening attachments to the list of things the old software does that the new software doesn't. ®

0c49eb4fc30298f0: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them.

AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility.

Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today.

As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine, we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability: the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely.

Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important.

With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions.

The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken.

Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it, and how long they took. And the bank must also analyze records of how the agent arrived at its refusal decision in order to ensure it did not use off-limits information, like details about the neighborhood the applicant is from.

Recording “what happened” and “how the agent decided” require different approaches, but both are feasible. The current lack of “what happened” records is mostly a software plumbing problem that can be addressed through OpenTelemetry, an open observability standard maintained by engineers across the industry and by the agent frameworks adopting it.

OpenTelemetry has launched a working group drafting shared formats for tracing agents, but they have yet to be finalized. The group should urgently incorporate standards for maintaining persistent agent identity and for recording human interventions and changes to agents’ permission or memory. And it should be done before these systems can scale, all the while attending to the privacy implications of agent ID that links to real people.

Preserving “how agents decided” records is more challenging. The issue raises open research questions for model providers and researchers: Does the step-by-step reasoning a model displays, known as chain of thought, reflect how the model actually made a decision? And do we have reliable ways to measure how confident the agent is in that decision? These questions need answers before anyone sets standards for how such observability records are used.
No single organization or sector can close the observability gaps on their own, but together, they can support the infrastructure required to prevent dangerous incidents and support safety.

AI developers building agent frameworks, like OpenAI, Anthropic, CrewAI, and LangChain, must integrate telemetry signals recording an agent’s persistent identity, any human interventions, and any changes to an agent’s permissions and memory. Meanwhile, enterprises adopting these agent frameworks have an influential role to play; enterprises in regulated industries, like banks and hospitals, can put pressure on the agent developers to supply these missing observability records where standards do not yet exist.

Enterprises must also define policies, permissions, and roles that set out what agents can safely do, since telemetry alone cannot assess whether agents broke specific rules. Finally, regulators and AI standards institutes must specify the observability records required for high-stakes AI deployments while leaving the technical details to industry. We have already seen initial momentum here: NIST’s agent standards initiative in the US is working on agent identity, one of the most salient gaps we found in our research.

No bank would let a thousand unbadged employees loose on customer accounts and hope to piece together what happened when something goes wrong. Yet that’s how we’re deploying AI agents. Making their behavior observable is the first step toward fixing this. And by building the regulatory and policy ecosystem that makes it possible to act on what we see, we can hold organizations accountable. Until then, every task we hand to an agent hands over our agency, too.

Madhulika Srikumar is the Head of the AI Safety Program at the Partnership on AI, a global non-profit partnership of leading industry, academic, and civil society organizations, advancing best practices in AI governance.
Claire Leibowicz is the Director of AI, Trust, and Society at the Partnership on AI and a doctoral candidate at Oxford University.

73686718715a7fd8: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals.

Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century.

A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs, and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding.

None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries.

A separate analysis published in One Earth in March, which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds.

Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group.

At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project, through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds.

But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue.

So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story). In addition, the Environmental Defense Fund’s Climate Innovation Initiative has backed lab research on the potential of adding sulfate, iron, or other compounds to wetlands to counteract fast-rising methane emissions.

Several startups are also exploring possibilities. They’re looking into suppressing the lightning strikes that are igniting more and more fires in high latitudes, placing synthetic mats above permafrost to prevent it from melting, and deploying autonomous drones to quickly suppress potentially high-emissions fires before they burn out of control.

Investigating all these ideas is worthwhile. But researchers are only in the earliest stages of figuring out how big a dent in emissions any such efforts could achieve across sprawling global ecosystems undergoing massive transformations.
The surest path to reducing the effect of warming-driven warming remains the one we’ve known all along: breaking society’s addiction to fossil fuels.
This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here.
2798037116d9ae43: <!--kg-card-end: html--> Oregon Senator Ron Wyden and Massachusetts Senator Edward Markey sent a letter to Meta on Wednesday demanding the company answer for the privacy concerns its smart glasses pose to the public.

The letter cites 404 Media’s October 2025 investigation into how people use Meta’s smart glasses to harass massage parlor workers. That investigation found Instagram accounts with hundreds of thousands of followers and millions of views uploaded videos filmed with Meta’s Ray-Ban glasses, where men entered massage parlors across the country and solicited the workers for sex work. The full letter is here.

“Meta’s own disclosures confirm that imagery processed through its glasses’ visual AI features may be retained and used to train AI systems, including with the assistance of human reviewers,” the letter says. “Using intimate imagery for AI development is itself an invasion of privacy when the people depicted have not consented to that use, as is inherently the case for most bystanders captured by Meta’s glasses. Retaining that material for AI development, thereby extending the period during which it can be accessed, disclosed, or misused, exploits people’s highly sensitive information for Meta’s commercial benefit.”
Researchers Show How Meta's 'Pervert Glasses' Are Used to Harass Women
A new study shows how pickup artist influencers use smart glasses to create content, and the connection between covert recording and harm.

Research published in August revealed how Meta’s platforms encourage an ecosystem of abusive, harassing content from pickup artists and influencers who use Meta’s smart glasses to capture interactions with people minding their own business in public or at their workplaces, who might not even know they’re being filmed. In a January report by the BBC, a woman who was recorded with the glasses said she was “bombarded” with phone calls because her phone number was posted with the video, and men who had seen the video stalked her at work.

Earlier this year, more than 70 people sued Meta, claiming that their intimate images and videos were exposed to workers hired by the company to label the data for AI. In March, Swedish journalists reported that Kenyan data labelers were viewing and annotating uncensored footage from Meta’s smart glasses, including sexual and violent content; Meta ended its contract with those workers less than two months later. These are labor conditions that groups like the Data Labelers Association in Kenya are fighting back against, and for the people whose images are in the videos and photos, it’s an obvious violation of their privacy. People have also been modding these glasses to disable the light that indicates they’re recording for years

Meta has played dumb about the difference between AI glasses you wear on your face and an iPhone for a long time. Now, these senators want the tech giant to answer for themselves. In the letter, Wyden and Markey demand answers about what safeguards, if any, Meta has in place to prevent the nonconsensual “capture, disclosure, or processing of sensitive and intimate imagery,” whether Meta specifically evaluated the potential for its glasses “to facilitate voyeurism, nonconsensual intimate image capture, or similar privacy invasions,” what imagery it uses for AI training, and whether people can request their biometric and other data captured by its glasses be deleted, along with several more questions about the glasses’ safety and design.

“The reported disclosure of intimate footage to contractors for the purpose of AI training is particularly disturbing. Human review to fulfill a service knowingly requested by the person depicted is one thing; exposing unsuspecting individuals’ intimate moments to strangers for AI training is quite another,” Wyden and Markey wrote. “The individuals whose naked bodies, sexual activity, and other private moments have reportedly been captured by Meta glasses did not knowingly agree to having those images shared with strangers, much less for the purpose of improving Meta’s commercial AI systems. That disclosure and processing is an invasion of privacy, regardless of whether the footage is subsequently published or misused.”

Do you know anything else about harassment and Meta's smart glasses? I would love to hear from you. Using a non-work device, you can message me securely on Signal at sam.404. Otherwise, send me an email at sam@404media.co.

In the last few weeks, Meta has come under fire for quietly changing its privacy policies for business accounts and granting itself permission to scrape user’s content and connected websites to develop its AI products.

Meta has been pushing its smart glasses over the years with ads featuring A-list celebrities, including Chris Pratt, Chris Hemsworth, and Kris Jenner (all three in a 2025 Superbowl ad), Doja Cat, Jennie Kim from K-pop group BLACKPINK, and most recently, Kylie Jenner. Guerrilla ad makers have countered with their own anti-AI glasses ads around the world, and people have started calling the smart glasses "pervert glasses" in response to these widespread invasions of privacy they've come to represent. In August, Meta filed a patent to add facial recognition and highlight reel features to its smart glasses.
4ba50ca79afa8cda: SEPANG, Oct 29 — Aprilia Racing’s Jorge Martin could add another dimension to the 2026 Malaysian Motorcycle Grand Prix (MotoGP) as championship leader Marc Marquez and third-placed Marco Bezzecchi welcome the Spaniard’s return to action at the Sepang International Circuit (SIC).

34781f222dc7f5db: JAKARTA: Pandu Sjahrir, the prominent Indonesian wealth fund executive who has publicly supported MSCI Inc.’s scrutiny of the nation’s stock market, is the co-owner of a brokerage sanctioned in connection with a stock-market manipulation probe.
Pandu, who as chief investment officer of Danantara has become a key liaison with global money managers, indirectly owns a 27.5% stake in PT Supra Sekuritas Indonesia, according to company records.

People with knowledge of the matter, who asked not to be identified discussing sensitive information, said Supra Sekuritas was the company referred to as “SS” by Indonesia’s Financial Services Authority this month when it announced sanctions against more than a dozen entities for violating regulations in cases related to market manipulation.

The statement, which only listed the firms by their initials, came in the wake of MSCI’s surprise threat to downgrade the country to standalone status — a more severe punishment than previously considered.

The previously unreported revelation risks complicating Indonesia’s efforts to regain New York-based MSCI’s confidence and prevent billions of dollars in capital outflows. The nation’s benchmark stock index has dropped around 10% since the index provider’s warning on Oct 15, the worst performance in Asia.

MSCI has repeatedly raised concerns about opaque ownership and the potential for coordinated trading in one of Southeast Asia’s biggest equity markets, while pressing authorities to strengthen regulation, surveillance and enforcement.
As a top executive at Danantara, which reports to President Prabowo Subianto, Pandu has pitched the country to investors at global forums in places like Washington, Davos and Tokyo.

“Pandu has increasingly become the face of Indonesia to the international investment community,” said Bhima Yudhistira Adhinegara, executive director of the Center of Economic and Law Studies, a Jakarta-based think tank.
A spokesperson for Pandu confirmed in a statement that he’s a minority shareholder of Supra Sekuritas in his personal capacity, noting that the investment is passive.

Pandu has never served on the company’s “board of directors, board of commissioners, or management, and has had no role in its daily operations, trading activities or compliance decisions,” the spokesperson said. “His ownership should not be confused with responsibility for the company’s actions.”

Pandu fully respects the FSA and “supports strong and fair enforcement of capital market regulations,” the spokesperson said, adding that he “remains committed to supporting transparency, good governance and investor confidence in Indonesia’s capital markets.”
In recent months, MSCI has privately signaled to Indonesian officials, including Pandu, that the market’s problems have not been fixed, according to people familiar with the matter.

Pandu has publicly supported MSCI’s scrutiny, describing its warning as a much needed wake-up call to improve the Indonesian stock market’s liquidity and transparency. The alumni of Stanford Graduate School of Business had estimated a downgrade to frontier-market status alone could trigger US$25 billion to US$50 billion in outflows.

Pandu met with MSCI Chief Executive Henry Fernandez in late September in New York and asked for recommendations on what Indonesia could do to avoid a reclassification, people familiar with that gathering said. On Oct. 13, Pandu participated in a Danantara-organized event on the sidelines of IMF meetings in Bangkok that MSCI also attended.

The announcement of fines earlier this month was part of the biggest series of financial penalties ever laid out by the FSA — a sweeping response to MSCI’s downgrade threat. The Indonesian regulator said on Monday that it will name sanctioned entities after an appeals period, but didn’t provide a timeline.

Pandu owns 99.99% of PT Asha Artha Sehati, which in turn holds a 27.5% stake in Supra Sekuritas, according to Bloomberg calculations of shareholding shown in company registration records. The brokerage, formerly known as Supra Securinvest, has been a trader of shares in Indonesian coal miner PT Dian Swastatika Sentosa, one of the companies at the heart of the recent regulatory sanctions.

His broader business career spans energy and private capital. Pandu spent 15 years helping run PT TBS Energi Utama, a listed group rooted in coal mining that has expanded into waste management, renewable energy and electric mobility. He directly held about 0.6% of its shares at the end of April.

Pandu was also a managing partner at Indies Capital and a founding partner of AC Ventures, which have reported managing more than US$1 billion and US$500 million, respectively. Those figures reflect capital managed for investors, rather than Pandu’s personal assets.
MSCI has said it will make a decision on Indonesia’s market status by the end of June 2027.

d0fc80649cae12ab: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — National triathlete Esther Joy Chen is eyeing an opportunity to compete in the marathon at the 2027 Kuala Lumpur SEA Games after emerging as Malaysia’s fastest female runner at the Standard Chartered Kuala Lumpur Marathon on October 4.

Esther, 22, clocked three hours, five minutes and 22 seconds (3:05:22) to win the Malaysian women’s category in her marathon debut, putting herself on the preliminary list of candidates for selection for the biennial Games.

She said the achievement had motivated her to continue improving her performance, particularly in terms of physical and mental preparation, as she pursued her dream of representing Malaysia on the international stage.

“In my mind, I am an optimistic person. I like setting high targets because I believe that whatever we set our minds to, we can achieve,” she said on Lensa Wanita on Siara Bernama Radio at Wisma Bernama here today.
On her preparations, Esther said she underwent specialised marathon training, with between one and three sessions a day depending on her training needs, each lasting between one and three hours.
She said nutrition during races also required attention, particularly the intake of energy gels and drinks, to help improve her performance.
“I think, in terms of performance, my race nutrition, especially energy gels and drinks, is still an area that needs improvement. Once I get that right, I believe I can go faster,” she said.

Esther, who began focusing more seriously on sports only last year, said the support of her partner and family had also played an important role in helping her get through difficult days during training.
She previously joined a wushu development programme in 2014 before quitting. She also had experience in gymnastics during her school days before turning her focus to triathlon.

Commenting on the challenges of triathlon, Esther said swimming was the most challenging discipline for her, as she had started swimming at the age of eight before stopping and resuming training at 18.

She hoped to continue addressing her weaknesses and building her self-confidence as she prepared to face greater challenges, including the opportunity to compete at the 2027 Kuala Lumpur SEA Games. — Bernama
6c7563d057b9fb20: TOKYO: Fast-fashion giant Uniqlo has cancelled a planned price hike for its popular socks in Japan, as consumers grow increasingly frustrated with inflation.
The company reversed its decision less than two weeks after announcing increases that led local media to suggest its reputation as a "symbol of affordability" was at risk.

The retail powerhouse said a planned jump to ¥390 (US$2.50) a pair for one popular category of basic socks was now officially off the board, instead opting to keep them at ¥290 and a bargain ¥990 for four pairs.

"As socks are an essential everyday item, in Japan we reconsidered our planned price revision and decided to continue our multi-buy offer," a spokesman for Uniqlo's parent company, Fast Retailing, said in a statement.
The company will still proceed with price increases for other selected items, including jackets and pants, from November largely because of soaring costs and a weak yen.
Japanese households are facing a spike in prices for everything from eggs to transport in a dramatic shift from deflation that plagued the nation for decades.
Many businesses that once prided themselves on low prices are now having to raise them.
The popular restaurant chain Saizeria apologised to its customers when announcing a hike this month.
Japan's core consumer prices rose 2.1% in September, and the Bank of Japan is soon expected to declare that the nation's underlying inflation has reached the 2.0% target.
Analysts have said Japanese firms are able to pass some costs onto consumers but not enough to fully cover them.
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi has identified fighting inflation as one of her top priorities.
