6027d0e7981f3043: Decentralized messaging platform Matrix is no longer the upstart it once was. The organization is now a serious challenger to the status quo as concerns about sovereignty and independence reach new heights.
At the organization's recent Malmo event, which grew attendance 30 percent year-on-year, the mood shifted from "yes, this is important" to "yes, we're rolling this out."

Matrix is an open standard for communication. It's a federated system, so there are no central hubs or overseas control to worry about, and it can be used for anything from messaging to voice over IP. Video is also supported.

The system is an alternative to services such as Microsoft Teams. It has become popular in the public sector as governments grow increasingly wary of relying on US tech giants for services that the Trump administration could switch off at will.

However, that increased interest and subsequent roll-outs have brought a level of scrutiny Matrix was not fully prepared for. A recent report regarding anonymous reaction to a roll-out of the technology by the European Commission took Element - the company that puts the lion share of the money into Matrix - by surprise.
One attendee at the Malmo conference observed, "First they [competitors] ignore you, then they laugh at you, then they fight you."
Matrix remains an open standard, however, the open source foundation behind it would certainly welcome more paying members.
"It's true that we're definitely getting more attention than we have had before," said Element CEO Matthew Hodgson.
"We are seeing Matrix ending up on the critical path of digital sovereignty as almost the poster child of the whole thing.

"I'm not sure that we necessarily do want to be the poster child," he added, "We didn't sign up to end up being ambassadors for digital sovereignty, roaming from government to government, but empirically that's where we've ended up, and yeah, that's going to attract attention from people who would rather everyone just kept in their traditional big tech systems."

This comes amid worries about the reliability of international partners, from early projects including France's Tchap messenger for the public sector and Germany's BundesMessenger through to more recent users, such as the Swedish public sector. Indeed, in one memorable demonstration during the Matrix event, messages were sent between French, Swedish, and NATO entities.

"I cannot overstate the strangeness," Hodgson added, "of having various national militaries phoning up every couple of days, saying, 'Look, we need to get on board Matrix too because we need to talk to this country and they're using Matrix, and we need to talk to that country, and they're using Matrix.'"
"It could be for defense, could be national security, could just be healthcare or education, public sector. But that is real. That is why there is a feeding frenzy."

Not that Element or Matrix is trying to build a better Teams than Teams. Patrick Alberts, Element's Chief Product Officer, said, "This is a digitally sovereign communication solution that, by and large, works like Teams in many aspects, but it's not set out to be the faster Porsche here..."

As for the reported complaints from the European Commission over Element's software implementation, Diana Gheorghe, EC head of sector for Communication and Collaboration Services, addressed them directly and described the anonymous complaints as "the natural friction of [a] high-profile rollout that we have done at scale."

Alexandru Vignide, EC service manager for Communication and Collaboration Services, who is very much at the pointy end of making the sovereign communication tools work, noted the speed of the rollout, which began with a proof of concept in Q4 2025, and hit laptops between July and September 2026.

The EC chose the Schengen Cloud Alliance (which includes OVHcloud) for hosting and, according to Vignide, "We wanted to provide a familiar experience for users." Not everyone is impressed with what is rolling out, but it's important to remember that change can be alarming, and this is still early days.

It is, however, a significant one. Gheorghe said that, as well as increasing resilience and business continuity, "We wanted to have vendor diversity. We also wanted to have data control and ownership of the platform."

Microsoft, as an example, would point to the sovereign capabilities of its system. As the Matrix conference kicked off, it announced new capabilities, including additional options for running AI, data services, and confidential workloads on customer-controlled platforms, and highlighted its sovereign partner ecosystem for customers who prefer local expertise.

However, Microsoft (and other tech giants) cannot escape concerns about who ultimately controls the data and what administrations might do with it. In 2025, a Microsoft representative memorably confirmed the US giant "cannot guarantee" data sovereignty to customers in France.

There is, however, a fly in the Matrix ointment. The platform is open source and, like so many open source projects, requires funding. Right now, Element accounts for much of the Matrix Foundation's funding. Hodgson finds this a little frustrating.

"If every government who is operationally dependent on Matrix put the smallest amount of money in the Foundation, the Foundation would have enough money to really start investing in the ecosystem and not be dependent on Element basically picking up the tab."
He acknowledged that things had improved in the last year, but said, "It's not good governance for an open standard to have one big player like Element effectively propping things up."

This isn't uncommon in the open source world, and it's a little disappointing given the ever-increasing importance placed on sovereignty in communications. Alberts commented: "There is confusion in the market that the thing somehow creates itself.

"No, it doesn't. It requires hardworking people. These hardworking people need to be paid, and that payment, in order to support government deployments going forward, ideally also comes from these governments. And some of them do a lot and do it in a great way, and that's amazing.
"But some don't." ®

c02963657f129c75: Welcome back to PWNED, in which The Reg offers cautionary tales from folks who’ve left their doors wide open to attackers and lived to tell the tale. This week’s misadventure involves unpatched older machines and a password that was supposed to send a message to crims.
Our story comes courtesy once again of leading red teamer and pen tester Dahvid Schloss of Suzu Labs.

A client asked Schloss to visit a factory and check the servers there for security holes. The company had been hacked six months prior, made some adjustments, and wanted to make sure that they were bulletproof now.
Schloss' mission, which he chose to accept, was to get domain admin rights.

Schloss drove over to the factory where he noticed a number of Windows 7 servers were connected to the CNC milling machines, even though Windows 10 was by then Microsoft's supported desktop OS. This was to be expected, as companies with proprietary software often use legacy OSes for fear of breaking apps.
At first, Schloss had a hard time breaking in because most of the servers were not connected to the domain. So there was no point in his running the EternalBlue zero-day that would have let him in.

“So I've been looking through these and most of them had been disconnected from the domain, so it's the right move,” he said. “Like, yeah, you could run EternalBlue on the network, but you really weren't going to be able to get anywhere with it, cuz you get on the device and what you find: you dump LSASS [the Windows Local Security Authority Subsystem Service], you’re like ‘All right, there’s local admin creds, but the local admin creds on those devices were different from the local admin creds on the majority of workstations.”

Finally, Schloss went onto one of the servers that was connected to milling machines and found that it was connected to the network and on the domain. It was vulnerable to EternalBlue and he went and dumped LSASS and found a pair of creds from WDigest, one of which looked like an admin account.
But Schloss thought that it must not be a legitimate admin account when he read the password : “heyhackergof***yourself,” but written in leet speak [l337 5p34k].

The resulting string was a strong password, but Schloss assumed that the admins were playing a game with him and left this credential there for him to find. Schloss assumed it wouldn't work and sat on it for a week.
During a briefing he had with the IT crew, he presented his findings and then asked who set up the admin account with this funny password.

“You could see everyone kind of looking at the senior manager of IT like ‘that was you, wasn’t it,’” Schloss explained. “He’s kind of got this face. I’m like ‘oh shit, like what?’ Turns out that ‘heyhackergof***yourself’ was the actual password for his admin account."

On Monday, Schloss tried the username and password combo and, lo and behold, it gave him complete control of the entire network. He was then able to get access to other passwords and many of them were also insults directed at potential hackers.

Schloss understood that the team was still angry about a breach they had suffered six months prior and, should they be breached again, wanted to give the finger to the hacker who did it. Unfortunately, their system was still vulnerable because of the outdated machine that was hooked up to the domain and he was able to gain control.
The lesson here is really to patch your systems and avoid using insecure legacy OSes whenever possible, because it was an old machine that let Schloss in, not a weak password.
Indeed, “hackergof***yourself” in leet speak isn’t a terrible password, just an embarrassing one if it's exposed. ®
9424cabcfddf9caa: HPE is giving its Alletra Storage MP X10000 another job: holding inference state that would otherwise be evicted from expensive GPU memory and recalculated later.

In testing validated by Kamiwaza using NVIDIA H200 GPUs, the Kamiwaza AI platform, and HPE Alletra MP X10000, the solution achieved up to 20× faster time to first token and 17× higher effective inference throughput versus running without KV cache offload.
The GPUs did not become cleverer. They had less repeat work to do.

The results move a storage decision directly into the discussion about AI economics. Model pricing gets plenty of attention. Paying expensive accelerators to process the same context repeatedly deserves some too.
Especially as enterprises move from chatbots answering individual questions to agents that can turn one request into a small committee’s worth of activity.
Your agents have a repetition problem

Agentic workflows repeatedly process documents, system instructions and conversation histories. One agent retrieves information, another evaluates it, a third checks the result, and subsequent steps revisit material the system has already processed.
Some repetition is necessary. Recalculating everything is not.

KV cache retains intermediate attention state, allowing compatible requests to reuse earlier computation. Keeping that cache available can reduce the work required before a model starts producing its next answer.
GPU memory, unfortunately, is neither infinite nor priced as though it were.

Long contexts and concurrent sessions compete for that memory. When reusable cache is evicted and later needed, the inference engine may have to rebuild it. More GPU work, more waiting, and no additional insight to show for either.

HPE Alletra MP X10000 provides a shared tier for offloaded cache, while RDMA for S3 accelerates the storage data path. The proposition: retrieve reusable context rather than make the GPU calculate it again.
Compute once. Reuse often. An unremarkable principle, until the alternative appears on the infrastructure bill.
Twenty times faster, with the denominator attached
The Kamiwaza-validated testing used NVIDIA Nemotron 70B and more than 30 concurrent agents under large-context, multi-agent inference.

That matters because this is precisely the sort of real-world workload where repeated context and memory pressure can make cache reuse valuable. Several agents consulting overlapping material create a different opportunity from unrelated, short prompts with little context in common.
Those headline gains are workload-specific. Context length, concurrency, cache hit rates and transfer overhead determine the return. Twenty times faster is a test result, not a universal entitlement.
Buyers should examine the comparison as carefully as the multiplier: the same workload, with and without KV cache offload, and enough concurrency to represent production conditions.
The useful question is how much repeated computation their applications can avoid, and whether retrieving cached context is faster than rebuilding it.
A large performance number without its test conditions is mostly a typography decision.
Garbage in still costs money
Cache reuse addresses repeated computation. It cannot rescue a retrieval system that feeds the model half the company’s document archive to answer one question.

HPE’s broader pitch pairs the X10000 with Data Fabric for governed access to distributed data. The X10000’s data intelligence node generates metadata, classification and embeddings at ingest to help applications retrieve relevant context.
That moves preparation closer to where data lands, rather than leaving every application team to assemble another downstream preparation pipeline.
The economic logic is straightforward. More precise retrieval can mean less irrelevant material in prompts and fewer attempts to obtain a useful answer.
Enterprise archives are rarely short of documents. Distinguishing the current policy from six superseded versions and a presentation called “FINAL_final_v7” is the more interesting problem.

Governance also matters when agents retrieve information and act on it. Relevant context still needs to be authorized context. Faster access to something an agent should never have seen is an awkward definition of progress.
That gives HPE two economic levers: improve what enters inference, then reuse computation where possible.

The distinction matters. Better retrieval can reduce prompt size and retries. KV cache reuse reduces processing work; it does not magically shrink generated answers or oblige an API supplier to lower its bill.
Beyond the cache checkbox
Cache offload is becoming a crowded market. HPE’s strength rests on combining it with data preparation and governance, rather than winning another feature tick.
The practical test for organizations looking to get more value from their AI is how smoothly data preparation, governance and cache reuse operate as a single system.

Can applications find relevant, permitted information without unnecessary copying and preparation? Can the inference engine retain and retrieve reusable context efficiently? Does the combination sustain useful throughput as context windows and agent counts grow?
Those questions connect the architecture to observable outcomes.

Buyers should ask for cache hit rates, time to first token and sustained throughput on their workloads. They should also examine retrieval quality and whether the system completes the intended task. A faster wrong answer remains a wrong answer, however attractive the benchmark chart.
Cost per terabyte remains relevant. So does the cost of making a GPU read the same briefing for the seventh time.
For more information, visit the HPE Alletra Storage MP X10000 web page.
Contributed by HPE
35eec45d08db9fb9: LONDON: British energy giant Shell said Thursday that its net profit more than doubled to US$12.1 billion in the third quarter as the Middle East war disrupted supplies and sent oil and gas prices soaring.
The company had posted profit after tax of US$5.3 billion in the third quarter of 2025.

"Shell's relentless focus on operational performance enabled very strong results in a quarter with continued severe disruption to the global energy system," chief executive Wael Sawan said in a statement.
Revenue rose sharply to US$92.8 billion from US$68.2 billion in the same period a year earlier.
Shell's refining margins, reflecting the spread between the price of crude oil and the fuels derived from it, surged to a record high in the quarter as the Middle East and Ukraine wars hit supplies.
The production and export of refined products in the Middle East have remained heavily disrupted since the war began in late February.
Logistical constraints have complicated the re-routing of fuel supplies, widening the gap between crude oil prices and refined products.
At the same time, Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have prompted Russia, a major player in the oil market, to ban the export of certain products, notably gasoline and diesel.
Refineries unaffected by the conflict are thus benefiting from the tightening global supply of such products.
Profit margins reached US$42 a barrel in the third quarter, up from US$24 a barrel between April and June.
At US$42, the level is far above the previous record set in 2022, just after the invasion of Ukraine by Russia, according to Bloomberg.
Shell also said it would boost its share buyback programme to US$5 billion.

cb637de114e6e7e1: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 29 — Microsoft shares popped more than five per cent yesterday afternoon after it reported better than expected revenue and profit, fuelled by its Azure cloud computing division which grew by 48 per cent in the September quarter.
“We are delivering greater capability, choice, control, and cost efficiency for customers across our entire stack,” Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella said in a statement.
The technology giant recorded US$92.3 billion (RM375 billion) in total revenue and more than US$36.6 billion in profit, the company said in a securities filing yesterday.
Analysts had expected around US$90.6 billion in revenue and US$35.1 billion in profit, according to FactSet.

The quarterly earnings report comes just days after Microsoft offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly a quarter of its workforce, as the tech giant spends heavily on artificial intelligence investments.
It’s the second voluntary buyout offer that Microsoft has offered employees this year, after giving seven per cent of its US workforce the option to retire early in April.
Microsoft had 223,000 employees globally at the end of June, down from 228,000 at the end of 2025, according to regulatory filings.
Earlier this month, Microsoft also announced a new Surface Ultra laptop that runs on Nvidia’s artificial intelligence chips and will cost more than US$2,500.

The launch is part of a broader push by tech companies to release hardware that can handle more AI computing on-device and offline, so users do not have to rely solely on remote cloud data centres, where running AI is slower and more expensive.
AI spending
One of the big questions looming over tech earnings is whether the industry’s heavy AI spending is paying off.
Analysts are expecting US$51 billion in overall spending by Microsoft from July to September, according to FactSet.
Microsoft nearly doubled its spending on “property and equipment” to US$39 billion compared to the same period last year, according to a press release.
The company added 24 new data centres across the world last quarter, Nadella said on a call with analysts yesterday afternoon.
Its overall capital expenditures reached US$45.2 billion, around three-quarters of which was spent on “short-lived assets” like memory chips and storage, Chief Financial Officer Amy Hood said.
In the final quarter of 2026, Microsoft expects capital expenditures to reach more US$50 billion, which will bring its total spending for the year to US$170 billion, she said.
Microsoft competes with Amazon Web Services (AWS) and Google parent Alphabet for cloud computing services customers.
AWS has dominated the sector and remained number one globally by revenue in the second quarter of the year, according to Synergy Research Group.
Microsoft is number two globally, followed by Google.

However, Google yesterday reported that revenue from its cloud division doubled to US$30.7 billion during the quarter, bringing it closer to Microsoft’s Azure revenue, which reached US$33.2 billion in the same period.
Tech companies are expected to collectively spend hundreds of billions of dollars on AI-related expenses this year.
Tech giants have also been taking on debt to fuel AI growth.
“To complement cash generated by the business and preserve financial flexibility, we will access additional sources of funding when we believe it is attractive to do so,” Hood said.
Alphabet recently raised US$85 billion through equity offerings to fund its AI data centre expansion.
On Monday, Facebook parent company Meta said it would raise US$35 billion through a stock offering to fund its own AI investments.

That stock offering is also a sort of financial carrot intended to keep CEO Mark Zuckerberg in California, where voters in November will decide whether to approve a temporary tax on wealth held by billionaires who reside in the state.
Amazon reports its quarterly earnings today. — AFP
a4a7292cb9d065d2: WASHINGTON, Oct 29 — Shares in Google parent Alphabet fell more than 10 per cent in after-hours trading yesterday as the company reported lower-than-expected profit and a slowdown in its advertising business while it maintained big spending on AI.
Net profit slid 25 per cent from a year earlier to US$26.2 billion (RM106 billion) in the July-to-September period, or US$2.12 per share, well short of expectations by analysts surveyed by FactSet.
Alphabet booked an US$8.7 billion loss on its equity investments, which it attributed to its stake in SpaceX, the Elon Musk-led company where shares have struggled since going public in June.
Revenue rose 25 per cent to US$127.6 billion, slightly below the roughly US$128 billion analysts had forecast.

Advertising revenue grew 11 per cent to US$82.0 billion, short of expectations. Revenue from Google’s search business, still the company’s largest source of income, rose 12 per cent to US$63.4 billion, slowing from 17 per cent growth in the previous quarter.

YouTube, now the most-watched content provider on American TV screens, saw advertising revenue grow nine per cent to US$11.2 billion, down from 13 per cent growth in the previous quarter. YouTube Music and Premium passed 150 million subscribers worldwide, including trials.
Google Cloud, which rents computing power and AI tools to businesses, saw revenue jump 103 per cent to US$30.7 billion, ahead of analyst expectations.
The company said sales of its in-house AI chips, known as TPUs, contributed significantly to that growth. Operating income for the unit tripled to US$11.1 billion.
Google is also selling its TPU chips to outside companies, in a growing challenge to market leader Nvidia. OpenAI plans to buy some of the chips, according to media reports this week.
Alphabet’s “Other Bets” division, which includes robotaxi company Waymo, posted revenue of US$372 million and an operating loss of US$2.0 billion.
Waymo now provides more than 500,000 paid rides per week across 15 US metropolitan areas and aims to reach one million weekly rides by the end of the year.
‘Long-range planning’
Alphabet spent US$51.4 billion on capital expenditures during the quarter, mostly on data centers and AI chips, more than double the US$24 billion a year earlier.

b7db9f0c18d3cdc5: A scientist working on data gathered by the Rubin Observatory has found a strong candidate for our solar system’s sixth known dwarf planet.

The Observatory is run by the USA’s National Science Foundation and Department of Energy, who built it on a remote hilltop in Chile and equipped it with the 3200-megapixel Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) Camera, which came online in June 2026.

As explained in a Tuesday announcement, Rubin Operations team member and project contributor Matthew Holman, of the Center for Astrophysics (CfA) at Harvard & Smithsonian, used search code he developed with CfA colleague Kevin Napier to analyze data captured before LSST operations commenced.
The Observatory says Holman’s and Napier’s code “is built to look at billions of detections of moving objects, compare them, and find the detections that correspond to the same object.”
On October 13, the code spotted an object so bright and distant that it is likely unusually large.
“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”
Other astroboffins sprang into action, dug into other records, and soon found ten years’ worth of relevant data.

Once they all checked their sums, the Minor Planet Center reviewed their work and announced the discovery of the romantically named 2026 ED138 and published lots of data about its orbit, which is at around 46 astronomical units (au). A single au is the distance from Earth to the Sun, and Pluto’s orbit averages 40 au.
Rubin Observatory revealed its part in the effort and declared that 2026 ED138 is a good candidate for certification as a dwarf planet.

The 2026 International Astronomical Union defines a dwarf planet as “an object in orbit around the Sun that is large enough to pull itself into a nearly round shape but has not been able to clear its orbit of debris.”

The Union’s definition of a full planet includes having “an important influence on the orbital stability of the other objects in its neighbourhood.” Dwarf planets whirl about the solar system in relatively close company with many rocky and/or icy objects that orbit under the influence of other bodies, not the nearby dwarf planet.

Rubin boffins think ED138 is between 600 and 1500 kilometers across. If the lower number is correct, it’s the smallest dwarf planet yet observed. Should the larger number be correct, it would be smaller than Pluto, Eris, and Haumea, but larger than Makemake and Ceres.

Scientists at the observatory think ED138 has evaded detection to date because it was found in a region of sky close to the plane of the Milky Way — meaning observers had to pick it out from light cast by billions of stars.

“Rubin Observatory’s regular and continuous monitoring of the entire Southern Hemisphere sky, combined with powerful algorithms that sift through millions to billions of points of light to identify those corresponding to small moving objects, enabled the team to spot ED138 within the crowded field,” the facility boasted. ®

64beab8743078d7b: Japan’s Fujifilm has decided the tape market has so much upside that it needs to boost production of its Linear Tape-Open (LTO) products by five times.
LTO is the sole surviving non-proprietary tape format and is kept alive by HPE, IBM, and Quantum Corp, who head the LTO Program.

As The Register recently reported, shipments of LTO cartridges went backwards during 2025, when buyers shelled out for 160.3 exabytes worth of LTO compared to the record 176.5 exabytes; worth of tape cartridges sold in 2024.
The LTO program attributed the 2025 result to difficult macro-economic conditions, noted that sales picked up strongly in the second half of the year, and predicted record sales in 2026.
Fujifilm seems to agree with that optimistic outlook, as it today announced a plan to spend ¥10 billion ($64 million) over the next two years to expand a tape plant in the Japanese city of Odawara.
The company said AI has made this a sensible investment.

“The rapid spread of generative AI and cloud services is driving exponential growth in the volume of data generated worldwide,” the company’s statement reads. “As a result, establishing environments in which the enormous amounts of data accumulated through AI training and inference as well as the digitalization of business activities can be stored and utilized securely and efficiently is becoming increasingly important in supporting the digital society.”

Fujifilm says its investment will go towards building more tenth-gen LTO tapes, which come in variants that boast native storage capacity of either 30TB or 40TB, and transfer data at 400 MB/s. Many LTO users employ data compression to more than double the capacity of each tape cartridge. Decompressing data takes time, and shifting data off tape doesn't happen in a hurry. Tape users, however, nearly always use it for offline or nearline archives, and understand that access times are not the medium's strong point.

The LTO Program has already defined four more generations of its format and delivers updates about every four years. LTO 11 is therefore due in about 2029 and will reach 70TB capacity. Version 12 will climb to 120TB, before unlucky version 13 shoots up to 210TB. Version 14 will jump to 365TB per cartridge!
The LTO program used to insist that tape drives could read the current past generations of cartridges. That ended with LTO-10 devices, which can only read the current generation of tapes. ®

1cb0b41065cb7013: Gadi Eisenkot or Benjamin Netanyahu – under whose direction will Israel head? Erik Marmor/picture alliance via Getty ImagesThe Israeli election of Oct. 27, 2026, was among the most highly anticipated votes in the country’s history. It was consequential, if not yet conclusive. With nearly all the votes counted, it is still unclear who will lead the country following the first national ballot since the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack, and the devastating wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran that Israel has launched since. The Conversation turned to Dov Waxman, an expert on Israeli politics at the University of California, Los Angeles, to walk us through the main takeaways and the process and difficulties facing anyone trying to form a coalition government following a divided vote. What can we take away from the election results? The first thing to note is simply the massive turnout – with a 77.7% turnout of those eligible voting, the highest turnout in more than two decades. That in itself is significant. It underscores how much importance Israelis attached to this vote. Before the election, many observers were saying that it was one of the most consequential – if not the most consequential – votes, and clearly many Israelis felt the same way. What drove this high turnout was different types of fears. Israelis of all persuasions were worried about how the outcome would affect what kind of country Israel becomes. The second big takeaway is that the ruling coalition, formed by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu after the 2022 election, was resoundingly rejected by the majority of Israeli voters – well over 50% cast their vote for parties opposed to the current government. Likud supporters at an election night event in Jerusalem, Israel. Alexi J. Rosenfeld/Getty Images The five parties that make up Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious coalition went into the election with 68 seats in the 120-seat parliament. That same bloc will now have 53 – and that is a significant loss, no matter how Netanyahu tries to spin this as a victory. It means that those five parties will not be able to form the next government, and as such, the vote stands as a repudiation of the Netanyahu government. Netanyahu’s Likud party will still be the largest in parliament. But its share of the national vote declined, and it looks like it will have six fewer seats in the next parliament, another blow to Netanyahu. Netanyahu’s far-right coalition partners fared worse than expected, too. In part, this was due to “wasted votes” going to a new far-right party that failed to make it above the 3.25% of the national vote needed to be represented in parliament. Also, Likud drew some voters away from these far-right parties who had voted for them in the last election. What drove the Arab parties’ surprise showing? The performance of the Arab majority parties – the more secular and left-wing Joint List and the more religious and conservative United Arab List – is very important. Combined, they currently look to have increased their representation by nine seats, bringing their total to 19, a historic high for them. The reason for that is the massive turnout of Arab voters – much higher than the last election. But also, a less noticed trend is the increase in Jewish votes that those parties received. It is important to note that these are Arab-majority parties, not simply Arab parties. Israeli left-wing protesters call for the formation of a government including Arab parties. Ilia Yefimovich/AFP via Getty Images Aside from Netanyahu, it was also a disappointing result for the main opposition party, Yashar; its leader, Gadi Eisenkot; and the anti-Netanyahu Change Bloc it was part of. The preelection polls suggested that the Zionist opposition bloc would do slightly better than the ruling coalition bloc. But Yashar ended up with over 200,000 fewer votes than Likud, winning a projected 21 seats compared to Likud’s 26, and the “Change Bloc” is heading to 48 seats, far short of a parliamentary majority. Ultimately, what is clear is that the Israeli public remains deeply divided. And the fact that there is still a good chance that Netanyahu will emerge as prime minister is remarkable given that many observers had already written his political obituary after the Oct. 7 attack. Was the vote a referendum on Netanyahu? Certainly many saw this as a referendum on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister. For his supporters, Netanyahu is the only person to be trusted with Israel’s security, especially given the threat from Iran. They credit him for weakening – albeit not defeating – the two non-state actors that most threaten Israeli security, Hezbollah and Hamas, and they praise him for ensuring President Donald Trump’s support for Israel. But for those who voted against Netanyahu, the fact that he has refused to take any personal responsibility for the Oct. 7 security failure – amid reports that he had advance warning of a major planned Hamas attack – factored into his poor election showing, as did his government’s refusal to establish a state commission of inquiry to investigate the Oct. 7 security failings. Many also blame Netanyahu for not prioritizing the release of the Israeli hostages held in Gaza and prolonging the war there. He is also held responsible by many for the precipitous decline in Israel’s international standing and for jeopardizing Israel’s crucial alliance with the United States. But it was domestic issues, rather than external ones, that motivated many of those who voted for anti-Netanyahu parties. Many fear that democracy in Israel is under attack, and they particularly oppose the effort by Netanyahu’s government to weaken the power and independence of the Israeli judiciary, which sparked massive street protests in 2023. They also strongly resent that Netanyahu’s government has allowed ultra-Orthodox men to avoid military service, despite the Israeli military’s growing manpower shortage. And on a personal level, Netanyahu is widely perceived as self-serving and dishonest – he is still on trial for corruption. Arab voters have other, more specific concerns that drove them to vote in record numbers, in addition to the Netanyahu government’s policies in Gaza and the West Bank, which they strongly oppose. Chief among them is the soaring rates of violent crime in their communities, which the government – particularly the far-right Itamar Ben-Gvir, who oversees the police – has done nothing to address, say his critics. More broadly, many Palestinian-Arab citizens of Israel fear that if the far-right parties remained in power, their civil rights would be under threat. What should we expect next? The key thing to underline is what happens on election day in Israel is just the first stage in the process of forming a new government. Since no party ever receives a majority of seats in the parliament, what really matters is what happens after the election when the coalition building begins. This can take weeks, if not longer. The party with the largest number of seats typically gets the first chance to assemble a governing coalition, but not always. Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, will choose who gets the first chance to form a government based on who is most likely to succeed. Right now, it looks like Eisenkot will get the first opportunity, but his only real option is to form a minority government that would depend on the parliamentary support of the Arab-majority parties – which some members of his Change Bloc adamantly oppose. Former Israeli military chief and Yashar party leader Gadi Eisenkot waves an Israeli flag as he addresses supporters on Oct. 28, 2026. Tomer Neuberg/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images Despite the success of the Arab-majority parties in the election, it is unlikely they will be invited to be formal members of any coalition – although that has happened once in the past, when the United Arab List joined the short-lived government of 2021-22 led by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid. If Eisenkot is unable to form a government, then Netanyahu will get the chance. He could try to entice some leaders of the parties in the Change bloc to defect and join a right-wing government under his leadership, or a broader “national unity” government with a rotating leader. Netanyahu did that in the past with Benny Gantz, but then he later prevented Gantz from becoming prime minister – so I doubt Eisenkot would agree to do this with Netanyahu. There are reports in the media that the Trump administration would like a national unity government in Israel, so that might increase the pressure on Eisenkot to accept this outcome. And should war with Iran heat up again, that would increase the pressure. The most likely scenario, I believe, is that neither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot will be able to form a government, and a new election will be called, with Netanyahu as caretaker prime minister until that vote. Netanyahu has reason to hope that his bloc will do better in another election, so that may well be his game plan. In which case, it will be many months until Israel has a new government. Dov Waxman does not work for, consult, own shares in or receive funding from any company or organization that would benefit from this article, and has disclosed no relevant affiliations beyond their academic appointment.
05fbd3b81be964a0: From Martin Vengadesan
I couldn’t help but be struck by the contrasting leadership styles on display in the run-up to the Melaka polls.
While neither is a candidate for chief minister, both PKR’s Adam Adli and Umno’s Dr Akmal Saleh are the faces of the future for their respective parties.
To me, Adam of PKR displays a soft-spoken, progressive style. There is backbone to his principles, and he was a student leader who was detained and harassed by the previous regime.
He chose to join a multiracial party and has progressed from PKR Youth chief to deputy minister of higher education after winning the Hang Tuah Jaya parliamentary seat.
While he often comes under the cosh over the failed PTPTN loan abolition, I have seen him at work trying to extend the benefits of our nation to its less fortunate.
On the other hand, there’s the rabble-rousing Akmal of Umno. The two men were born a year apart but represent very different ways of thinking.
Indeed, his career reads to me like a hall of shame. But presumably, it has some appeal among the rempit crowd.

Just last week came another defamation suit loss, as the Melaka High Court ruled in Teresa Kok’s favour over his September 2024 remarks slamming her for questioning a proposed mandatory halal certification.
Kok was awarded RM250,000 in general and aggravated damages, plus RM50,000 in costs. He had called her an “old Nyonya” and suggested placing a non-halal logo on her forehead.

Now he says he is prepared to give up his bid to defend the Merlimau state seat in the Melaka election on Nov 14 if the court case he faces over a charge under Section 505(b) of the Penal Code hurts Umno and Barisan Nasional’s chances at the polls.
Akmal is charged with making statements on his Facebook page that allegedly caused public fear, alarm, or disruption to public order.
The charge stems from a viral Facebook video and post made around Aug 11, 2025, regarding an incident in which the Jalur Gemilang was displayed upside down.
Akmal said he had conveyed his position to Umno president Ahmad Zahid Hamidi, stressing that the party’s interests must come before his personal ambitions.
This is, of course, merely the latest transgression by a man who has positioned himself as an ethnic champion. Akmal was also previously involved in a defamation suit brought by his sibling.

In 2024, he called on the prime minister to sack tourism, arts and culture minister Tiong King Sing after bak kut teh was recognised as a national heritage food. In the same year, he was involved in a dispute over vernacular schools that led to an insinuation that his opponent, P Ramasamy, was drunk.
And of course he led the KK Mart boycott campaign after socks bearing the word “Allah” were discovered on sale there. Is his brand of politics toxic or constructive? I leave you to decide.

Adam has been working quietly to build consensus. The fact that he cares about all Malaysians does not make him any less of a member of his race or religion. In fact, that is one of the great false assumptions in Malaysian public life.
In his roles at the higher education ministry and the youth and sports ministry, Adam has supported several public-facing initiatives, including PTPTN loan repayment flexibility.

Under the repayment measures announced in the 2027 budget, borrowers earning between RM2,501 and RM3,000 a month are required to make minimum monthly payments of RM50, while those earning below RM2,500 a month are eligible for repayment exemptions.

Other initiatives for students include support for transit passes like My50 and MyKomuter50, alongside the FlySiswa flight subsidy of RM500 for students who travel between Peninsular Malaysia and East Malaysia.
He has promoted technical and vocational education and training (TVET) to bolster graduate employability and supported the revival of the Rakan Muda programme for youth development.
He has also been involved in local infrastructure and welfare projects in Hang Tuah Jaya, such as local flood mitigation.
More than anything else, he views the future with a keen mind and open heart. These are the leaders we need if we are to stop going around in circles.
Martin Vengadesan is a former editor who currently serves as a strategic communications consultant to the communications ministry.

7929e6ff65cd98ce: Shares in Google’s parent company Alphabet dived by almost ten percent on Wednesday, after the web giant admitted AI-powered searches earn it less money than it earns by serving ads with its old-school search engine.

Alphabet on Wednesday reported its Q3 results, which included news that its year-over-year search query growth rate is the highest it’s been in the last five years. Some of that growth comes from users adopting “AI Mode” – Google’s latest LLM-powered search system.
Google’s revenue from search rose 12 percent year-over-year to $63.25 billion, a little lower than the 14.5 percent growth the company reported in last year’s Q3.
During Alphabet’s earnings call, chief business officer Philipp Schindler said the slowdown was caused by “lower monetization we were seeing in AI Mode.”

That’s a worry given that Google is spending enormous sums on infrastructure. $51.4 billion went out the door in Q3, around two thirds of it going towards servers and networking equipment. The rest funded datacenter builds.

That spending appears to have impacted profitability, as Alphabet reported $26.17 billion net income for the quarter. Last year’s Q3, during which Google revenue was $102.35 billion, produced $35 billion net income.
Schindler argued that AI search will pay off.

“On AI Mode, many of these queries are upper funnel queries, allowing us to capture new, high-value commercial intent,” he told investors. “In addition, the majority of AI Mode queries are incremental, creating more monetization opportunities over time.”
Google tried to seize one of those opportunities today, by turning on ads alongside AI Mode searches around the world, after first testing them in the US only.
But for now, AI Mode searches aren’t as lucrative as Google’s existing search business, which brought in just under half of Alphabet's $125.8 billion quarterly revenue.

Google’s cloud is its next-best earner, at $24.75 billion for the quarter, but it has troubles too because the Big G doesn’t have enough capacity to serve all its customers. The company has started to offload some customer workloads to third parties, and warned that will dent its future margins.

Thomas Kurian, Google Cloud’s CEO, said the company has over 100 companies using its TPU silicon, adding that “All of the inventory for TPU systems are associated with committed contracts” – meaning Google can see some revenue to cover some capex. The company expects to book revenue from TPU sales to third parties in coming quarters.

CEO Sundar Pichai was full of optimism for future AI revenue, noting that Google’s Gemini app has won a billion users faster than any other product in the company’s history, and praising the performance of its models. He said Google is moving fast to create agentic AI tools, but will focus on business customers for starters, “because the bar for security, safety, and governance is extremely high.”
“As a next step, we are bringing these features to Search and also, of course, to our billion users on the Gemini app,” he added.
Pichai didn’t say when agentic AI will come to search or if he expects it will avoid the monetization issues AI Mode has already caused.
Yet the company also stuck to its $195-$205 billion capital expenditure forecast for this year and said it intends to spend “significantly” more in 2027. ®
883754d3b0d62fe2: KUALA LUMPUR, Oct 29 — The ringgit opened higher against the US dollar today, supported by the possibility of overnight policy rate (OPR) normalisation at Bank Negara Malaysia’s (BNM) Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) meeting next week.

Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the unchanged OPR at 2.75 per cent could provide support for the local currency.

“It appears that the Federal Reserve is taking a guarded approach to reach its price stability goal at a time when the economy is deemed to be growing at a robust rate.
“On that note, we foresee the ringgit could be well supported,” he told Bernama.

The ringgit gained vis-a-vis the Japanese yen to 2.5798/5851 from 2.5812/5843 at Wednesday’s close, but edged down against the British pound to 5.4268/4374 from 5.4130/4190 and fell against the euro to 4.5427/5516 from 4.5337/5387.

270aee5ea45a14da: Melihat senarai calon wanita untuk PRN Melaka saya sebetulnya terkedu. Ia cepat membawa saya kepada watak-watak wanita ikonik dalam sejarah Kesultanan Melayu Melaka. Sukar untuk memadam watak-watak seperti Tun Kudu, Tun Teja dan Tun Fatimah dari benak. Malangnya wanita yang saya sebutkan ini dihinjak dalam politik.

Ambil sahaja Tun Kudu yang menjadi sekadar 'alat' untuk kepentingan penguasa. Tun Kudu adalah puteri kepada Bendahara Seri Wak Raja dan merupakan permaisuri kepada Sultan Muzaffar Syah yang memerintah Melaka (1446-1459). Namun demikian untuk meredakan perseteruan dua kem politik orang Melayu yang berebutkan kedudukan sebagai bendahara, Sultan Muzzafar Syah telah menceraikan Tun Kudu dan mengaturkan baginda untuk menjadi isteri Bendahara Seri Nara Diraja yang sudah tua kerepot, lagi berusia.

Seri Nara Diraja memang menyebabkan Sultan Muzaffar sakit kepala kerana enggan bersara, membolot jawatan tersebut setelah Bendahara Seri Wak Raja dan hanya sedia melakukannya dengan syarat diberi hadiah gundik sultan. Makanya dalam percaturan Sultan Muzaffar, Paduka Raja Tun Perak, iaitu kekanda Tun Kudu terpaksa mengambil sikap damai. Tun Ali atau Seri Nara Diraja itu adalah bapa saudara Sultan Muzaffar Syah dan pembesar yang bertanggungjawab mengatur dan meletakkan Sultan Muzaffar di atas takhta pada 1446.

Watak kedua pula adalah Tun Teja iaitu anak Bendahara Pahang Seri Amar Bangsa Diraja dan disebut sebagai tunangan kepada Sultan Pahang, Sultan Abdul Jalil. Akan tetapi Sultan Mahmud Syah yang gila perempuan telah berusaha mendapatkan Tun Teja lantas bertitah kepada pembesar; "Barang siapa membawa anak Bendahara Pahang itu ke mari, apa yang dikehendakinya ku anugerahkan akan dia. Jikalau ia hendakkan sekerat kota dengan kerajaan sekalipun kita anugerahkan".

Dalam riwayat, Tun Teja dilarikan oleh Hang Nadim (menantu kepada Laksamana Hang Tuah) demi menebus kesalahannya terhadap sultan. Untuk melakukannya, Hang Nadim merasuah seorang pelulut untuk memujuk Tun Teja agar kelak berkahwin dengan Sultan Mahmud Syah. Berdasarkan Hikayat Hang Tuah, Tun Teja merupakan seorang yang bermaruah tinggi dan bukanlah gilakan kedudukan. Beliau malah menolak lamaran sultan Melaka, sebaliknya memilih menjadi isteri Megat Panji Alam Terengganu.
Perbuatan pelulut membujuk Tun Teja ini gagal. Oleh sebab Tun Teja liat dan berkeras, malangnya baginda disihir dengan ubat guna-guna lantas dipaksa berkahwin dengan Sultan Mahmud tanpa kerelaan.

Sultan Mahmud Syah selaku raja dan sultan yang gila perempuan seterusnya mensasarkan pula Tun Fatimah. Baginda adalah anak Tun Mutahir dan baru berkahwin dengan Tun Ali. Sultan Mahmud Syah menggunakan kuasa baginda untuk membunuh Tun Ali sebelum merebut Tun Fatimah. Ini juga didorong oleh fitnah Raja Mendaliar kononnya Tun Mutahir sedang merancang untuk menggulingkannya. Sultan menitahkan Tun Sura Diraja dan Tun Indera Segara untuk menghabisi seisi keluarga bendahara. Kesan atau trauma kehilangan seisi keluarga dan suami itu, Tun Fatimah hidup berendam dendam. Dalam riwayat disebut Tun Fatimah itu 'selama ia duduk dengan Sultan Mahmud Syah jangankan ia tertawa, tersenyum pun tiada pernah'. Bahkan setiap kali mengandung, baginda menggugurkan kandungannya.

Kisah raja gila seks, termakan fitnah dan pertelingkahan politik antara kem pembesar untuk berebut kedudukan dan jawatan bendahara ini adalah satu renungan yang penting untuk kita memahami pula konteks semasa.

Hari ini Melaka menyaksikan sekali lagi perebutan kuasa dalam bentuk pilihan raya. Dengan mengambil ingatan, Melaka melayan watak wanita sebagai alat percaturan politik, pemuas nafsu dan sekadar di pinggiran; saya dengan berhati-hati mencari parti politik yang tidak melakukan hal-hal sedemikian. Saya juga menyuruhkan kaum keluarga saya yang terdiri dari pengundi wanita untuk tidak memilih mereka yang melayan wanita dengan buruk.

Sudah tentu kita telah menjauhi era kesultanan Melayu yang penuh malapetaka seperti di atas. Iklim politik kita juga harapnya tidaklah setoksik itu. Pun tenung punya tenung saya mesti memastikan parti politik manakah yang tidak menjadikan wanita sekadar melukut di tepi gantang. Saya benci perlakuan Melaka di zaman lampau tersebut.

Mengapakah saya memberi tumpuan kepada wanita? Jawapan mudahnya, ini adalah kerana dalam rekod, terdapat 348,849 orang pengundi di PRN Melaka kali ini adalah perempuan, iaitu 50.73% daripada jumlah keseluruhan pemilih. Justeru saya berpandangan penting untuk kita melihat komponen parti manakah yang paling bersungguh memperjuangkan wanita.

Letak duduk wanita dalam politik adalah penting terutama setelah ucapan kontroversi di Persidangan Agung Umno 2026, iaitu apabila Presiden Zahid Hamidi berseloroh mengatakan Ketua Wanita Noraini Ahmad nampak macam 'nenek-nenek'.

Pakatan Harapan menjanjikan lima orang calon wanita untuk membawa mandat rakyat Melaka di kawasan masing-masing. Parti Keadilan Rakyat (PKR) mengetengahkan tiga orang calon wanita dalam PRN Melaka, pada 14 November ini. Menurut Setiausaha Agung Fuziah Salleh, daripada sembilan calon yang diketengahkan parti itu, tiga calon wanita telah diberi kepercayaan untuk bertanding, dan ini mewakili 33.3% daripada keseluruhan calon PKR pada PRN. Calon wanita ini adalah Ketua Pemuda Tangga Batu, Farzana Hayani Nasir di Klebang; Ketua Penerangan Wanita Ginie Lim Siew Lin yang sekali lagi bertanding di DUN Machap Jaya, dan Esma Eazreen Husin di Rim. Farzana, seorang Gen Z baru-baru ini mendapat perhatian ramai apabila diusir seorang anggota wanita Umno dari menghadiri program Kampung Angkat Madani di kawasan masjid Bukit Rambai.

Dalam pada itu, Amanah di Merlimau membawakan Rahayu Hamzah. Beliau akan membawa tugas besar untuk menewaskan Ketua Pemuda Umno, Dr Akmal Saleh yang baru-baru ini kalah dalam saman berkaitan isu cadangan pensijilan halal, di mana Akmal merujuk Ahli Parlimen Seputeh, Teresa Kok sebagai 'nyonya tua'. Akmal diperintahkan membayar ganti rugi berjumlah RM250,000 kepada Teresa. Ini termasuklah kos perundangan sebanyak RM50,000 (jumlah keseluruhan RM300,000). Dalam vonis hakim, iaitu Isa Aziz Ibrahim; Akmal malah ditegur dengan kata-kata bahawa adab itu membentuk keperibadian.

Menariknya jumlah peratusan pengundi wanita di DUN N.27 Merlimau, Melaka ini adalah sebanyak 52.45% berdasarkan data rasmi Suruhanjaya Pilihan Raya Malaysia. Justeru kita akan mengetahui minda atau kognitif pengundi wanita di Merlimau, bagaimana mereka melayan wanita itu sendiri. Apakah misalnya 'adab membentuk keperibadian' akan dijadikan pedoman.
Sebuah lagi parti komponen Pakatan Harapan, DAP pula menaruh harapan menerusi Leng Chau Yen yang bertanding di kerusi DUN N22 Bandar Hilir.

Umno terus tampil meletakkan calon-calon lelaki yang berusia di kebanyakan kerusi. Parti ini juga sekadar meletakkan tiga calon wanita untuk bertanding. Hal ini tentulah menyedihkan. Calon wanita dikemukakan di Pengkalan Batu (menggugurkan penyandang wanita sebelum ini yang agak cekatan). Dalam pada itu, muka lama Tuminah Kadi dikitar semula di Pantai Kundor; sementara bekas pengacara rancangan hiburan dikekalkan di Rim, iaitu Khaidhirah anak ketua menteri Melaka kelapan, Abu Zahar Ithnin.

Adalah menarik untuk kita melihat bagaimana hampir separuh pengundi wanita di Melaka kelak mengundi. Yakni apakah mereka akan membiarkan watak seperti Tun Teja, Tun Kudu dan Tun Fatimah menjadi igauan politik di Melaka; atau melakukan sesuatu yang beradab.

bea6ae276ae0bb55: When a child refuses to share a table with another child because one eats pork, we are no longer talking about a minor classroom incident. We are talking about a failure of national education.
Malaysia’s schools are now producing children who see difference as contamination, faith as a barrier, and fellow Malaysians as people to be avoided.
This is not unity. It is segregation being taught early, quietly and dangerously.
A warning from the classroom

Puncak Borneo MP Willie Mongin recently revealed that some primary school pupils had refused to sit beside classmates of another faith. Among the reasons were that a classmate was eating pork or wearing a cross.
Let that sink in.
Children young enough to still be learning multiplication tables are already being taught, directly or indirectly, that another child’s food, religion or symbol makes them unworthy of friendship.
Do not hide behind the excuse that “children repeat what they hear at home”. Of course, families matter.
But schools are where society either corrects prejudice or normalises it. If a child can carry such intolerance into a classroom without being firmly challenged, then the classroom has failed.
Unity cannot remain a slogan
For decades, Malaysia has recited the Rukun Negara, held unity-themed assemblies and printed national slogans on walls, banners and exercise books.
Yet what is the value of a national principle if a child will not sit beside another child because of what that child eats or believes?

The Rukun Negara is not decoration. It is not a mural. It is not a slogan for official events. If it means anything, it must be visible in how children treat one another every day, in classrooms, canteens, playgrounds and school buses.
Our education system has become too comfortable with symbolism. It celebrates diversity on stage but often fails to build genuine relationships across communities in daily school life.
Separate childhoods, divided futures
Malaysia’s national, Chinese and Tamil primary schools reflect our multicultural reality. Preserving mother tongues and cultural identity is legitimate and necessary.
But preserving identity must not mean raising children in social isolation.

When pupils spend their formative years largely among those who look, pray, eat and speak like them, anything different becomes unfamiliar. And unfamiliarity easily induces fear. Fear becomes prejudice. Prejudice breeds rejection.
How can we expect adults to build a united Malaysia if, as children, they were never given real opportunities to know one another?

Joint sports, debates, arts, science projects, community service and shared classrooms must not be occasional photo opportunities. They must be routine, structured and compulsory parts of school life, not pleasing politicians for their occasional visit to school.
Stop pretending the system is fair
We must also stop pretending that education policy is neutral.
For too long, access to opportunities, scholarships, school placements and pathways has been viewed through racial lenses.
Whatever the original intention, the consequence is clear: many young Malaysians grow up believing that their future depends more on their ethnicity than their effort, talent or need.

Helping the disadvantaged is right. But assistance must be transparent, needs-based and accountable. A system that leaves one community feeling privileged and another feeling excluded cannot claim to be building unity.
A child who believes the system does not value them equally will not easily believe the nation values them equally.
Malaysia built on community effort

Our history lessons must stop being exercises in memorising dates and names. They must teach the harder truth: Malaysia was built through negotiation, compromise and cooperation among communities that did not always share the same faith, language or customs.
Tunku Abdul Rahman, Tun Tan Siew Sin and Tun VT Sambanthan came from different communities, yet they worked towards one national objective: independence.
If our founding leaders could sit at the same table and build a nation, why should a child today refuse to sit beside a classmate because of pork or a cross?
No community owns Malaysia. Every community helped build it. Every community has a stake in protecting it.
The education ministry must answer
This is not a problem to be passed to the national unity ministry while the education ministry (MoE) hides behind curriculum documents.
The MoE must answer directly:
Why are children absorbing religious intolerance in schools?
Are teachers trained to identify and confront prejudice early?
Are schools required to create meaningful interaction across communities?
Are incidents of discrimination investigated, recorded and corrected?
Are school leaders held accountable when unity exists only in speeches?
If the ministry cannot enforce the values it preaches, then it is not merely failing pupils. It is failing Malaysia.
Make unity measurable
National unity must become part of every subject, every school and every level of education.
Kindergartens must teach children to play, share and cooperate across backgrounds. Primary and secondary schools must run regular joint programmes with schools of different streams.
History, literature and civics must teach shared nationhood, not narrow narratives. Group work must deliberately bring children out of familiar ethnic and religious circles.

Teachers need training in inclusive classroom practices, religious literacy and conflict resolution. Textbook writers must be held accountable for accuracy, balance and the removal of stereotypes, not mere focus on any one community.
And the ministry must publish measurable indicators: pupils’ sense of belonging, participation in cross-community activities, teacher preparedness, complaints handled and corrective action taken.
Unity must be assessed, not merely announced.
The future is sitting in our classrooms
A child who refuses to share a table today may become an adult who refuses to share a country tomorrow.
This is the harsh truth Malaysia must face: our education system is not merely underperforming academically; it is failing in its duty to mould Malaysians.

We can continue producing students with excellent grades but shallow citizenship. Or we can rebuild schools into places where children learn that faith, food, language and culture must never determine who deserves their friendship.
Malaysia’s future will not be decided only in parliament or boardrooms. It will be decided at classroom tables, where children either learn to see one another as strangers, or as fellow Malaysians.

3f40214d76a7be3b: SAN FRANCISCO, Oct 29 — No startup has ever grown so fast. In five years, Anthropic has become an AI giant valued at US$1 trillion (RM4.08 trillion), and it is now aiming for a record-breaking stock market debut.
But it faces three threats: rivals that are catching up, prices that are collapsing, and bills that keep climbing.
Anthropic spells out the risks in its Wall Street prospectus, published Monday.
The first is commoditisation: “the degree of differentiation among advanced AI models may narrow,” the company warns.

The San Francisco-based firm also says “substantially all of our revenue” comes from its AI tools. Unlike Google or Meta, it has no advertising empire to fall back on if business takes a hit, and no cloud business like Microsoft’s or SpaceX’s.
Investors have already grown nervous. In mid-August, shareholders were floating a valuation of US$2 trillion.
But quarter-on-quarter growth slowed from 145 per cent in the second quarter to 45 per cent in the third, cooling expectations to around US$1.5 trillion.
Cheap and open
So-called open AI models, which anyone can download and modify, are close behind closed models such as Claude or ChatGPT, which are available only through their owners’ paid services.
The performance of open models trails by only about four months on average, according to research institute Epoch AI.
They include Kimi K3.1 Pro from Chinese company Moonshot, which costs half as much as Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s current flagship.
And among paid models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, none has stayed on top for long.
Anthropic also acknowledges it is holding itself back: its safety measures “could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints.”
Still, the company says each new version of Claude has boosted sales. More than 80 per cent of its revenue last quarter came from models less than six months old.
Prices collapsing

When products look alike, prices fall. According to Morningstar, the price of having AI process the same amount of text, at the same level of performance, has dropped 97 per cent, from US$17 at the end of 2024 to 50 cents today.
Anthropic itself cut the price of Claude Opus by 20 per cent in September, and OpenAI cut the price of one of its flagship models by a factor of five in July.
The effect is already visible at Vercel, a developer platform that routes requests across AI models.
In August, more than half of the text it handled was processed by open models, up from 13 per cent in April.
Even so, Anthropic still captured nearly two-thirds of spending on the platform.
Even a 90 per cent price cut would not shrink total spending on AI as long as usage keeps growing at its current pace, said Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Traffic transits past Anthropic’s headquarters in San Francisco, California October 27, 2026. — Benjamin Fanjoy/Getty Images/AFP pic
‘Triple whammy’
Anthropic’s costs, by contrast, are largely locked in. To stay ahead, each new Claude model has to be bigger than the last, trained on more data using more computing power.
Since late 2025, the company has committed to paying at least US$417 billion to rent chips and servers.
That is nearly 13 years of sales at its first-half 2026 pace, and the total could nearly double if cancellable or planned contracts are included.
These commitments are due no matter the state of its business, Anthropic warns.
The bet involves the entire industry: Google and Amazon are at once Anthropic’s shareholders, its suppliers and its resellers.

If AI turns out to be less profitable than expected, the International Monetary Fund fears a “triple whammy” from these intertwined investments: falling stock prices, debts that are harder to repay, and promised revenue that never materialises.
The independent research firm New Constructs called the listing “an unprecedented test of investor gullibility.”
To pay these bills, Anthropic is counting on money from the stock market, which is not unlimited.
SpaceX, Elon Musk’s rocket and AI company, raised record sums there in June, while Google and Meta, which are pouring fortunes into data centres, are also seeking fresh capital.
OpenAI, whose chief Sam Altman called a listing “ill-advised” this year, has chosen to wait until 2027, giving it time to see how Wall Street treats its big rival. — AFP

867089db0a112536: Anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy has unilaterally passed a rule that will allow specialty pharmacies to sell six specific peptide drugs, overruling scientists at the Food and Drug Administration.

The peptides are popular among members of Kennedy's Make America Health Again movement, and many prominent MAHA figures and Kennedy allies sell them. Kennedy said he uses some of the peptides and called himself a "big fan." But FDA scientists continue to say there is insufficient evidence to show if they're effective, and they are potentially dangerous. In 2023, the safety concerns led the FDA to remove the six peptides from a list of drugs that can be made by specialty pharmacies called compounding pharmacies—which make customized formulations of drugs for patients, or, in cases such as this, specialty drugs in bulk.

Kennedy's new rule sidesteps the need to formally undo that FDA action. The rule is titled "Enforcement Discretion Policy Regarding 503A Compounding Using Certain Peptide Bulk Drug Substances" and was made available Wednesday on the Federal Register, with the final publication date set for October 30. The rule does not change the regulatory status of the peptide; instead, it states the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) will no longer take enforcement action against compounding pharmacies for making the peptides, essentially giving them a green light to freely produce and sell them. Kennedy had quietly proposed this rule earlier this month.
30c1e927c6551931: Google is working with NASA to develop a robotic medical assistant that could help astronauts on future deep-space missions.

Chocolate Factory's public sector VP Jim Kelly said in a Tuesday blog post that the company's latest moonshot could take its technology far beyond the lunar surface, with Google's public sector arm partnering with NASA's Human Research Program, Johnson Space Center's robotics team, and the Jet Propulsion Laboratory to develop a robot that could assist astronauts with medical tasks, cargo handling, and routine maintenance.

The robotics project builds on the Crew Medical Officer Digital Assistant (CMO-DA), an AI-powered medical decision-support system Google has been working on with NASA since last year. CMO-DA, which is powered by the Red Hat-supported open source local AI tool RamaLama, is already being evaluated on Earth-bound copies of computers used aboard the ISS. It’s designed to run AI models locally for evaluation of medical issues, which will be a key part of future space missions due to the communications lag between Earth and astronauts in deep space.

“An astronaut on a future deep space mission to Mars could face severe operational challenges—including round-trip communication latencies of up to 44 minutes, making real-time medical guidance for crew nearly impossible,” Kelly said in this week’s blog post.
Google and NASA envision the robot as an assistant to a human crew medical officer, helping with medical tasks and doing other work when bedside assistance isn't required.

“To maximize its utility for a lean crew, the robotic system is designed as a versatile 'payload' handler capable of managing cargo, logistics, and equipment,” Kelly explained. “When not needed for routine maintenance like organizing tools or securing compartments, it can pivot to medical support.”

As one example of its potential use, the Google public sector VP explained that, were someone to experience severe back pain potentially caused by kidney stones, the robot could fetch and prep an ultrasound machine, leaving the crew medical officer to interpret the scan and decide on treatment.

“The ultimate goal is to build a robotic system that can execute a variety of tasks via simple voice instructions, under the astronauts’ direct supervision and command,” Kelly said. “For instance, the robot might be directed to assist with routine health monitoring—such as capturing basic vitals or simple ultrasounds—under the strict guidance of a human crew medical officer.”
So, not a full-fledged digital medical officer as much as an extra set of hands for an overworked human doc.

As for the status of the project, it doesn't appear to have advanced too far yet. Google outlines several technologies being explored, including JPL's work adapting satellite situational-awareness tools originally used to track objects in orbit to help the robot navigate 3D spaces. The project remains at the proof-of-concept stage, with early laboratory demonstrations conducted, but Google hasn't confirmed whether a fully integrated, space-ready robot exists.

Kelly explained that Google used DeepMind's MuJoCo physics simulator to test the robot's movements, and that the system scored an initial 85 percent success rate in early lab tests involving locating and moving a medical bag – not exactly proof that it's ready to assist with medical procedures, but it's a start.

Google referred us to NASA for questions, but the space agency declined to get into specifics. The agency only told us it's working on a variety of "super intelligence" (eye roll - that's AI to those of us operating in reality) projects for its many missions, and that it's working with partners to assess them for future applications. ®
d29f179e903a044f: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments.

An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all.

Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes.

“There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.”

The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says.
