35ef08cfc995907f: Now, Russian disinformation fuels the memory of violent historic conflicts, and Polish empathy is burning out
Originally published on Global Voices

Folkowisko during the “Borderland Memory” project, bringing Ukrainian and Polish youth together to preserve shared historical heritage, restore historic cemeteries, and strengthen cross-cultural friendship. Photo: Folkowisko. Used with permission.

Marcin Piotrowski remembers the beginning of his work in Ukraine through the Budomierz-Hruszów border crossing in February 2022, days after the launch of Russia’s war on Ukraine. “We crossed the border on the second day after the full-scale invasion,” he says, “and there were hundreds of people there. Nobody was helping them.”

People were waiting for days to enter Poland, some in cars and some on foot, as temperatures fell to around minus 15 degrees Celsius. On the Polish side, food and transport had been organised, but the queues on the Ukrainian side had become a challenge of their own. Piotrowski and volunteers from his Polish association, Folkowisko, decided to intervene. “We had experience because our association organises festivals,” he explains. “We put up tents, brought volunteers, and our medical service from the festival came as well. Later, we started helping at other border crossings, then in Lviv at the railway station, and we began working with volunteers from different parts of Ukraine.”

What began as emergency assistance developed into a network of projects across the Polish-Ukrainian border. Folkowisko helped establish a medical clinic and education centre in Nakhachiv, near the Polish border, where Polish and Ukrainian cultural workers have held joint workshops. The organisation has also supported psychological care, trained Ukrainian psychologists and social workers, and brought Ukrainian families affected by the war to Poland for temporary respite.

But Folkowisko's work is not only about the present. Piotrowski is also interested in the history of the border region, and in what happens when difficult memories are discussed through contact rather than isolation. “Before the Second World War, there were more than a thousand Ukrainians in the village where we work,” he says, referring to a locality in what is now eastern Poland. “Today, there are 43 people and they are all Polish. People were resettled in 1945 and 1947, during Operation Vistula. This was a place where Jews, Poles and Ukrainians lived together, and 80 years ago you could not really say where the border was.”

The history separating the two societies is particularly painful. During World War II, tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed by Ukrainian nationalist formations in the Volhynia region. Polish nationalist groups retaliated, killing thousands of Ukrainian civilians. The competing memories of these events have remained politically sensitive, especially in families whose relatives were victims.

After the fall of communism, the history of Volhynia became increasingly prominent in Polish public debate. In Ukraine, meanwhile, the Ukrainian Insurgent Army (UPA) acquired an important place in national memory because of its role in the struggle for Ukrainian independence against Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union. Disputes over monuments, commemorations, exhumations and historical figures have repeatedly affected relations between Warsaw and Kyiv.

The subject is also vulnerable to manipulation, according to Łukasz Wojtkowski, an assistant professor at Nicolaus Copernicus University in Toruń, who researches information operations and disinformation. He argues that historical grievances can be connected to contemporary fears and used to deepen divisions: “Volhynia is a playbook for propaganda and disguised disinformation,” he explains. “It is basically the only open case between those two nations that can spark the engine of disinformation and hatred. Russia can put two irons in the fire at the same time: it can increase the hatred between Poland and Ukraine, and it can reinforce the Russian narrative that there is a fascist regime in Kyiv.”

Anna Mierzyńska, a Polish journalist and social media researcher specialising in disinformation, has studied similar narratives targeting Polish audiences. “Reliable historical debate,” she stresses, “is always based on listening to both sides and taking new developments into account. Its purpose is not to attack or create hatred, but to explain what happened and find an understanding.” While there is such a debate among historians and experts, she adds that in the Polish information sphere, “many of the posts on this subject are designed to provoke hatred toward Ukrainians.”

Recurring narratives portray Ukrainians as a physical threat to Poles, Mierzyńska continues, using descriptions of the Volhynia crimes to create fear, or to suggest that Ukrainians could seek Polish territory. Existing social problems can also be folded into the same narrative. Long waiting lists for healthcare, for example, existed before the arrival of millions of Ukrainian refugees, but online claims blamed Ukrainians for them. Housing, employment and public services have been framed in similar ways.

The scale of Ukrainian displacement makes the relationship especially important. In 2026, nearly a million Ukrainians took temporary protection in Poland, representing 21.8 percent of all people from Ukraine under temporary protection in the European Union.

We need good contacts between Poles and Ukrainians, integration, getting to know each other and building trust. When we know each other well and trust each other, outside influence becomes much less important. – Anna Mierzyńska

For Piotrowski, the first months after the invasion demonstrated what such contact can look like. “Ordinary citizens living on the border with Ukraine were the first ones to provide immediate support,” he recalls. “I have never seen so much kindness in my life on both sides of the border, and so much reconciliation and understanding.”

Five years into the full-scale war, however, the border has also revealed the limits of that extraordinary solidarity. “I understand that when Poles opened their homes, it could become difficult,” Piotrowski says. “Someone comes who speaks another language, has slightly different customs and wants to stay for a long time. This is what I call empathy burnout.”

He does not regard that exhaustion as proof that the solidarity of 2022 was false, but rather, as a relationship being tested by time. His response is the same one that drives Folkowisko’s cultural work: more contact. “Poles don't know Ukrainians, Ukrainians don't know Poles,” he says. “Our job is to make people meet each other and understand each other.”

This approach means bringing difficult history into conversations in much the same way that Folkowisko’s festivals and programmes bring Polish and Ukrainian participants together while addressing the violence and displacement that transformed the region.

Wojtkowski is more cautious about whether historical reconciliation alone could resolve the wider conflict over competing narratives. “Imagine that tomorrow Poland and Ukraine commemorate every victim, Ukraine admits who was killed and how many people died, Poland admits what happened on its side, and all the exhumations are completed,” he posits. “It would not change everything, because Russia has other narratives.”

He maintains that, when it comes to history, both Polish and Ukrainian society did not do their homework properly. “In Poland, we learned the story of the interwar period as the restoration of the Polish state after more than a hundred years without independence,” he says, “but we did not always learn enough about the Ukrainian experience within that state. Ukraine has its own work to do in confronting everything that happened during the Second World War.”

Wojtkowski further advises that both Poland and Ukraine “should step very carefully, as if on very thin ice.” According to him, there should be signs of goodwill and a willingness to cooperate, but there is still a lot to do politically, academically and socially.

For Piotrowski, however, governments and historians do not have to resolve everything before ordinary people can build relationships: “We are trying to connect people who live ten or 15 kilometres from each other. They have different memories, different histories, but they can still meet and work together.”

As Ukraine moves toward the European Union, and as Polish and Ukrainian lives become increasingly intertwined, those everyday relationships may shape how the two societies handle their shared past. “If we lose the contact between ordinary people across both countries,” Piotrowski maintains, “then it becomes much easier to build the walls. And once the walls are there, it is much harder to build the bridges again.”

Anna Romandash is an award-winning journalist and co-author of “Women of Ukraine: Reportages from the War and Beyond.”
Nata Yasevych is a multimedia producer, media maker, and journalist, covering social issues and politics.

f3b6de314f91f101: Each year, Climate Week NYC brings together more than 100,000 people in more than 1,000 events across the city to discuss climate challenges, explore solutions, and spur action. Participants come from industry, academia, philanthropy, nonprofits, government, and finance and venture capital. And this year, the mix included a strong, cross-campus presence from MIT. The MIT community could be seen multiple days during Climate Week, with appearances by Evelyn Wang, vice president for energy and climate, at the official opening ceremony discussing artificial intelligence and the climate equation; an event co-hosted by MIT and the Bezos Earth Fund on climate innovation; and 14 sessions organized by the MIT Climate Project and eight MIT departments, labs, centers, and initiatives — including the Abdul Latif Jameel Water and Food Systems Lab (J-WAFS), the MIT Sloan Sustainability Initiative, the Center for Transportation and Logistics (CTL), MIT Lincoln Laboratory, MIT Open Learning, the MIT Initiative for New Manufacturing (INM), the MIT Climate Policy Center, and the Priscilla King Gray (PKG) Center for Social Impact. “The MIT Climate Project is a whole-of-MIT mobilization, but no single institution can deliver the climate solutions the world needs — from reducing greenhouse gas emissions to adapting to a changing climate and building more-resilient communities and systems,” said Wang, who is also the Ford Professor of Engineering in the Department of Mechanical Engineering. “Climate Week New York is important because it convenes the range of stakeholders and sectors that must work together to confront these challenges. When we connect the MIT community with this global network, we uncover powerful possibilities to strengthen not only our own efforts, but the world’s capacity for change.” One location, numerous events Climate Week NYC was held Sept. 21-27 at venues across Manhattan and other New York boroughs. Utilizing multiple spaces at the Dream Downtown Hotel in the Chelsea neighborhood of Manhattan, the MIT coalition attracted more than 700 attendees for events ranging from small, private conversations to workshops and panel presentations. Larger sessions included “The Future of Data Centers: Technologies to Change the Paradigm.” “Data centers are at an inflection point, facing interconnected technical, operational, economic, and community constraints that demand cross-sector dialogue and innovation,” says Gang Chen, the Carl Richard Soderberg Professor of Power Engineering and faculty director of the Climate Project at MIT. Chen, who leads the Data Centers of the Future frontier for the Climate Project, convened a panel of experts across research and industry to address technologies that can change the paradigm. “Technology can't solve all the challenges we’re facing with data centers, but technology has a significant role to play in shaping a future role that is more sustainable and better for the communities that are home to these facilities,” Chen says. “This session was a productive conversation on data center challenges and the potential solutions to overcome them.”  The workshop “Next-Generation Super Pollutant Solutions: Challenges and Opportunities,” hosted by Jesse Kroll, a faculty director and lead for the Super Pollutants frontier for the Climate Project, convened speakers from the Environmental Defense Fund, Spark Climate Solutions, and across MIT labs and initiatives.  Accounting for nearly half of all global anthropogenic warming to date, super pollutants currently lack viable solutions for adequate abatement. Many super pollutants have shorter atmospheric lifespans than carbon dioxide, with solutions providing an “emergency brake” to decrease peak warming in our lifetimes. Investments in tackling super pollutants can generate economic benefits, including lowering health-care costs and increasing productivity, and require cross-disciplinary teams to develop and advance the next-generation solutions to meaningfully address super pollutant emissions.  “Super pollutant mitigation is getting a lot of attention as an ‘emergency brake’ for near-term climate warming. But a huge fraction of our super pollutant emissions simply cannot be mitigated with current technologies and approaches,” said Kroll, the Peter de Florez Professor in the Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering. “Our session focused on the innovation — technical and otherwise — needed to tackle these hard-to-abate pollutants.” Other events included: “2026 State of Supply Chain Sustainability Report” with the MIT CTL “Building Flood Resilience” with MIT Lincoln Laboratory “Climate Communication for Impact” from the MIT Climate Project “Climate Impact Founder and Funder Connect” with the PKG Center for Social Impact “Educating Tomorrow's Climate Leaders: An MIT Perspective” from the MIT Climate Project “Trading for Food Security in a Changing Climate” with J-WAFS  “Industrial Decarbonization: Pathways to Productivity and Growth” with MIT INM “Mobilizing Climate Knowledge for Action” with MIT Open Learning “Rethinking Climate Innovation” from the MIT Climate Project “What is Sectoral Acceleration and How Do We Fund It” with the Sloan Sustainability Initiative   Rethinking the climate innovation pipeline with the Bezos Earth Fund A critical climate challenge is moving from breakthrough technology to real-world impact at scale. MIT and the Bezos Earth Fund brought together leaders from industry, venture capital, government, academia, philanthropy, and startups to explore solutions for a stronger innovation pipeline.  A panel of MIT faculty and alumni spinout leaders Asegun Henry, Seonghoon Woo, Ariel Furst, and Assil Halimi, moderated by Ray Rothrock, venture capitalist and life member of the MIT Corporation, explored the period between a promising scientific invention and commercial deployment. For many breakthroughs that can benefit climate and nature, that journey requires more early-stage science and engineering research, specialized testing infrastructure, validation, patient capital, and pathways to demonstration and pilot projects. “A breakthrough in the lab is not yet impact in the world. For climate and energy technologies, we need to think about the entire journey — from discovery and invention through validation, commercialization, and deployment — and build better pathways through the gaps along the way,” Wang said in a conversation with Tom Taylor, Bezos Earth Fund president and CEO.  Tapping into global nexus to find and scale solutions New York Climate Week is a global nexus for climate, where the connections required to develop, test, and scale potential solutions form. Across the board, MIT sessions addressed the need for solutions to be large in magnitude, technically feasible, and contextually realistic.   “Even when a technology is low-cost, it doesn’t mean it will diffuse naturally or get widely adopted,” said Claire Walsh, global director of policy and communications at MIT’s Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab. “Frontier technologies are often more expensive to start, so that means it’s even more important for scientists and engineers to think about end user adoption, and their incentives and constraints, from the start.”

ccba086c286d7466: A fourth presidential victory gives Lula another chance to defend democracy, protect the Amazon and deliver for Brazil’s working people Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s win in Brazil’s presidential election is a triumph for him, his country and the world. The 80-year-old incumbent snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, blocked the rise of the far right and saved the planetary air-conditioning system of the Amazon from irreparable destruction. Known universally as Lula, he made history by becoming the first candidate to win a presidential run-off after finishing second in the opening round. In triumphing against Flávio Bolsonaro, the leftist stopped what could have been the most dangerous consolidation of authoritarian rule in Brazil since military rule ended. bc04c10d0ff7f2c5: Getty ImagesIf we’re to follow the philosophy of organiser extraordinaire Marie Kondo, a tidy home is a better home. Albert Einstein, however, might have contested that point. “If a cluttered desk is a sign of a cluttered mind,” goes a quote widely attributed to the famed physicist, “of what, then, is an empty desk a sign?” My newly published research, which studied 22 New Zealand households, also challenges the conventional wisdom that mess is a problem which must be fixed. Far from being a symptom of poor organisation, mess can help families function and make life run more smoothly. When mess makes life easier Consider the spaces in our homes that serve more than one purpose, and where things tend to pile up. A living room that doubles as a play area, or a bedroom that also serves as a study. One couple told me how their dining table becomes a “drop zone” for belongings such as bags and drink bottles, before it’s cleared each evening. Another person described how leaving something on his kitchen island made him less likely to forget it when leaving the house. Disorderly as each of those spaces might have appeared, they served daily routines which might have been disrupted for the sake of a tidier-looking home. We might think of clutter as stuff that simply gets in our way. But often, a messy space is just one that is being useful to us. For one mum, her kitchen counter served as a dining table and a workspace for her and her daughter. Pens, toys and other items might accumulate, but “as long as there’s still space to eat, then I kind of just let it be”. Look familiar? Often messy spaces, such as dinner tables and kitchen counters, can also just be useful spaces. Getty Images Mess can also tell us much about family relationships. One dad would leave his daughter’s jumper hanging on the back of a chair rather than pack it away. She had previously left it on the floor, and he wanted to acknowledge her progress. “So I regard that as a win,” he said. Another person told me she put up with some of her partner’s mess because “he also lives here”. For her, a shared home should not be organised only around one person’s idea of tidiness. Leaving some things alone was a way of recognising that the space belonged to both of them. These might be modest examples, but they show us that the seemingly simple act of tidying can run up against the encouragement we offer our children or the respect we show our partners. When we’re making room for other people’s ways of living, putting everything in its “proper” place sometimes isn’t the most considerate thing to do. Knowing when to tidy up So, should we just stop tidying and embrace chaos? Not quite. Previous research has linked household clutter to stress, embarrassment and conflict between family members. Mess can make things harder to find, prevent us from using a space or create more work for someone else. Our study doesn’t dispute these problems. Rather, it suggests we need to look beyond how messy a space appears to understand whether that mess is actually causing difficulties. We found households used three main approaches to managing disorder: clearing things away, tolerating them or simply hiding them from view. One woman described pushing her partner’s golf balls and other belongings beneath a cabinet, where they were less visible. Another kept her daily supplements on the kitchen counter rather than in the pantry, because putting them away might mean she forgot to take them. Organising consultant Marie Kondo is famous for creating the KonMari Method, a decluttering and organising philosophy centered on keeping only items that ‘spark joy’. Michael Buckner/Getty Images These decisions reflect something earlier research has tended to overlook: keeping a home tidy involves balancing different needs, routines and expectations. What one person regards as clutter might be important to someone else’s daily life. Our findings also suggest tidiness is rarely a permanent state. Spaces become messy as people use them, are cleared when needed, then become messy again. Trying to maintain constant order can mean repeatedly undoing arrangements that serve a useful purpose. This doesn’t mean all mess should be tolerated. But a home that looks perfectly organised isn’t necessarily one that works best for the people living in it. Perhaps the better measure of a well-organised home isn’t how tidy it looks, but how well it works for the people who live there. a3e5e3993999079e: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world.

It also warns that there’s a fair chance that its tech could “erode trust, harm society and destabilize the geopolitical order” and, if things don’t go to plan, “pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

“We encourage you, as a prospective owner of our stock, not to think of your purchase in purely transactional terms,” the company writes. “We hope you will see it instead as an opportunity to be part of something greater. The advent of machine intelligence is one of the seminal moments in human history.”

This kind of public messaging is a master class in narrative capture. But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here.

Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers.
Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation.

And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience.

The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?)

If you skim through the long sections about risks in the IPO prospectus, it’s clear this is no ordinary offering and no ordinary company. The way Anthropic tells it, business success depends not only on the firm’s ability to translate its technology into profitable products but also to save the world from what it has made.

Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.”

Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. This view of its technology makes its way into the prospectus as one more risk to its business. Anthropic states that: “In addition, given our focus on developing frontier AI, and the way we approach model sentience and moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications.”
In other words, if Claude wakes up, it could be a problem.

I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this (although it’s pretty wild to read about machine sentience in an IPO prospectus.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum. When so little seems certain, what it says is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship.
It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think.

The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation. Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked).
Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said. But why should we trust it? “What is Anthropic?” he asked.
Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth.

But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that. As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free. Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because they have big egos.

In fact, Anthropic is all of these things. As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post: “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.”

Amodei makes it sound as if he’s got it all tied up, but playing multiple roles is hard. There are huge tensions between the priorities of an AI safety organization and a profit-driven megacorp, for example. (Amodei admits in his post that he has made mistakes.)

Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us. They should help us figure out how much to trust it to self-regulate or whether we should be forcing it to give external safety testers access to its models on our terms rather than theirs. They should help us give it the benefit of the doubt (or not) when what looks like a self-serving piece of legislation comes to light.

But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra. Anthropic is many things to many people, and I’m not sure that makes it more trustworthy. In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read.
This article has been updated with additional details from the IPO prospectus.

e2358621b2dbc832: Highway thieves are using sophisticated digital tactics that investigators worry make it easy to rob trucks carrying millions in expensive data center equipment.

NBC News spoke to “several industry leaders, consultants, and investigators advising law enforcement” offices probing the biggest thefts yet and reported that since June, thieves have “made away with more than $100 million in data center freight.”

Here’s how they said thieves get away with it: First, thieves hack freight brokers’ accounts on shipment-listing websites and post fake shipments to lure real bids, then send a malicious link to any trucking companies that respond. Once victims click, thieves install software to take control of their accounts and start bidding on real shipments. Sometimes, a real delivery driver is hired to collect the cargo, unaware of the scam, and other times fake driver’s licenses are used to get accomplices hired. Either way, the goods are eventually transferred to a driver working with the thieves to resell the gear, and, in one of the largest thefts, tracking coordinates were spoofed to prevent digital monitoring.
b4870627c1eeff0d: Serbia’s student-led political movement has secured a historic election victory. Preliminary results suggest the so-called Student List has won 141 of the 250 seats in parliament, with the ruling Serbian Progressive Party taking 104. The result brings the 12-year rule of Alexander Vučić to an end. The Student List’s story is remarkable. It has no standalone leader and fielded candidates without political experience from across Serbian society. Stemming from student-led protests against the entrenched corruption and creeping authoritarianism of the ruling regime, it has now achieved an improbable dream. In late 2025, one of us (Gavin Brent Sullivan) conducted focus groups with members of the student protest movement as part of the Pledge EU Horizon project. The project explores the emotional dynamics of political grievances and their democratic implications. The protesters’ grievances were centred on the 2024 collapse of a roof at the newly renovated Novi Sad train station in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. Allegations of state involvement through corruption in the procurement process and lowered building standards have been denied by the government. But they nonetheless sparked large nationwide protests. Focus group participants expressed anger and underlying fear about harassment during the protests by what they said were government-funded gangs. They also spoke of their concern at the threats and violence directed towards them, not only as they protested but also when walking in areas near government buildings in main cities. Several students reported feeling threatened even in their own homes. At the same time, the students voiced dissatisfaction with teachers who were not supportive of their movement, and other students who opposed them. This dissatisfaction extended to older family members and relatives who repeated government-controlled media fabrications about the protests. These included claims that the students were being paid by foreign anti-Serbian groups. Despite the fear of arrest or worse, and despondency that change could really occur, the students who took part in the focus groups were resilient. They were focused on their long-term goal of regime change, with many students talking with pride about creating a leaderless movement that was organising candidates to challenge Vučić in an election. Several participants reported feeling spontaneous, intense experiences of national pride when taking part in the protests. Some spoke of taking back national symbols such as the Serbian flag to counter propaganda that they were not patriotic and wanted to destroy the country. Feelings of solidarity were also experienced when minority Bosniak Muslim students from Novi Pazar University in south-western Serbia joined the protests. As one participant said: They’re a minority which was at odds with Serbia, with Serbian nationals actually. So now we had that part of reunification with them and they’re a Muslim minority. They are really active in these protests and student protests and it’s been wonderful. Another member of the focus group noted that they expected elections to be “brutal”. But they were optimistic about the prospect of unseating the Vučić government. They said: “I see the glimpse of hope that this is our future and that actually we can say to our kids, our grandkids, we changed the system, we were the change.” At the same time, most of the students did not dare to dream that they would succeed in ousting a government that had held a 12-year grip on power. It is stunning now after Vučić’s concession speech in which he admitted “it is clear that we have lost these elections” to know that they were successful just one year later. What’s next? The remarkable victory of the Student List should give hope to any group opposing a corrupt, authoritarian regime that a core commitment to democracy is precisely what attracts voters to choose progressive change. However, while there will be euphoria, pride and tears of joy in Serbia as the election result sinks in, there may also be groups who are fearful of change and that the new government may seek accountability for members of the ousted regime. Some theorists of political emotions talk about the possibility for revenge to be enacted by winners, especially when a fight for power has been bitter. For those on the losing side, meanwhile, electoral defeat can bring grief, anxiety and anger. But acknowledging these emotions and coming to terms with loss can bring openness to change. In his concession speech, Vučić said: “I do not want unrest, I do not want killings, I do not want anything like that on the streets.” The Student List’s commitment to democracy, pluralism and justice should also override any desire for redress. The movement has actively avoided developing a victim identity, taking responsibility for enacting change themselves. As one focus group participant said: Of course, they [the government] are the problem. I’m not trying to deny that. But I would blame us more … because, I mean, we chose them, we keep choosing them. Okay, they do steal when it comes to the elections, they do many things, they hide, they try to control the media and everything. But at the same time, we don’t have the opposition and we have that state of mind that is allowing them to do everything they’re doing. There are various other challenges facing the Student List. These include adapting the movement’s leaderless organisational assemblage into a government capable of delivering the reforms required for EU membership. But regardless of what happens next, it was certainly a privilege to talk to the students at a time when change did not seem possible and to provide encouragement and support when there was little outside recognition of their struggles and sacrifices. MASTERS IN BUSINESS: Robin Wigglesworth Editor, FT Alphaville · Author, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World
Bloomberg Radio · Interview transcript · Running time 1:24

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:00:07] I’m Barry Ritholtz. You are listening to Masters in Business on Bloomberg Radio. My extra special guest, returning to us, is Robin Wigglesworth, editor of FT Alphaville, one of my favorite sites on the web. It’s the Financial Times’ finance blog, which he runs from Oslo, Norway, with a team of writers both in London and New York.

He co-hosts The Story of Money, a financial history pod, and writes the newsletter Buy the Dip. His new book, A Fabulous Debt: The Epic Story of How Bonds Built the Modern World, is out. It frames bonds as the world’s largest, most powerful financial engine. I’m halfway through it and I’ve been loving it.
The conversation was fascinating. I think you’ll really enjoy it. With no further ado, my interview of Robin Wigglesworth. Robin, welcome to Bloomberg.
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:01:15] Well, it’s a massive honor to be here, so thanks for that, Barry.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:01:19] So before we talk about the book, I want to spend a little time discussing your very interesting background. You get a bachelor’s in journalism and contemporary history from City University and then a master’s in history of international relations from the London School of Economics, focused on political Islam. Was the original career plan always journalism?
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:01:44] No, I always dreamt of being a physicist, maybe specifically an astrophysicist.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:01:48] There is zero physics in international relations. I guess that’s really intergalactic relations.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:01:55] Well, weirdly, you know, when you try to self-analyze it always gets a little bit weird. But I like figuring out how the world worked. And I liked physics. I loved understanding and learning about the galaxies. And I realized I was pretty good at maths and physics, up until a point I realized I would be nothing other than a mediocre physicist.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:02:12] It’s amazing. You could be great at the secondary level, and suddenly in college, oh, those guys are really good.
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:02:18] Yeah, those guys are good.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:02:18] I had that same experience.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:02:19] Yeah. And it’s fine. It’s kind of knowing your limitations, what you’re good at. But journalism in many ways, I’ve kind of come to see, is similar in that you’re just figuring out the world from a different perspective. And financial journalism has at least a little bit of math, albeit not quite on the level of PhDs in physics.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:02:36] So am I correct in saying your first gig out of LSE was Bloomberg News? Is that right?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:02:42] No, I had one intermediate step. I was a financial journalist for a small trade mag in Dubai, and they just ingest journalists and then spit them out if they’re bad. And I didn’t know anything, but it was kind of this first awe-inspiring moment where, like, oh my God, I get paid to ask smart people about stuff. And it was so fun.
I knew nothing. And luckily I didn’t embarrass myself, so they kept me around. But I quickly moved to Bloomberg because I knew that was a great place to learn.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:03:09] So the Middle East and Dubai is a theme that comes up. You’re the Gulf correspondent in Abu Dhabi, covering the Arab Spring from both Bahrain and Libya. How do you go from that to covering finance?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:03:24] Well, so the first job had been covering bonds. Islamic bonds, actually, sukuk. And I worked at Bloomberg as an economics and politics reporter, but also, you get roped into everything. Bloomberg’s a great place if you want to spread your wings. So I covered FX and rates a lot as well. So at the FT I was a Middle East correspondent, a Gulf correspondent, but you kind of do a bit of everything then.

And it was a lot of Dubai going bankrupt. This was 2008. Dubai was having a hard time. It was fascinating. It was also covering things like labor movements in Bahrain and Saudi Arabia. But when the Arab Spring happened, I did get to cosplay as a war correspondent for a bit. And it was a wild time. I actually interviewed for a financial journalist job at the FT back in London from the army barracks of the rebel government in Benghazi.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:04:09] Oh my God. So how do you end up covering capital markets in New York for the Financial Times?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:04:16] Well, I went to London. I did get that job, despite the slightly bad backdrop of the Benghazi army barracks. Got the job covering capital markets for the FT in Europe. And it was the euro in crisis. And it was an incredible time. You learn so much more, so much more quickly, in a crisis. So it’s terrible for the world, great for us.
And after a few years, I got moved to New York to head up the markets team there. And for me, that’s the Premier League, or the World Series. It’s New York finance. It doesn’t really get better.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:04:51] You know, I love quoting Robert Duvall in Apocalypse Now during the financial crisis to some young analysts. There’s a line, “Someday, son, this war’s gonna end,” he says wistfully. And in the middle of a crisis, there’s very much that experience. Like, you better appreciate this, because these only come along every 20 years or so. And they’re amazing learning experiences. You experience that repeatedly.
First with the Arab Spring, then with the Great Financial Crisis. What was the next big economic crisis that really affected how you saw the world?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:05:32] I’d say COVID is the obvious one. There were lots of little mini things in between. I remember all the brouhaha about the first time the Fed was going to raise interest rates. That was a big deal, but it actually ended up being a bit of a nothingburger. But COVID was incredible, just on the personal but also the professional level.

I remember talking to one of our best young, promising journalists who was feeling quite stressed out at the time. And I said, look, it’s tough, it’s difficult, but this will make your career. If you just throw yourself into it, you will grow by leaps and bounds over the next days, weeks, months. We don’t know how long this is going, but just try to enjoy it, get enough sleep, and just try to almost revel in it. Try to turn it around. This isn’t just stress, it’s something that will shape you. And it shaped me as well. And it was incredibly exciting.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:06:23] So your last book was about index funds. This book is about bonds and debt, which occasionally blow up and cause a crisis. I’m curious how fundamental was the Dubai debt crisis you mentioned to how you frame the world of debt and credit, and how you think about the bond market, which you’ve described as the most powerful financial engine in the world.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:06:49] That’s a great question, actually. My first job was covering these Islamic bonds, and I had to learn about the bond market that way. And they’re really quite funky. They’re kind of structured to have…
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:00] No interest rates. Right.
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:01] No interest rates in theory, but it walks, talks and quacks like a fixed income…
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:05] Bond. You’re buying it at a discount. So it’s like a zero coupon bond. So there is interest.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:09] Yeah. They’re sale-leasebacks, basically. Like, I’ll lease you, you buy a house, the bank will buy it for you and lease it to you at fixed payments for the next 20 years, for example. And…
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:19] Then you own it.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:19] Yeah. And then they own it, and then you own it. Then for Bloomberg, I covered most of the rate space, so it was quite exciting. Because Iceland was part of it. And you remember Iceland really blew up during the financial crisis.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:30] Oh, it was completely wiped out.
ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:32] Yeah, it was. And again, it’s terrible because obviously, you know, people in Iceland had a terrible time, but…
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:07:38] But fantastic at the same time.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:07:39] So interesting. But yes, Dubai I think was the first time I really covered distressed debt and realized the full panoply of crazy stuff that can happen with fixed income and how much it pays to read the bond docs. Lots of investors don’t really read the documentation, as we’ve seen again and again. There was one Islamic bond issued by Dubai. It was backed by land that was actually supposed to be reclaimed from the sea, but it literally was the seabed. And good luck trying to seize that if you’re a creditor.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:08:10] Right, right. It’s underwater, both literally and figuratively.

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:08:13] So it was a wild time. And the characters in that world were just very different. The credit investors, the special situations people, from the rates people I’d kind of mostly known. So it was fascinating. So it definitely deepened my love affair with fixed income.

BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:08:30] And we’re going to talk more about the book, but I love all the examples you pull and these great narrative tales throughout history to illustrate. I found the book really fascinating. You must have studied, I want to say centuries, but maybe it’s millennia, maybe it’s a thousand years of government borrowing, of bond issuance, of debt, of credit. Why do we see the same patterns happen over and over again?

There’s credit. Sometimes you have people creating frauds. Sometimes there’s a mania. Like, who would’ve imagined, wait, railroad bonds? Why is that sexy? And yet we see the same things over and over and over again. Is it just, this is our nature, you have to accept it?

ROBIN WIGGLESWORTH: [00:09:24] I think that’s exactly it. I mean, there’s a famous quote, I never remember which British philosopher said it, but “from the crooked timber of mankind, never a straight thing was made.” And, you know, the technology changes, society changes, human nature doesn’t change that much.

And we can see the patterns again and again. And, you know, that’s great for financial journalists like us, but it’s bad for society. But, broadly speaking, despite those big crises, those big cycles, those huge mess-ups along the way, we’re still better off now than we were before. So I think that’s part of the magic of maybe even modern capitalism.
BARRY RITHOLTZ: [00:10:05] No longer living in caves. Indoor plumbing.

f4f84bb256f7090a: In all of West Africa, te voting age is 18, but presidential eligibility ages vary widely
Originally published on Global Voices
Youth mobilized in Africa. Screenshot from DW Africa's YouTube channel

In West Africa, young people can vote for the first time at 18. In some states, they are eligible to serve in parliament by age 25. However, depending on the country, they must wait until they are 35, 40, or even 50 years old before being eligible to run for the highest office. Although these age limits are beginning to shift, the real challenges often lie deeper in the electoral structure.

Young people are deemed mature enough to elect their leaders, yet not to replace them. They drive political movements forward by voting, advocating, campaigning, and protesting, yet cannot run for office themselves. The question is, can democracy really be called inclusive when it gives young people the right to elect but not to be elected?
Age: A shifting barrier

Across the region, the voting age is 18. However, presidential eligibility ages vary widely. In Gambia, it’s 30; in Senegal, Nigeria, and Côte d’Ivoire, it’s 35; and in Benin, Ghana, and Guinea, it’s 40. In the legislative assemblies, the bar is even lower. In Togo, Benin, Senegal, and Nigeria’s House of Representatives, it’s 25, while in Ghana it’s 21.

The situation in Togo requires closer inspection. On May 6, 2024, the country legally became a parliamentary republic. Under the 2024 Constitution, the eligibility age for President of the Republic is 50. Parliament also now elects the president, whose powers are limited. Authority now rests with the President of the Council of Ministers, who must be at least 40 and is not elected in public presidential elections. Faure Gnassingbé has held this position since May 3, 2025, the day parliament also elected the country’s oldest-ever incoming president of the Republic, Jean-Lucien Savi de Tové, 86.
However, the country’s legal age limit is hardly set in stone. In 2002, the National Assembly lowered it from 45 to 35 — a reform the opposition called tailor-made for Faure Gnassingbé.

More recently, in Ghana’s capital, Accra, on July 30, 2026, the Ghanaian government agreed in principle to lower the minimum presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35, defying the Constitutional Review Committee’s recommendation of 30. This legislation will ultimately go to a referendum, requiring a 40 percent turnout and a 75 percent approval.

In 2018, Nigeria set a regional precedent. Under pressure from the youth-led Not Too Young To Run campaign, the law lowered the presidential eligibility age from 40 to 35 and the House of Representatives’ eligibility age from 30 to 25.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union, lowering the minimum presidential age leads to younger parliaments. However, Côte d’Ivoire tells a very different story. In 2016, after removing the maximum age limit of 75 to run for office, incumbent President Alassane Ouattara, 83, ran for another term in 2025. The law rarely protects younger generations.
Youths particularly active in street movements

Even though young people have the right to vote across the continent, that does not mean all young people exercise that right. In August 2025, an Afrobarometer survey found that those aged 18 to 35 were less active than their elders in almost all traditional means of political participation. Overall across the continent, they trailed by 18 percentage points in voting, but by a record 29 points in Senegal. Protests were the only exception.

In Togo’s capital of Lomé, the June 6 Movement, sparked by the rapper Aamron’s arrest, brought thousands of people onto the streets. According to the Media Foundation for West Africa, the subsequent crackdown, for which the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) blamed government-backed militiamen, left seven dead.

Similarly, in Madagascar, the September 2025 protests toppled President Andry Rajoelina’s government, resulting in a military takeover. According to the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS), the overthrown president himself came to power in 2019 on the back of a protest, at just 34 years old.

Comparably, in Kenya, street protests forced the withdrawal of the 2024 Finance Bill. Meanwhile, in Morocco, youth-led protests prompted the authorities to announce youth candidacy incentives and prosecute specific ringleaders.
Although leaderless movements wrest concessions, they rarely last without political parties or trade unions to sustain them.
The gap between participation and representation

The Inter-Parliamentary Report, published on April 9, 2026, found that elected officials aged 30 and under account for just 2.8 percent of all parliamentarians worldwide. Since 2023, progress has stalled for the first time since 2014. More than a third (37.1 percent) of legislative houses have no parliamentarians in this age group.

The lack of youth representation and participation is a significant challenge considering young people under 35 account for roughly 70 percent of West Africa’s population, according to the West Africa Youth Democracy Conference.

According to data from the Inter-Parliamentary Union (IPU), at the start of Ghana’s 2025 parliamentary term, despite the legal minimum age of 21, no parliamentarians were aged 30 or under. What’s more, those aged 31 to 40 held just 46 of the 269 parliamentary seats, or 17.1 percent. After Senegal’s 2024 legislative elections, the National Assembly had only five members under 30, accounting for just 3 percent. Although almost 38 percent of registered voters were aged 18 to 35, the Assembly’s average age was 47. Elected at just 44, the country’s youngest-ever president, Bassirou Diomaye Faye, only became an official candidate after his mentor, Ousmane Sonko, was disqualified.

In Nigeria, International IDEA, an intergovernmental organization that supports sustainable democracy worldwide, reported that in 2015, only three of the 360 members of the House of Representatives were between the ages of 18–25, rising to 14 in 2019 — a positive but modest development.
In Dakar, the head of Yiaga Africa, the organization behind the Not Too Young to Run campaign, summed up the situation, stating that the political arena is more open on paper than in reality.

However, Afrobarometer has identified a paradox. While young people do vote less than their elders, they are also excluded from seats of power and the polls. This representation gap is anything but passive; it breeds disengagement. The IPU warns that young people’s absence from parliamentary assemblies undermines institutional legitimacy and jeopardizes trust in democracy. Senegal, listed in the 2026 IPU report as one of the countries where parliament grew younger in the most recent elections, shows that rejuvenation is possible when a political agenda empowers a generation.
Rewriting the deal: money, parties, obstacles

High age limit proponents demand experience. Across the 34 countries that Afrobarometer surveyed, citizens favor an average leadership age of 39. Those calling for a lower age limit seek proven engagement measures, such as lowering the eligibility age, quotas, and forums for young parliamentarians. However, as Nigeria shows, often, the main obstacle is financial.

Nigeria’s ruling party, the All Progressives Congress (APC), has set the total cost of its 2027 presidential nomination and expression-of-interest forms at NGN 100 million (USD 75,000), NGN 30 million (USD 22,521) for the expression of interest, and NGN 70 million (USD 52,550) for the nomination. The Senate will cost NGN 20 million (USD 15,014) and the House of Representatives NGN 10 million (USD 7,507).

Young people will receive a 50 percent discount only on nomination fees, leaving the presidential bill at NGN 65 million (USD 48,789). A Nigerian civil society group calculated that workers earning the minimum wage, NGN 70,000 (USD 52) per month, would have to work for more than a century to buy some of these forms.

The Electoral Act, 2026, signed on February 18, also doubled the presidential candidate’s campaign spending limit to NGN 10 billion (USD 7.5 million) and tripled that of governorship candidates to NGN 3 billion (USD 2.2 million).

At the initiative of ECOWAS and the youth-led advocacy organization Legis360, delegates from 12 countries gathered in Dakar to bring these obstacles to the forefront. In their communiqué, they launched the West Africa Youth Observer Network (WAYON) and called for youth quotas, reduced candidate fees, and spending limits. ECOWAS later announced it would deploy youth-only election observers for Nigeria’s upcoming presidential election on January 16, 2027.

Other countries exemplify how laws can directly impact nominations. According to the IPU, Ecuador owes much of its progress to a 2022 law, which required 25 percent of its candidates to be young adults. Countries with term limits also have considerably more young parliamentarians than the global average. In 2023, the IPU also noted that limited youth funding and a lack of spending limits contributed to aging parliamentary assemblies.

Elsewhere, the obstacles are political. Take, for example, Benin. After disqualifying the main opposition candidate (Les Démocrates) for failing to meet election requirements, current President Romuald Wadagni faced only one opponent (Paul Hounkpe). On April 12, 2026, Wadagni subsequently won the presidential election with 94.27 percent of the vote. In 2024, a constitutional reform that extended the presidential term from five to seven years also raised the minimum vote threshold for securing seats in the National Assembly from 10 percent of parliamentary election votes to 20 percent. This regulation far outweighs a candidate’s date of birth when they have no party machine behind them.

Another example is Burkina Faso. In January 2026, the military junta dissolved all political parties. Meanwhile, in The Gambia, President Barrow will run for a third term in the December 5 presidential election.
Inclusive voting, but flawed representation

Is a system that gives young people the right to elect their leader but impedes their ability to become one themselves fully inclusive? The findings speak for themselves. Although Nigeria has lowered its age limits and Ghana has committed to doing the same, these limits are more a symptom than a cause. Age is not the sole contributing factor.

Critics argue that lowering age limits without also addressing nomination costs, party regulations, and the openness of the political arena would only be the first step on a seemingly endless staircase. What stands between young people and decision-making positions are exceedingly high costs, restrictive nomination practices, candidate exclusions, and even the lack of parties.

Until street movements have credible institutional representatives, they will continue to wrest temporary concessions or, as seen in Madagascar, give way to powers other than those they had hoped for. The primary challenge of the West African Democratic Pact is making young people not only the promised future of politics, but also an active part of today’s representation.
Written (Français) by Jean Sovon

e5ac04ec0f826185: We had a feast of economics in early October with Budget 2027 from Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim and two days before, a shadow budget from Rafizi Ramli and Bersama.
For economists and policy analysts this laid out the economic agendas for the next general election (GE16) expected next year.

When it comes to government debt and the fiscal deficit both Rafizi and Anwar recognise the importance of proper fiscal management, cutting wastage, leakages and above all corruption and making sure that budgets are efficient and clean.
Beyond that Bersama sets out a whole new approach to economic policy and fiscal management to free income for the specific aim of improving social policy.
They target reducing the deficit and moving to a budget surplus by 2035 which is a very sound approach.

Anwar’s approach sees sound fiscal management as setting targets for debt and deficit and trying not to breach them. Often this is achieved because GDP rises faster than borrowing so the ratio falls even if the debt is stagnant or rising.
There is no statement on why this is important except that meeting targets signals fiscal conservatism, for its own sake.
On taxes, Anwar was silent on the goods and services tax (GST) in his budget speech because he opposes it and I agree with him on that.

He had also previously announced a review to adjust the sales and services tax (SST) to make it more like GST, which to me is a compromise to silence those calling for GST rather than an exercise in tax reform.
He did raise tax thresholds and cut rates, which I applaud but there were no substantive reforms.

Bersama on the other hand put reintroducing GST front and centre but fixed the rate at 5% for 10 years while evaluating new taxes such as the retail electronic payments tax (REPT) which is something I support and will work.
This is a step towards substantive reform of taxation, and it is much needed.
On incomes, both support raising the minimum wage but Bersama will also extend Rafizi’s progressive wage policy (PWP) to 2.5 million people at a cost of only RM1.8 billion. This is transformative.
Anwar on the other hand stuck to raising STR-Sara handouts with no real structural reforms to help middle-income groups raise their monthly take-home pay.
On social assistance, Bersama announced universal child assistance, universal basic pensions, universal monthly cost of living to help raise incomes irrespective of ethnicity or interest groups.
Concentrating social support into one ministry provides focus while cutting 189 separate agencies.

Anwar’s budget stuck to the same-old “Duit Raya” schemes and maintaining low petrol and diesel prices whereas Bersama wants to stop those wasteful subsidies and provide help targeted on incomes rather than keeping prices down artificially.

Anwar’s budget was administrative with normal handouts to specific interest groups, especially civil servants but no sense of universal vision or reform for everyone else. It was very similar to any budget of the past.

For business, especially MSMEs there is also a big difference. Anwar’s budget relies heavily on the state through the GLCs with private sector support in the form of soft-loans, easy finance and “you pay first, we match later” on so-called priority areas.
For Bersama, the entrepreneur in Rafizi shows through in reducing red tape and liberalising the business landscape to encourage competition, innovation and agility directly.
Overall, Anwar’s budget is last season, Bersama’s shadow budget has a vision for changing economic policy to free business and save money which is refocused on raising incomes.
Their reforms are universal, refreshing and new, unlike anything we have seen before.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.
f0ec4cd2fbceb27e: What if I told you that the most important meeting Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim had in China last month wasn't with officials of Alibaba, Huawei or Geely, but with a company that didn't exist four years ago?

In Hangzhou, Agibot, a Shanghai humanoid robot maker founded only in 2023, pledged a potential RM1 billion investment in Malaysia by 2035 along with 5,000 jobs, according to The Edge. Sure, a potential pledge is not money in the bank, but the company making it is no minnow.

Agibot shipped more humanoids than any other firm last year - 5,168 of them according to research firm Omdia; and International Data Corporation (IDC), an American market intelligence firm, has it on top again so far this year. To boot, it rolled its 20,000th robot off the line in September. A company not yet old enough for kindergarten is out-building every rival.

I've spent years in the robotics industry, between Silicon Valley, Shenzhen and Singapore, and if there's one thing I've learnt, it's that the products which end up defining an era almost always start out clumsy, expensive and easy to laugh at, right up until they aren't.

The personal computer, the internet, the laptop, the smartphone and now artificial intelligence (AI) all followed that script. Case in point: in 2007, Microsoft's then chief executive Steve Ballmer told USA Today that "there's no chance that the iPhone is going to get any significant market share. No chance." Within a decade, Apple had become America's biggest smartphone brand.

Today it's driverless cars, with Alphabet's Waymo giving more than 500,000 paid rides a week across more than a dozen American cities, and next, I would wager, comes the humanoid robot, the defining product of the next five to 10 years.
From stumbling to sprinting
If that sounds far-fetched, consider that in April last year, the winner of the world's first robot half marathon in Beijing limped home in two hours and 40 minutes.

This April, a robot built by Chinese phone maker Honor completed the same race on its own, more than six minutes faster than the men's world record. That's right, in a single year robots went from stumbling to beating the best time any human has ever run. Let that sink in for a bit.
And this is no lone show pony. IDC estimates that nearly 25,000 humanoids were shipped in the first half of this year, up a whopping 432%, with Chinese makers building more than 95% of them.

Here's the kicker: they're getting cheaper at a mind-blowing pace. Unitree's G1 launched in 2024 at 99,000 yuan (RM60,500), yet just over a year later its smaller R1 arrived at 39,900 yuan (RM24,400), less than half the price.

The Americans aren't sitting still either, with Tesla saying it is converting part of its Fremont, California, car plant to make its Optimus robot, which Elon Musk calls "probably the biggest product ever".
So how big could this get? IDC expects annual shipments to pass 750,000 by 2030, and Morgan Stanley reckons more than a billion could be in use by 2050.
Not quite ready for your living room

Mind you, none of these machines is ready to babysit your children, and electric vehicle news site Electrek reported that it could find no evidence Tesla built even hundreds of the 5,000 to 10,000 Optimus robots Musk had talked of making last year.

Even Agibot's founder, Deng Taihua, has said that robots in the home face different challenges from those in factories, since they have to weave between furniture and everyday clutter. That's precisely why factories and warehouses will come first, then hospitals and hotels, and only then the gloriously messy Malaysian home, shoes piled at the front door and all.
Why Malaysia should grab this with both hands

Six years ago, I wrote that jobs demanding dexterity in unpredictable surroundings were among the most resilient to automation for the next 20 years. With robots now loading car parts on a BMW line, I can't help but feel I was far too generous with my timeline.

But here's the thing: for Malaysia, that is mostly good news. We relied on about 2.1 million documented foreign workers as of October 2025 and the government has capped their share of the workforce at 13% and wants it down to 10% by 2030. Meanwhile, economy minister Akmal Nasrullah Mohd Nasir told Parliament this month that we will become an aged nation, with 14% of the population aged 65 and above, by 2048.

We're short of hands and greying fast, and a machine that can lift, sort and fetch around the clock eases both problems. Agibot is already on the ground here, running an experience centre with developer I-Berhad at i-City in Shah Alam.

So what should Putrajaya do now? Get that "potential" RM1 billion signed, sealed and delivered. After Budget 2027, Treasury secretary-general Johan Mahmood Merican said the government was open to using foreign worker levies to "finance mechanisation", and that money could help pay for the first humanoids on Malaysian factory floors, on condition that some of them were assembled here.

Agibot did not exist four years ago, and today it wants to spend RM1 billion in Malaysia. Give its robots five to ten more years and the question on our factory floors won't be whether to hire one, but how soon we can do it.

eb58e7e8a5694b2b: As the term “middle powers” has gained currency this year, it has forced us to ask which countries actually belong to this grouping. After all, shouldn’t most states be described that way?
With his much-cited speech at the World Economic Forum in Davos in January, Canadian prime minister Mark Carney revived a debate about shifting power structures in today’s world.
He believes we are seeing a “rupture” in the global order, one that will require middle powers to cooperate to resist economic coercion and political domination by others.
Although he did not mention the US, President Donald Trump immediately sensed, correctly, that some of Carney’s remarks were directed against him.
But, again, how should the middle powers that Carney had in mind be distinguished from the other powers of our time, if at all? Perhaps one should start by discussing those other powers.

It was some time ago that “superpower” was applied to nation-states that wielded powers well beyond any others on the global stage. After World War II, this term was used to describe not only the US and the Soviet Union, but also, for a very short period, the British Empire.

In the decades that followed, the two unquestioned superpowers were defined by their massive nuclear arsenals—with each commanding tens of thousands of warheads—and their ability to deliver them anywhere in the world in a matter of minutes, with no possibility to defend against an attack. Each had the power to annihilate the other within a half-hour.

Over time, other states acquired nuclear weapons, but none had the capacity or the will to develop arsenals that would put them on the same level as the two superpowers. Then came the collapse of the Soviet Union, after which the term superpower started to fall out of use.

The US was occasionally still described as such, but during this brief “unipolar era,” it was also bestowed with a new term: Hubert Védrine, France’s foreign minister between 1997 and 2002, called it a hyperpuissance.

Today, the US remains very powerful, and Russia still commands huge military resources, including the world’s largest nuclear arsenal. Yet both countries’ powers have increasingly come to be defined by their obvious limitations.

Despite having mobilised its vast conventional arsenal, Russia has not been able to subjugate its substantially smaller neighbour, Ukraine. And despite Trump constantly boasting about his country’s military might, his war on Iran has so far yielded little more than higher oil prices and a destabilising stalemate.

The failure to achieve victory in their respective wars of choice demonstrates that the US and Russia no longer qualify as “superpowers”. Are they even great powers, or do they ultimately belong to the same, broad category of middle powers?

Whatever the case, the age of superpowers is over. Even the most nominally powerful countries are highly constrained. The limits of their powers have been laid bare, regardless of whether they realise it yet.

Though middle powers come in many different shapes and sizes, most are at least aware of their status. Neither India nor Brazil nor Canada can use military power to shape its political environment to its liking.

Instead, each must rely on economic engagement and political relationship-building to exert influence. But the same applies to the US, Russia, and other larger, more powerful players like the European Union.
The late Joseph Nye still has much to teach today’s middle powers. He famously introduced the concept of “soft power” to draw a distinction between persuasion and coercion in international relations.

While military capability confers “hard power,” soft power—what Nye termed “the power of attraction”—comes from cultural exports, economic ties, diplomacy, goodwill, and trust built up over many years. Perhaps the world’s middle powers can be defined along these lines, namely as those who must rely primarily on soft power.

Of course, some countries will still harbour visions of grandeur, having convinced themselves that hard power is enough to bend others to their will. It might take some time for recognition of their reduced status to sink in. But whatever those in Moscow or Washington tell themselves, the fact is that the world has changed. There are no superpowers any longer.
Carl Bildt is a former prime minister and foreign minister of Sweden.

4b22ee1f7844c295: Being Mozambican is a matter of belonging — regardless of one’s origin, appearance, or surname
Originally published on Global Voices
Indians in Mozambique celebrating the Hindu festival of Navratri. Image by Kash_if via Flickr. CC BY 2.0.

In Mozambique, the word monhé has a much deeper history than its everyday use might suggest. Depending on who says it and the context, it can simply be a reference to the population of Indian origin, an identity marker, or a prejudiced remark. But behind the word there is a history of migration, trade, colonialism, independence, displacement, and, above all, belonging.

The question of who is Mozambican gets particularly interesting when we look at the communities of Indian origin, who have lived in the country for several generations. Are they Mozambicans? Indians? Foreigners? Or, in some cases, stateless persons? The answer cannot be found in appearance, surname, religion, or family origin alone. It is found in the country’s history and, particularly, in its nationality law.
A presence older than modern borders

The presence of people originating from the Indian subcontinent in the lands we now call Mozambique predates the country’s independence and, in many instances, predates the demarcation of the current political borders. The Indian Ocean’s trade networks connected the East African coast to South Asia long before 1975, the year Mozambique gained its independence. Over time, merchants, families, and whole communities settled in different parts of the country.

During the Portuguese colonial period, this took place within a political structure that gave people nationalities and legal statuses according to the rules of the empire. As such, “being of Indian origin” never meant automatically “being an Indian citizen.” A person can have Indian ancestry and at the same time hold Portuguese, Indian, Pakistani, or any other nationality, which could leave people in a complex bureaucratic situation. This distinction became especially important when the empire came to an end.
1975: When the question “Whose country is this?” took on a new meaning

Mozambique’s independence, made official on June 25th, 1975, did not just mean a transfer of political power. It also implied the need to define who would legally receive the new state, which was known as the New State. The Nationality Law of 1975 was key to answering that question. Among its provisions were rules that recognized as Mozambicans certain people born in the territory and resident in Mozambique at the time of independence, as well as other criteria related to birth, family links, and residence. The legislation would thus transform a heterogeneous imperial population into a national political community.

For many families of Indian origin who lived in Mozambique for decades or generations, this transformation would mean a fundamental change: no longer being legally associated with a colonial power or a foreign nationality and becoming part of the new Mozambican nation. But the experience of this transition was not the same for everybody.
When identity doesn’t fit neatly into a passport

Decolonization created situations where identity, origin, and nationality did not match. Imagine a family history across three generations: the grandparents born in India, the parents born in Mozambique during the colonial period, and the children born after independence. Which nationality should each generation have? The answer may depend on specific legal circumstances: place of birth, the parents’ nationality, residence in Mozambique at its independence, existing documentation, and any decisions to opt for or relinquish nationality.

Here, the issue of statelessness arises. A stateless person is somebody who is not considered a national by any state’s legislation. It is not an ambiguous cultural identity or feeling divided between two countries, but a legal status.

After decolonization, some people in former colonial territories, such as Angola and Mozambique, faced this problem: some were no longer recognized as nationals by the former colonial power without any other nationalities automatically being granted. This does not mean, though, that the whole Indian community in Mozambique became stateless. This generalization would be historically and legally incorrect.
‘Monhé’ is not a nationality

This may be where everyday language misleads us. The term “Monhé” may be used as an identity category, but it is not a legal category. Somebody called a monhé can be as Mozambican as anybody else born or naturalized in the country. They may have been born in Maputo, Nampula, Beira, or Quelimane, speak Portuguese or another Mozambican language, have had family in Mozambique for several generations, and never have lived in India. Your ancestry does not disqualify your citizenship.

Likewise, a person of Indian origin living in Mozambique can be a citizen of another country. And, in certain cases, they may have difficulties in proving or acquiring a nationality. As such, it is important to distinguish three concepts that are often confused: origin, nationality, and citizenship. A person’s origin may be Indian. Their identity can be simultaneously Mozambican and Indian. Nationality, though, is a legal relationship between an individual and a state.
A community across oceans
The history of so-called monhés in Mozambican identity also challenges an overly simplistic view of nationality.

Mozambique has always been a space where people cross paths. Africans, Arabs, Indians, Portuguese, and other peoples participated, at different moments, in the country’s social, economic, and cultural development. The Mozambican coast, in particular, cannot be understood without movements across the Indian Ocean.

This is why it may be inappropriate to think of the Indian diaspora as forever an “outsider” population. For many of these families, Mozambique is not simply the country where they live. It is the country where they were born, where their parents were born, where their ancestors are buried, and where they built their lives. India may be their family origin. Mozambique is, for many, a homeland.
The ongoing question

Around half a century after independence, the question of nationality continues to be more than a matter of just documents. It is a question of recognition. Who has the right to say “I am Mozambican”? Is it enough to have been born in the country? Have Mozambican parents? Have lived in the country for decades? Participate in society? Speak its languages? Share a collective memory? Or will some people continue to be seen as foreigners by many, despite legally being citizens? It is in this space between the law and general perception that many identities exist.

This evokes the concept of a “bridge” — Mozambique’s Indian-origin community historically finds itself between different spaces: Africa and Asia, family tradition and national identity, migratory memory and territorial belonging. But being between two shores does not necessarily mean not belonging to either. Sometimes it means belonging to both. And, for some, it means discovering that their family history crossed oceans long before modern passports decided which country a person belonged to.

The history of Mozambique’s monhés is thus also a history about the very meaning of being Mozambican. Not a story of people who simply “came from outside,” but a story of people who, over generations, helped build the country, while continuing to negotiate, within their families and wider society the fundamental question that follows all those who migrate: where, in the end, is home?
